tables.grain: one row per Sale record — one register ticket/transaction, in any state (open, completed, voided, archived). Refunds are NOT a separate resource: a refund is a Sale whose lines carry negative unitQuantity and whose payments carry negative amount, so it is also one row here.
tables.description: The transaction header for the whole domain: totals, tax, discounts, cost of goods, and every foreign key that gives a sale its who/where/when. This is the source of truth for revenue, margin and ticket counts at sale grain. It is NOT a takings/cash table (that is ls_sale_payments), NOT a product table (that is ls_sale_lines), and it contains open shopping carts and voided tickets that must be filtered out before any money question.
gotchas: Every money question needs BOTH `completed = true` AND `voided = false`. Open tickets carry totals but no payments; voided tickets keep their money columns fully populated. Omitting either filter inflates revenue.

VERIFIED LIVE (2026-08-01, Ashburton Cycles): Sale.json ACCEPTS `archived=true` but SILENTLY IGNORES it — identical sale ids return with and without the filter. Do not schedule a second archived pass; it is a full duplicate history walk (thousands of rate-limited requests) for zero new rows.
VERIFIED LIVE: walk-in sales store customerID = 0, not NULL. Normalise 0 to NULL or COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) collapses every anonymous sale in history into one phantom customer.

VERIFIED LIVE: the live payload and query parameter are `updateTime` (camel case) even though the reference field table prints `updatetime`. A mirror keyed on the documented spelling silently fetches nothing.
VERIFIED LIVE: `Note` is NOT an allowed load_relation on account-level Sale.json, so sale notes cannot be bulk-mirrored from this endpoint at all.

VERIFIED LIVE: live Sale payloads carry extra fields the published reference omits (a ticketNumber, a tax-inclusive flag, a receipt-preference value). They are deliberately NOT columns here because they are not in the published field table — confirm them against your own account before adding.

Refunds are ordinary Sales with negative lines and negative payments, not a separate resource. SUM(calc_total) therefore already nets refunds out; a true 'gross sales' figure needs an explicit calc_total > 0 split.

FOUR overlapping total columns exist: calc_total (grand total inc tax, what the POS shows), total (the documented arithmetic restatement, can disagree), displayable_total (adds gift-card face value, double counts) and total_due (subtracts gift-card/store-credit movement). Pick one, document it, never mix them in a single query.
`balance` is the only non-additive column here: it is money outstanding right now. Summing it over a date range mixes layaway balances that were later paid off.
Cost columns are ex-tax and calc_total is tax-inclusive. Gross profit MUST be calc_subtotal - calc_fifo_cost. Blending the bases overstates margin by roughly the tax rate.

tax1_rate and tax2_rate are FRACTIONS (0.1 = 10%), and they are only sale-level defaults. Any line with its own TaxClass overrides them, so reconstructing tax as calc_subtotal * tax1_rate is wrong on mixed baskets — use calc_tax1 + calc_tax2.

complete_time is empty on open sales, so a WHERE on it implicitly restricts to completed sales. This makes the `completed = true` filter look redundant when it is not — add it anyway, because it also documents intent and survives a switch to create_time.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: Immutable numeric ticket id, unique within the account. The join key for every child table (lines, payments, voids, CC charges, ShipTo, quotes). NOT the human receipt number the customer sees — the Refund endpoint accepts a ticketNumber in its URL path, but no ticketNumber field is published on this object.

columns.name: completed
columns.description: True once the ticket was finalised: inventory has been deducted and payments sum to the total. False = an open/parked ticket sitting on a register (or the working sale behind a saved quote) with NO payments at all. Almost every money question must filter completed = true; omitting it silently mixes unpaid shopping carts into revenue.

columns.name: voided
columns.description: True when the sale was voided. Documented meaning: voided sales do not count toward totals or payments received and all inventory was restocked — but the money columns on this row are NOT zeroed out, so a voided sale still carries a full calcTotal. Summing without voided = false inflates revenue by the value of every reversed ticket.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the sale is archived (hidden from the POS UI). Archived is NOT voided: an archived completed sale was real revenue and must stay in the numbers. See the VERIFIED LIVE gotcha — the archived=true query filter is silently ignored on this endpoint.

columns.name: create_time
columns.description: When the ticket was first opened at the register, store-local, read-only. This is when shopping started, not when money changed hands — on layaways and parked tickets it can precede completion by months. Never use it as the revenue period.

columns.name: complete_time
columns.description: When the sale was completed — THE canonical revenue timestamp, store-local. Empty/NULL on open tickets, so any date predicate on this column implicitly drops uncompleted sales. Documented as changeable (staff can back-date a completion), so it is not monotonic with sale_id and a re-run of last month's report can legitimately move.

columns.name: update_time
columns.description: Last modification, read-only, store-local. Use for incremental mirroring only, never for reporting periods — a two-year-old sale touched by a refund gets today's stamp. Note the reference field table spells it `updatetime` (lower-case t) while the live payload and query parameter are `updateTime`.

columns.name: time_stamp
columns.description: Marked *legacy* in the reference. Dual-purpose stamp whose meaning switches on `completed`: last-modified while the sale is open, completion time once it is complete. Because the semantics change per row it is the classic source of wrong date filters — use complete_time for revenue and update_time for change tracking. Still accepted as a sort/filter parameter, which is why it survives.

columns.name: reference_number
columns.description: Order number assigned by the external system that created the sale (webstore, Amazon, marketplace). Empty for tickets rung up in-store. Free text, not guaranteed unique, and not a Lightspeed identifier — never join on it without also matching reference_number_source.

columns.name: reference_number_source
columns.description: Name of the external system that owns reference_number. The nearest thing to a sales-channel dimension on this object: empty means the sale originated in the POS, non-empty names the ecommerce/marketplace channel. Values are whatever the integration writes, so normalise before grouping.

columns.name: tax1_rate
columns.description: Default first tax rate for the sale, expressed as a FRACTION (0.1 = 10%, not 10). Lines without a specific TaxClass rate fall back to this. Reading it as a percentage is a 100x error; deriving tax as calc_subtotal * tax1_rate is also wrong on any mixed basket because lines override it.

columns.name: tax2_rate
columns.description: Default second tax rate as a fraction, for jurisdictions with two components (e.g. GST + PST). 0 in single-tax territories such as AU/NZ. Total tax collected on the sale is calc_tax1 + calc_tax2, never a rate multiplication.

columns.name: change_given
columns.description: Cash handed back to the customer; cash sales only. Purely informational — it is already reflected inside the cash SalePayment amount and is NOT a deduction from revenue. Subtracting it from totals double counts.

columns.name: tip_enabled
columns.description: True when the tipping feature was active on this ticket. A configuration flag, not evidence a tip was actually left: the money is in calc_tips and SalePayment.tipAmount. Can be true with calc_tips = 0.

columns.name: enable_promotions
columns.description: True when automatic Promotions were run against every line added to this sale. Write-once: settable only at creation and immutable thereafter, so it describes how the ticket was priced historically, not a toggle you can reason about as current config.

columns.name: calc_discount
columns.description: Total money discounted on the sale, store currency, as a POSITIVE number representing value given away. Aggregates line-level markdowns plus the sale-level discount from ANY source — named rule, automatic price rule, loyalty redemption, manual override. Therefore it is NOT attributable to discount_id alone.

columns.name: calc_total
columns.description: The grand total the customer pays: after discounts, INCLUDING tax. The canonical per-sale revenue figure and the one the POS UI shows. Refund sales carry a negative value so SUM() nets refunds out automatically. Never pair it with the cost columns (which are ex-tax) — use calc_subtotal for margin.

columns.name: calc_subtotal
columns.description: Sale total EXCLUDING tax, after discounts. The correct revenue base for gross-margin arithmetic because calc_avg_cost and calc_fifo_cost are also ex-tax. Mixing calc_total with cost overstates margin by roughly the tax rate (about 9% of revenue at 10% GST).

columns.name: calc_taxable
columns.description: Subtotal of only the lines that were actually taxed (SaleLine.tax = true AND their TaxClass carries a rate). calc_taxable + calc_non_taxable should reconcile to calc_subtotal; a gap means mixed tax treatment worth investigating.

columns.name: calc_non_taxable
columns.description: Subtotal of the non-taxable lines (tax-exempt customers, zero-rated goods, some labour classes). The reason tax collected is usually less than subtotal x rate — quote this rather than accusing the data of being wrong.

columns.name: calc_avg_cost
columns.description: Cost of goods for the whole sale at weighted-average unit cost, ex tax, summed across lines. The cost-basis choice silently changes reported profit: Lightspeed's own profit reporting uses FIFO, so pick one basis and never blend the two within a report.

columns.name: calc_fifo_cost
columns.description: Cost of goods at FIFO, ex tax — the basis that matches Lightspeed's native profit reports. Gross profit = calc_subtotal - calc_fifo_cost. Can be 0 on migrated history and on non-inventory/service lines, in which case gross profit is silently reported as 100% — fall back to calc_avg_cost when this is 0 and subtotal is not.

columns.name: calc_tax1
columns.description: Tax collected at the first rate across all lines, in store currency. A money amount, not a rate — the name pairs confusingly with tax1_rate.

columns.name: calc_tax2
columns.description: Tax collected at the second rate, in currency; 0 in single-tax jurisdictions. Total tax on the sale = calc_tax1 + calc_tax2.

columns.name: calc_payments
columns.description: Sum of every SalePayment.amount on this sale, tips included. On a completed sale this equals the total; on a layaway or on-account sale it is only the portion paid so far. This is takings, not revenue — the two diverge whenever deposits or instalments exist.

columns.name: calc_tips
columns.description: Sum of SalePayment.tipAmount across the sale. Tips are INSIDE the payment amounts, not additional to them, so merchandise money taken = calc_payments - calc_tips. Tips are not revenue and are typically owed to tip_employee_id.

columns.name: total
columns.description: The documented arithmetic restatement: calcSubtotal - calcDiscount + calcTax1 + calcTax2. Reads as a near-duplicate of calc_total but is derived differently, so the two can disagree depending on whether calc_subtotal is already net of discount on your account. Choose ONE total column for reporting (calc_total is what the POS shows) and never mix them within a query.

columns.name: total_due
columns.description: Total minus credit-account and gift-card deposits (deposits subtract, withdrawals add) minus credit-card refunds. The amount of NEW money the ticket demands, which diverges from total whenever gift cards or store credit are involved. It is NOT money outstanding — that is `balance`.

columns.name: displayable_total
columns.description: total plus gift-card deposits. Issuing a gift card is not revenue, so its face value is excluded from total but must still be printed on the receipt. Use this only to reproduce a printed receipt; using it for revenue double counts every gift card once at issue and again at redemption.

columns.name: balance
columns.description: total - calc_payments: money still owed on the ticket. Non-zero on layaways, special orders and on-account sales, ~0 on a settled ticket. The ONE non-additive column in this table — it is an outstanding balance at a point in time, so summing it across a date range mixes in layaways that were subsequently paid off.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: Customer attached to the ticket. VERIFIED LIVE: walk-in sales store 0, not NULL. Normalise 0 to NULL before COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) or every anonymous walk-in in history collapses into one phantom mega-customer and customer counts are badly wrong.

columns.name: discount_id
columns.description: DEPRECATED per the reference. Historically the named sale-level Discount rule applied to the whole ticket. Still populated on older rows and still worth joining to ls_discounts for a rule name, but it can never fully explain calc_discount, which also contains line-level, price-rule and manual markdowns with no rule id.

columns.name: discount_percent
columns.description: DEPRECATED per the reference. Legacy whole-sale percentage discount. Where present it is a FRACTION of 1 (0.2 = 20%), consistent with the Discount object's documented <= 1.00 cap. Use calc_discount for money actually given away.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Employee who processed (rang up) the ticket — the attribution for 'sales by staff member'. Distinct from ls_sale_lines.employee_id (which can differ when several staff touch one ticket) and from tip_employee_id.

columns.name: tip_employee_id
columns.description: Employee assigned the whole tip amount for this sale. Frequently 0/NULL even when calc_tips > 0, because tipping is often configured without an assignee. Never use it as the seller.

columns.name: quote_id
columns.description: The Quote this sale was created from. Non-zero means the ticket originated as a saved quote — THIS is the direction to measure quote conversion from, because the inverse pointer (Quote.saleID) is reassigned on every quote edit and is meaningless for conversion.

columns.name: register_id
columns.description: Register (till) the sale was processed on. Maps to the `register` canonical entity. 0/NULL for sales created via the API or an integration with no register context, so register splits will show an unattributed bucket for ecommerce orders.

columns.name: ship_to_id
columns.description: The ShipTo (shipment/delivery) record for this sale, present when goods were shipped rather than carried out. Non-zero is the practical marker of a delivered order — there is no explicit fulfilment-type field on Sale.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: Shop (physical location) where the sale was processed — the `location` dimension for every revenue split. Note lines carry their own shopID, so a multi-shop ticket is technically possible and line-level splits can disagree with this.

columns.name: tax_category_id
columns.description: TaxCategory governing which tax rates apply to this sale; it is what determines the tax1_rate/tax2_rate defaults. 0 when the account has a single implicit category. Maps to the `tax_code` canonical entity.

tables.grain: one row per SaleLine — one charge on one sale. That is a catalog item line, a miscellaneous/non-inventory charge, an item-fee surcharge line, or a refund line (negative unitQuantity). Layaway, special-order and workorder lines share this same grain.
tables.description: The product-level truth for the domain: units, per-product revenue, per-line discounts and per-line cost basis. Every product ranking, sell-through, return-rate and item-margin question belongs here, never on the sale header or the item catalogue. It is NOT a tax table (rates are line-level but tax categories live in the org domain) and it carries NO completed/voided flag of its own — those must be joined from ls_sales.
gotchas: Refund lines are NEGATIVE unit_quantity at a POSITIVE unit_price. Never flip the price sign — quantity * price already yields negative revenue, and doing both turns returns into extra sales.

VERIFIED LIVE: avg_cost and fifo_cost behave as LINE totals, not per-unit costs, despite the reference calling them unit costs. Multiplying either by unit_quantity double counts COGS. Validate against one known line on your account before trusting either reading.

The reference defines calc_subtotal as unitQuantity * unitPrice (gross of discount) while displayable_subtotal explicitly subtracts the discount. Confirm which one your account returns net before using it as the margin base; the difference is exactly calc_line_discount.

discount_percent is a FRACTION (0.2 = 20%), matching the Discount object's documented <= 1.00 cap. VERIFIED LIVE across every 20% rule at the reference store. This is the single easiest 100x error in the domain.

customer_id on the LINE is set only for layaway, special-order and workorder lines. The buyer of an ordinary line is on the parent Sale. Grouping revenue by ls_sale_lines.customer_id silently drops nearly all sales.
VERIFIED LIVE: item_id is 0/absent on miscellaneous and some labour lines. Product rankings must filter item_id IS NOT NULL or an unnamed bucket wins.
line_type is documented as NOT distinguishing layaway / special order / workorder — those need the is_* booleans. line_type only ever carries item-fee style values.
item_fee_id non-null means the row is a category surcharge, not merchandise. Include or exclude it deliberately: counted as a product it inflates units and drags down average selling price.
Total markdown on a line = calc_line_discount + calc_transaction_discount. Using only the first under-reports every time a whole-sale discount was applied.
This table has NO completed/voided of its own. Every revenue query must join ls_sales and filter completed = true AND voided = false, or the flags must be carried down during load.

VERIFIED LIVE: exploding this table out of Sale pages is expensive. The account-level SaleLine collection accepts itemID / saleID / customerID / employeeID / shopID as direct filters, after which parent Sales can be batch-hydrated by saleID — always push down at least one filter for per-item or per-line lookups.
require_full_reservation is a request-only flag; expect it false/absent on read and never use it analytically.

columns.name: sale_line_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id for the line. Stable across edits to the parent sale; the target of parent_sale_line_id on refund lines and of ls_sale_accounts.sale_line_id on gift-card lines.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: The sale this line sits on. This table has no completed/voided/complete_time of its own, so every revenue query MUST join ls_sales through this key (or carry those three columns down at load time).

columns.name: create_time
columns.description: When the line was first added to the ticket, store-local. On a parked ticket or a layaway this can be days or months before the sale completes — it is 'when the item was put in the basket', not the sale date.

columns.name: time_stamp
columns.description: When the line was last modified. Not the sale date: a line touched during a later exchange gets a fresh stamp, so filtering revenue periods on it back-dates nothing and double counts amended sales. Filter on the parent sale's complete_time instead.

columns.name: unit_quantity
columns.description: Units on the line. NEGATIVE on refund lines — that is how R-Series expresses a return. SUM(unit_quantity) therefore already nets returns out, and filtering to > 0 overstates sell-through. Documented as integer, so fractional quantities (weight/length) are not expressible on this field.

columns.name: unit_price
columns.description: Per-unit price actually charged, after price rules. May be negative for rebates or credits, but NEVER for refunds — a refund is a negative quantity at a POSITIVE price. Flipping the price sign on refunds produces a double negative and turns returns into revenue.

columns.name: normal_unit_price
columns.description: Per-unit price before any price rules were applied — the 'was' price. (normal_unit_price - unit_price) * unit_quantity approximates automatic markdown only; manually keyed discounts land in discount_amount / calc_line_discount instead, so the two measures do not add up.

columns.name: discount_amount
columns.description: Dollar discount entered on the line. Mutually exclusive with discount_percent — exactly one of the two is non-zero. This is the operator's INPUT, not the resulting money off; the realised money off is calc_line_discount.

columns.name: discount_percent
columns.description: Percentage discount on the line, expressed as a FRACTION of 1 (0.2 = 20%), matching the Discount object's documented <= 1.00 cap. VERIFIED LIVE across every 20% rule at the reference store. Reading 0.2 as 0.2% is a 100x error. Mutually exclusive with discount_amount.

columns.name: avg_cost
columns.description: Weighted-average cost of the product on this line, ex tax. The reference calls it the current average UNIT cost, but VERIFIED LIVE it behaves as the LINE total cost. Multiplying it by unit_quantity therefore double counts COGS and can halve reported margin — validate against a known line on your own account before doing any arithmetic with it.

columns.name: fifo_cost
columns.description: FIFO cost for the line, ex tax — the basis Lightspeed's own profit reports use. Same unit-vs-line ambiguity as avg_cost (VERIFIED LIVE as a line total). It is 0 on non-inventory/service lines and on some migrated history, which silently reports those lines at 100% margin; fall back to avg_cost when this is 0 and calc_subtotal is not.

columns.name: taxed
columns.description: Whether the line is taxed at all. If false, no tax applies regardless of any rate. If true, tax still only applies when the line's TaxClass actually carries a rate — so taxed = true does NOT guarantee calc_tax1 > 0, and using it as a proxy for 'tax was collected' overstates taxable turnover.

columns.name: tax1_rate
columns.description: First tax rate for THIS line as a fraction, after TaxClass and TaxCategory customisation. Overrides the sale's tax1Rate — this is why a mixed basket cannot have its tax reconstructed from the sale-level rate.

columns.name: tax2_rate
columns.description: Second tax rate for this line as a fraction, where the jurisdiction has one. 0 in single-tax territories.

columns.name: is_layaway
columns.description: Line sits on a layaway: goods are reserved (see ls_sale_line_inventory_allocations) and paid for over time, so the money is a balance rather than settled revenue. Settable only via the SaleLine endpoint or the app, never through the Sale endpoint.

columns.name: is_workorder
columns.description: Line originated from a workshop/service job — the marker that separates SERVICE revenue from goods revenue. Effectively read-only: the docs state it must not be set through the Sale or SaleLine endpoints and cannot be used to create a workorder.

columns.name: is_special_order
columns.description: Line is a special order (stock brought in for a named customer); setting it creates a SpecialOrder record. Settable only via the SaleLine endpoint or the app. Special-order lines can sit on an open ticket for weeks, so they distort 'time to sell' metrics.

columns.name: displayable_subtotal
columns.description: Receipt-facing line subtotal, documented as (unitQuantity * unitPrice) - discount. Use it to reproduce a printed receipt. For analytics prefer calc_subtotal so the tax treatment is unambiguous — but note the two differ by exactly the line discount (see the calc_subtotal gotcha).

columns.name: displayable_unit_price
columns.description: The unit price shown to the customer after price-rule PERCENTAGE discounts ONLY — fixed-amount price rules are deliberately excluded. Because of that exclusion it can disagree with unit_price; never use it as the cash-per-unit basis for revenue.

columns.name: calc_line_discount
columns.description: Money taken off by the line's own discount, in currency. Only half the story: add calc_transaction_discount to get the total markdown on the line, otherwise whole-sale discounts are invisible at line grain.

columns.name: calc_transaction_discount
columns.description: This line's allocated share of a whole-sale (transaction-level) discount. calc_line_discount + calc_transaction_discount summed across lines reconciles to Sale.calcDiscount; using either alone under-reports markdown.

columns.name: calc_total
columns.description: Line revenue INCLUDING tax, after all discounts. Sums across lines to the sale's calc_total. Negative on refund lines.

columns.name: calc_subtotal
columns.description: Line revenue excluding tax. TRAP: the reference defines it as unitQuantity * unitPrice — i.e. GROSS of the line discount — whereas displayableSubtotal explicitly subtracts the discount. Confirm on your own account which behaviour you get before using it as the margin base; the gap is exactly calc_line_discount.

columns.name: calc_tax1
columns.description: Tax charged on this line at the first rate, in currency. A money amount, not a rate.

columns.name: calc_tax2
columns.description: Tax charged on this line at the second rate, in currency; 0 in single-tax jurisdictions.

columns.name: tax_class_id
columns.description: TaxClass of the line, which determines its specific rates. The practical dimension for goods-vs-labour tax splits (accounts commonly define a 'Labor' tax class). Maps to the `tax_code` canonical entity.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: Customer on the LINE — populated ONLY for layaway, special-order and workorder lines. This is NOT the buyer of an ordinary sale line; that lives on the parent Sale. Grouping revenue by this column silently drops nearly every normal sale and produces a tiny, plausible, wrong answer.

columns.name: discount_id
columns.description: The named Discount rule applied to this line specifically. Joins ls_discounts. NULL/0 for automatic price rules, loyalty and manual markdowns, so it explains only part of calc_line_discount.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Employee responsible for this line, which can differ from the sale's employee when staff split a ticket or a workshop tech adds parts. Use this for per-line commission and the sale's employee_id for per-ticket attribution — mixing them double counts.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: Catalog item the line charges for; maps to the `product`/`product_variant` canonical entities. VERIFIED LIVE: 0/absent on non-catalog lines (miscellaneous charges, some labour), so product rankings must filter item_id IS NOT NULL or an unnamed bucket tops the chart. On write an itemCode (UPC/EAN, or the itemID itself) may be sent in its place, but reads always return itemID.

columns.name: note_id
columns.description: The single Note object attached to this line; notes print on the receipt. At most one per line by design, so this is a scalar FK not an array. The Note object's own fields are not published in this extract.

columns.name: parent_sale_line_id
columns.description: For a REFUND line, the original sale line it reverses — the API uses it to stop cumulative refunds exceeding the original quantity. Non-null is the most reliable marker of a refund line, more reliable than sign alone (rebate lines are also negative-valued). NULL on ordinary lines.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: Shop where the line was added. Normally equal to the parent sale's shopID, but it is stored per line, so a cross-shop ticket is representable and line-level location splits can disagree with sale-level ones.

columns.name: tax_category_id
columns.description: TaxCategory applied to this line — the jurisdiction-level container that sits above TaxClass. Together they resolve tax1_rate/tax2_rate.

columns.name: item_fee_id
columns.description: The ItemFee this line represents, when the line is a fee rather than merchandise (e.g. a recycling or environmental levy attached by category). Non-null means this row is a surcharge: it inflates unit counts and distorts average selling price if treated as a product.

columns.name: line_type
columns.description: Descriptor of what the line represents. Explicitly NOT a discriminator for layaway/special-order/workorder — the docs say so outright, and using it that way returns zero rows. Use is_layaway / is_special_order / is_workorder for those, and line_type only to isolate item-fee rows.
columns.enums: item_fee = an item-fee surcharge line; item_fee_refund = reversal of an item fee. Documented as NOT currently used to differentiate layaway, special order or workorder lines. Empty/absent on ordinary item lines.

columns.name: require_full_reservation
columns.description: Request-payload-only flag that makes a write FAIL if there is not enough inventory to reserve the whole unitQuantity. Layaway lines only, defaults false. It carries no analytical meaning on read — expect it absent or false on every stored row and never filter on it.

tables.grain: one row per SalePayment — one tender applied to, or refunded from, one sale. A single sale can have many (split tender, layaway instalments); a credit-account deposit is deliberately recorded as TWO rows.
tables.description: How money actually moved: cash, card, gift card, store credit, cheque, on-account. This is the takings/tender-mix table and the cash-reconciliation table. It is NOT revenue: layaway instalments, deposits and on-account payments land on the day the money moved, whereas ls_sales recognises revenue at complete_time. Refund payments appear here as negative amounts.
gotchas: archived = true payments are effectively voided and must be excluded from every takings figure. This is INDEPENDENT of the parent sale's voided flag — filter both.
tip_amount is INSIDE amount, not additional to it. Merchandise money taken = SUM(amount - tip_amount). Reporting SUM(amount) as sales overstates by the tip pool.

Credit Account sign convention is inverted from intuition: positive DEBITS the account, negative DEPOSITS to it. The docs also state a deposit is written as TWO payments — a positive real-tender payment plus a negative Credit Account payment of the same amount — so SUM(amount) over a deposit sale correctly nets to the tender taken. Do not 'fix' the apparent double entry.

Takings is not revenue. Layaway instalments, deposits and on-account payments land on create_time here, while ls_sales recognises the sale at complete_time. The two will never tie for a store that offers layaway.

VERIFIED LIVE: stores on an external EFTPOS terminal have cc_charge_id NULL on every card payment, because the card never touches Lightspeed's integrated processing. A NULL cc_charge_id does NOT mean 'not a card' — read the tender from payment_type_id.
ref_payment_id is the only reliable pairing between a refund tender and the charge it reverses; do not match on amount plus card last-four.

Gift-card issuance appears here as a negative payment paired with a ls_sale_accounts row, and the later redemption appears as a positive payment on a different sale. Counting both as money earned double counts the gift card.

The documented sortable fields for this endpoint include `timeStamp`, but NO timeStamp field appears in its published field table (only createTime). Sort by salePaymentID or saleID; treat timeStamp sorting as unverified.
salePaymentID is described in the reference as 'the unique numerical ID for the payment type'. That is a documentation error — it identifies the payment. The payment type is payment_type_id.

columns.name: sale_payment_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id for this tender line. The reference calls it 'the unique numerical ID for the payment type', which is a documentation error — it identifies the PAYMENT, not the payment type (that is payment_type_id). Target of ref_payment_id on reversals and of ls_processing_fees.sale_payment_id.

columns.name: amount
columns.description: Amount tendered in store currency, INCLUDING any tip (see tip_amount). Negative for a refund going back to the customer. On a Credit Account payment type the sign meaning INVERTS: positive = debit from the account (customer spends stored value), negative = deposit to it — see credit_account_id before trusting any sign-based logic.

columns.name: create_time
columns.description: When the payment was taken, store-local. On layaways and on-account sales this can be far later than the sale's createTime and is the correct date for 'takings by day' / cash-up reconciliation, whereas revenue uses the sale's complete_time.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: Archived payments are effectively voided and, per the docs, must NOT count toward totals. This is INDEPENDENT of the parent sale's voided flag: a perfectly live sale can carry an archived (reversed and re-taken) payment. Filter archived = false on every takings figure or you count reversed tenders twice.

columns.name: remote_reference
columns.description: Optional client-generated unique identifier supplied by an integration when creating the payment — an idempotency key for reconciling against an external system. Empty for POS-entered payments; not a Lightspeed identifier and not guaranteed unique unless the integration enforces it.

columns.name: tip_amount
columns.description: Tip portion of this tender, negative for a refund. IT IS INCLUDED IN `amount`, not additional to it — merchandise money = amount - tip_amount. Rolls up to Sale.calcTips. Treating tips as revenue overstates sales and understates the liability owed to staff.

columns.name: payment_id
columns.description: Reference to the charge held by the payment SERVICE (the processor's own handle). A string despite the -ID suffix, and unrelated to sale_payment_id — never join or cast it numerically.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: The sale this payment settles. Join to ls_sales for the completed/voided filters — this table has none of its own.

columns.name: payment_type_id
columns.description: Tender type of this payment or refund (Cash, Credit Card, Gift Card, Credit Account, ...). The tender-mix dimension; the PaymentType reference table lives in the org domain. Its value is what flips the sign convention on amount when credit_account_id is set.

columns.name: cc_charge_id
columns.description: The CCCharge (gateway transaction) backing this payment, when the card ran through Lightspeed's integrated processing. VERIFIED LIVE: NULL/0 on every card payment at stores using an external EFTPOS terminal — absence does NOT mean the payment was not a card.

columns.name: ref_payment_id
columns.description: Points at the ORIGINAL salePaymentID this row reverses; set when refunding a previous credit card charge. The only reliable way to pair a refund tender with the payment it reverses — matching on amount and card last-four is guesswork.

columns.name: register_id
columns.description: Register the payment was received at. Can legitimately differ from the parent sale's registerID — a layaway instalment is often paid at a different till from where the ticket was opened, which is why cash-ups must group by THIS column, not the sale's.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Employee who received the payment; may differ from the employee who rang the sale. Use this for till accountability and the sale's employee_id for sales attribution.

columns.name: credit_account_id
columns.description: The CreditAccount (store credit or gift card) this deposit/withdrawal applies to. Sign semantics are documented and easy to invert: with paymentType = Credit Account, POSITIVE amount = debit FROM the account (customer spends stored value), NEGATIVE = deposit TO it. With Cash/Check/Credit Card and this set, a positive amount is a REFUND of the customer's deposit paid out in that tender.

tables.grain: one row per SaleAccount — one gift-card (CreditAccount) association linking a single SalePayment to the SaleLine that created or funded it. Documented one-to-one with SalePayment, so a payment has zero or one row here.
tables.description: The bridge that makes gift cards and store credit interpretable: it ties the negative payment that funded a card to the sale line that sold it and to the CreditAccount that holds the balance. Without it you cannot distinguish a gift-card ISSUE (money in, no revenue) from a gift-card REDEMPTION (a payment on a later sale). It holds no money of its own and must never be aggregated.
gotchas: Zero-or-one row per SalePayment by design. This is a bridge table, not a fact table — it has no amount column and must never be aggregated for money.

This is the ONLY way to separate a gift-card ISSUE (a negative SalePayment plus the line that sold the card: money in, no revenue) from a gift-card REDEMPTION (an ordinary positive payment on a later sale). Counting both as sales double counts the card.
Gift-card face value is excluded from Sale.total but INCLUDED in Sale.displayableTotal. Use this table to explain the difference rather than switching total columns to make a receipt tie out.

Reachable from two directions (SalePayment.SaleAccounts and SaleLine.SaleAccounts) but it is ONE object with one grain, so it is modelled once. Loading it from both relations without de-duplicating on sale_account_id creates phantom duplicates.

columns.name: sale_account_id
columns.description: Primary key of the link record. Has no business meaning on its own — it exists only to identify the association.

columns.name: credit_account_id
columns.description: The CreditAccount (gift card / store credit account) used in the SalePayment. This is the identity of the physical gift card, and the key that lets you follow one card's balance across issue, top-up and redemption on different sales.

columns.name: sale_payment_id
columns.description: The SalePayment linked to the sale line — specifically the NEGATIVE-amount payment that created or topped up the gift card. Relationship is documented one-to-one, so this is effectively an alternate key: at most one SaleAccount per payment.

columns.name: sale_line_id
columns.description: The SaleLine that sold the gift card. This is the half that makes the record useful: pairing the line (what was sold) with the payment (money in) is the ONLY reliable way to classify a gift-card issue versus a redemption.

tables.grain: one row per SalePaymentSignature — one captured signature image belonging to one sale payment.
tables.description: Evidence that a customer signed for a payment, stored as a pointer into Lightspeed's image storage service. Used for chargeback defence and audit trails. It is NOT a measure of anything: there is no amount, no sale id and no approval status here, and a signature can exist on a payment that was later archived/reversed.
gotchas: file_path is a pointer into an image storage service, not a URL and not the image. Do not present it as a link and do not expect to render it without a separate authenticated fetch.
No amount and no sale_id: this table is evidence, never a measure. Reaching a sale requires joining through ls_sale_payments.
A signature can exist on a payment that was later archived (reversed). Joining it to takings without filtering ls_sale_payments.archived = false overstates 'signed' revenue.

Absence of a row is weak evidence: signature capture depends on terminal configuration and tender type, so most cash payments will never have one. Do not report an un-signed rate without first restricting to card tenders.

columns.name: sale_payment_signature_id
columns.description: Primary key of the signature record. Addressable at SalePayment/{salePaymentID}/SalePaymentSignature/{id} — it is a child resource of the payment, not a top-level collection.

columns.name: file_path
columns.description: Path to the signature image inside Lightspeed's image storage service. A storage pointer, NOT a public URL and NOT the image bytes. Its presence proves a signature was captured; it says nothing about whether the payment was authorised or settled. Treat as personal data — a signature is biometric-adjacent.

columns.name: create_time
columns.description: When the signature was captured, store-local. Normally within seconds of the payment's createTime; a large gap indicates a signature added retrospectively, which is exactly what a chargeback investigation cares about.

columns.name: sale_payment_id
columns.description: The payment this signature was captured for — the ONLY link this table has to the rest of the domain. There is no sale_id, so reaching the sale requires going through ls_sale_payments.

tables.grain: one row per InventorySale — one allocation of units from ONE inventory lot to ONE sale line. A line that draws from three lots produces three rows.
tables.description: The bridge from a sale line to the specific inventory lots it consumed or reserved. This is what makes a FIFO cost audit reconstructable, and what shows how much stock an open layaway or special order is holding hostage. It is NOT a stock-on-hand table and NOT a general inventory movement log — it only covers allocations tied to sale lines.
gotchas: quantity means TWO different things depending on the parent line's state — units SOLD from a lot (immutable) on a sold line, units RESERVED (mutable, rewritten as the order changes) on an open layaway / special-order / workorder line. Always split on the parent's is_layaway / is_special_order / is_workorder plus ls_sales.completed before aggregating.

InventorySale carries NO saleLineID of its own. Its grain exists only because the row is exploded out of its parent SaleLine, so it must be loaded via the SaleLines.InventorySales relation on Sale.json — there is no standalone collection that would give it identity.
create_time on a layaway allocation is when the stock was ring-fenced, which can precede the sale completing by months. It is not a COGS date.
This is the bridge from a sale line to a specific cost lot, and the only way to make a FIFO cost audit reconstructable — ls_sale_lines.fifo_cost alone cannot be traced back to lots.
Reservations on open lines are effectively a stock balance, not an event. If you snapshot this table over time, do not sum the same inventory_sale_id across snapshots.

columns.name: inventory_sale_id
columns.description: Unique numeric identifier for the allocation. The only field on this object that is stable — quantity is rewritten in place while the parent line is open.

columns.name: quantity
columns.description: Units drawn from this lot. MEANING DEPENDS ON THE PARENT LINE'S STATE: on a sold line it is the quantity SOLD from that lot (immutable, realised COGS); on an open layaway / special-order / workorder line it is the quantity currently RESERVED and will be rewritten as the order changes. Summing both together silently mixes realised cost with open commitments.

columns.name: create_time
columns.description: When the allocation or reservation was made, store-local. For a layaway this is when stock was ring-fenced, which can precede the sale completing by months — so it is the right date for 'how long has this stock been tied up' and the wrong date for COGS periods.

columns.name: inventory_id
columns.description: The Inventory lot the units were pulled from. The join key into the inventory domain and the reason this table exists: it is the only published link between a sale line and the specific cost lot behind its FIFO cost.

columns.name: sale_line_id
columns.description: The sale line this allocation belongs to. NOT a field on the InventorySale object itself — it is carried down from the explode parent. Without it the row has no grain and no meaning, which is why this object cannot be loaded from a standalone collection.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: The sale the allocation ultimately belongs to, carried down from the top-level Sale envelope. Denormalised purely so allocations can be filtered by sale state without a second hop through ls_sale_lines.

tables.grain: one row per SaleVoid — one void event recorded against one sale, with the operator's stated reason.
tables.description: The audit trail for voided transactions: who voided what, where, when and why. This is the loss-prevention table. It is NOT the voided state itself — that lives on ls_sales.voided — and it is NOT a money table: the value voided has to be pulled from the parent sale.
gotchas: create_time is the VOID date, not the sale date. A sale rung Monday and voided Tuesday lands in both periods — state which you mean.
employee_id here is who VOIDED. ls_sales.employee_id is who rang the original sale. Comparing them is the standard void-abuse check; conflating them misattributes every manager override.
The voided STATE lives on ls_sales.voided; this table only records the event and reason. Treat the join as LEFT in both directions and never assume a 1:1 correspondence.
De-duplicate with COUNT(DISTINCT sale_id) before counting voided sales — the resource is keyed on saleVoidID.
reason is operator free text and is often empty. Do not fill blanks with a placeholder before analysing: the blanks are the finding.
The sortable-fields list published for this endpoint is truncated in the reference ('saleVoidID, saleID, ---'). Assume only those two are safely sortable.

columns.name: sale_void_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the void record. Note the resource is keyed on the VOID, not the sale, so counting rows is not the same as counting voided sales.

columns.name: create_time
columns.description: When the void happened, store-local. This is the VOID date, not the original sale date — a ticket rung Monday and voided Tuesday appears in Monday's sales history and Tuesday's void report. Use it for 'voids by day/shift/staff member'.

columns.name: reason
columns.description: Free-text note the operator gave for the void. No enum — values are whatever staff typed, including empty. Loss-prevention gold: blank or boilerplate reasons on high-value voids are the classic fraud signal, so never coalesce empty to a placeholder before analysing.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: The sale that was voided; joins ls_sales where voided = true. Because the resource is keyed on saleVoidID, a sale can in principle carry more than one void record — COUNT(DISTINCT sale_id), not COUNT(*), when counting voided sales.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Employee who PERFORMED the void — frequently NOT the employee who rang the original sale (that is ls_sales.employee_id). Comparing the two is the standard void-abuse check, and treating this as the seller misattributes every manager override.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: Shop where the void was performed. Can differ from the original sale's shopID when a void is processed at a different location, so location-based void rates must decide which of the two they mean.

tables.grain: one row per CCCharge — one credit-card transaction ATTEMPT at the processing gateway, including declines, gateway voids and authorisation-only holds.
tables.description: Gateway-side truth for integrated card payments: what was authorised, captured, declined, voided or refunded, and the reference ids needed to reconcile against a processor statement. It is NOT the POS payment record (that is ls_sale_payments) and it is NOT a settled-money table — most rows on a busy account are failures and holds. Empty on any merchant using an external terminal.
tables.additivityAxis: time, per cc_charge_id — `refunded` is a cumulative-to-date total restated in place on the same row, so you may not sum it across successive syncs of the same charge (summing across distinct charges at one point in time is fine)
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: the reference store (Ashburton Cycles) has ZERO rows here because cards run on an external EFTPOS terminal, never Lightspeed's integrated processing. Empty is NORMAL — answer card questions from ls_sale_payments plus the PaymentType reference, and say the gateway data is unavailable rather than reporting zero card sales.
Rows include failures and holds. Settled card money requires declined = false AND voided = false AND auth_only = false. Any one omitted overstates card volume.
`refunded` is a cumulative running total restated on the row, not an event. Never sum it across sync snapshots of the same charge.
entry_method's documented description ('The card type: Visa, Mastercard, etc.') contradicts its name. Do not build a card-brand mix on it without live verification.
VERIFIED LIVE: the docs' own sample response returns the raw gateway blob under `rawResponse` while the field table calls it `response` — the column can extract NULL on some accounts.
xnum, exp and cardholder_name are cardholder data. Mask or exclude them from shared output; xnum is not unique and is worthless as a key.
time_stamp moves when a refund is applied, so it is not the charge date. Use ls_sale_payments.create_time for when the customer paid.
This charge's voided flag is gateway-side and independent of ls_sales.voided. Filtering one does not filter the other.

columns.name: cc_charge_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id for the charge attempt. ls_sale_payments.cc_charge_id joins here. Existence of a row does not imply money moved — check declined, voided and auth_only.

columns.name: gateway_trans_id
columns.description: The processor's own transaction id — the key for reconciling against a merchant statement. Opaque string whose format varies by gateway, so never parse it or assume it is numeric.

columns.name: xnum
columns.description: Last four digits of the customer's card. Never a full PAN and NOT unique — thousands of cards share a last-four, so it is useless as a customer or card identity key. Cardholder data: mask in any shared output.

columns.name: response
columns.description: Raw response received from the gateway. Documented as possibly XML, a URL, or another format — unparsed, bulky, and not analytics data. VERIFIED LIVE caveat: the docs' own sample response returns this blob under the key `rawResponse`, so extraction against `response` can yield NULL on some accounts.

columns.name: voided
columns.description: The charge was voided AT THE GATEWAY before settlement — no money ever moved. INDEPENDENT of Sale.voided: a gateway-voided charge can sit under a perfectly live sale (the customer simply re-tapped) and a voided sale can contain a settled charge that was refunded separately.

columns.name: refunded
columns.description: CUMULATIVE amount refunded back to this card so far — a running total restated on the same row, NOT a per-refund event. Remaining balance = amount - refunded. Summing it across sync snapshots of the same charge double or triple counts refunds.

columns.name: amount
columns.description: The original amount authorised/captured on the card. The current remaining balance of the charge is amount - refunded. Includes any tip that was added at the terminal, so it can exceed the sale total.

columns.name: exp
columns.description: Expiration date of the credit card as recorded by the gateway. Cardholder data with no analytical value — exclude it from any shared output; its only legitimate use is chargeback dispute paperwork.

columns.name: auth_only
columns.description: True when the transaction was an AUTHORISATION HOLD only and was never captured. No money settled. Counting auth-only rows as takings inflates card revenue, and they are common on pre-auth flows (workshop deposits, hire bonds).

columns.name: auth_code
columns.description: Authorisation code returned by the gateway on approval. Presence is a weak approval signal; use declined = false as the actual test.

columns.name: time_stamp
columns.description: When the record was last modified, store-local. The closest thing to a charge timestamp this resource exposes, but it MOVES when a refund is later applied — so it is not the original charge time. For the payment date use ls_sale_payments.create_time.

columns.name: declined
columns.description: True when the gateway declined the charge. DECLINED ATTEMPTS STILL CREATE ROWS. Settled card money requires declined = false AND voided = false AND auth_only = false — omitting any one of the three overstates card volume.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: The sale this card payment belongs to. A single sale can have many charges (retries after declines, split tender, tip adjustments), so this is many-to-one.

columns.name: entry_method
columns.description: CONFLICTED FIELD: the reference documents it as 'The card type: Visa, Mastercard, etc.' while the field name says how the card was presented (swipe/chip/contactless/keyed). One of the two is wrong. Treat values as untrusted until observed on a live gateway-integrated account, and never build a card-brand mix on it without verifying first.

columns.name: cardholder_name
columns.description: Name appearing on the card. Cardholder data. Do NOT use it as a customer identity key — it comes from the card track/chip and will not reliably match Customer records in spelling or format.

columns.name: communication_key
columns.description: Undescribed in the reference — gateway plumbing, most likely a credential or session handle. No analytical meaning, and it should be treated as a secret: never expose it in output or logs.

tables.grain: one row per ProcessingFee — one fee record the payment processor assessed against one SalePayment.
tables.description: What card acceptance actually costs, per payment, broken into fixed/variable components with interchange and scheme sub-breakdowns. The only place in the API where merchant cost of payment acceptance appears. Only populated for merchants on Lightspeed's integrated payments; empty for anyone on an external terminal. It is NOT a payment table — its `amount` column is a notorious trap.
gotchas: `amount` is the PAYMENT amount the fee was assessed on, NOT the fee. The fee is fixed_fee + variable_fee. This is the single most common misread on this table and it silently reports card volume as card cost.
interchange_* and scheme_* columns are BREAKDOWNS of the total fee, not extra charges. Adding every fee column together roughly doubles the reported cost.
VERIFIED LIVE: the reference store has ZERO rows (external EFTPOS, so processor fees never reach Lightspeed). Report 'not available in this data' rather than estimating card costs from a rate.
The *_pct columns' fraction-versus-percentage format is unverified live. Always sanity-check variable_fee / amount before using any pct column in arithmetic.
processing_time (processor-side settlement) lags create_time (Lightspeed-side ingest). Statement reconciliation must use processing_time.
Fees can be RESTATED by the processor — update_time moving on a closed period is expected, so a re-run of last month's cost report can legitimately differ.

columns.name: sale_payment_processing_fee_id
columns.description: Unique identifier of the processing fee record. Note the sortable-fields list for this endpoint is truncated in the reference ('salePaymentProcessingFeeID, ---'), so assume this is the only safe sort key.

columns.name: sale_payment_id
columns.description: The SalePayment the fee was assessed on. The endpoint supports a direct ?salePaymentID= lookup, making per-payment fee retrieval cheap without a full scan.

columns.name: processing_fee_ref
columns.description: The processor's external reference id for this fee line — the key for tying a fee back to a line on a processor statement. Opaque; format is processor-specific.

columns.name: processor
columns.description: Name of the payment processor handling the transaction. Only populated for integrated-payments merchants, and the grouping dimension if an account has moved between processors — fee rates are not comparable across processors.

columns.name: amount
columns.description: TRAP: this is the total PAYMENT amount the fee was linked to, NOT the fee itself. The reference wording ('the total payment amount linked to the processing fee') is easy to skim past. Summing this column gives card VOLUME, not card COST. The fee is fixed_fee + variable_fee.

columns.name: fixed_fee
columns.description: The fixed, per-transaction component of the fee, in store currency. Together with variable_fee this is the actual money the merchant lost on the payment.

columns.name: variable_fee
columns.description: The rate-based component of the fee, in store currency. Total fee for the payment = fixed_fee + variable_fee; the interchange_* and scheme_* columns explain how that total was composed, they are not additional charges.

columns.name: variable_pct
columns.description: The rate used to calculate variable_fee. Whether it is stored as a fraction (0.017) or a percentage (1.7) is NOT verified live — no rows exist at the reference store. Sanity-check it against variable_fee / amount before using it in any arithmetic, or you are 100x out.

columns.name: interchange_fees_fixed_fee
columns.description: Fixed portion of the interchange component (the part paid to the card-issuing bank). A BREAKDOWN of the total fee, not an addition to it — adding it to fixed_fee double counts.

columns.name: interchange_fees_variable_fee
columns.description: Variable portion of interchange, in currency. Breakdown component; do not add it to variable_fee.

columns.name: interchange_fees_variable_pct
columns.description: The rate behind the variable interchange portion. Same fraction-vs-percentage uncertainty as variable_pct — unverified live.

columns.name: scheme_fees_fixed_fee
columns.description: Fixed portion of card-scheme fees (the part paid to the Visa/Mastercard network, distinct from interchange). Breakdown component.

columns.name: scheme_fees_variable_fee
columns.description: Variable portion of card-scheme fees, in currency. Breakdown component.

columns.name: scheme_fees_variable_pct
columns.description: The rate behind the variable scheme portion. Format unverified live, same caveat as variable_pct.

columns.name: processing_time
columns.description: When the processor remotely processed the fee — the settlement-side date. It LAGS the payment date and determines which processor statement period the fee lands in, so statement reconciliation must use this column, not create_time.

columns.name: create_time
columns.description: When the fee record was created inside Lightspeed. A sync artefact: it tracks when Lightspeed learned about the fee, not when the fee was charged.

columns.name: update_time
columns.description: Last modification of the fee record. Fees CAN be restated by the processor after the fact, so a fee report re-run for a closed month may legitimately change — use this column to detect restatements.

tables.grain: one row per Quote — one saved, uncompleted sale held for a customer so it can be reloaded at the register later.
tables.description: The pre-sale pipeline: quotes/invoices staff saved for customers. A deliberately thin resource — it has no customer, no totals and no line detail of its own, all of which live on the sale it points at. It is NOT a conversion log: its sale_id is reassigned on every edit, so conversion must be measured from the other direction (ls_sales.quote_id).
tables.additivityAxis: time, per quote_id — the row is overwritten in place (sale_id is REASSIGNED on every edit and archived flips), so it holds current state only and carries no history. COUNT(*) by issue_date is still a valid event measure.
gotchas: sale_id is REASSIGNED every time the quote is modified — the reference says so explicitly. It points at whichever sale currently stores the contents. Using it as a conversion signal marks every edited quote as converted.
Measure conversion the other way: JOIN ls_sales ON ls_sales.quote_id = ls_quotes.quote_id AND completed = true AND voided = false.
The object has no customer, total or line detail of its own. Any quote-value or quote-customer question MUST join ls_sales through sale_id.
archived does not mean lost — staff also archive quotes after they convert. Open pipeline = archived = false AND no completed sale referencing the quote.
There is no expiry or accepted-at date, only issue_date. 'Stale quote' definitions have to be imposed by the analyst, not read from the data.
The two joins to ls_sales point in opposite directions and mean different things. Mixing them in one query produces a fan-out that silently double counts pipeline value.

columns.name: quote_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the quote — the ONLY stable identifier here. ls_sales.quote_id back-references it when a quote is turned into a sale, and that reference is what conversion should be measured on.

columns.name: issue_date
columns.description: When the quote was issued, store-local. The only date on the object: there is no expiry, no accepted-at and no converted-at field, so quote age can only be computed as issue_date to now, and 'time to convert' must come from the converted sale's complete_time.

columns.name: notes
columns.description: Free-text notes on the quote. Usually the ONLY human description of what was quoted, because the line detail lives on the linked sale — so this is what a rep actually reads when reopening a quote.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the quote is retired. Archived does NOT mean lost: staff routinely archive quotes AFTER they convert as well as when they go cold. Open-pipeline questions need archived = false AND no completed sale referencing the quote — the flag alone is not a lost/won signal.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Employee who started the quote. The attribution for quote-pipeline-by-rep. Note this is who CREATED it — the employee who eventually completes the resulting sale is on ls_sales.employee_id and can be a different person.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: The Sale record CURRENTLY holding this quote's contents. The reference states outright that a quote gets a NEW saleID every time it is modified, so this is a content pointer, not a conversion signal. Read the quote's value, customer and lines through it; measure conversion from ls_sales.quote_id on completed sales instead.

tables.grain: one row per named Discount rule that staff or the system can apply to a sale or a sale line.
tables.description: The catalogue of reusable discount rules — their names, amounts/percentages, and what kind of discount they are (price rule, loyalty, or manual discount rule). A row is the RULE, not money given away: actual markdown lives in ls_sales.calc_discount and ls_sale_lines.calc_line_discount, which also include price-rule and manual discounts that carry no rule id.
gotchas: discount_percent is a FRACTION (0.2 = 20%). VERIFIED LIVE at the reference store on every 20% rule, and the docs cap it at <= 1.00. This is the easiest 100x error in the domain.
Exactly one of discount_amount / discount_percent is non-zero per rule — branch on which side is > 0 rather than assuming one shape.

source_id separates price rule (0) from loyalty (1) from discount rule (2). Loyalty redemptions are the cost of a loyalty programme, not a promotional markdown; blending them misstates both margin and programme cost.
VERIFIED LIVE: names carry trailing whitespace — TRIM before grouping or one rule appears twice.

VERIFIED LIVE: DELETE archives rather than deletes, and Discount.json accepts archived=true. Historical sales keep referencing archived rules, so do not inner-join with an archived = false filter when explaining old markdowns.

A row is the reusable RULE, not money given away. Actual markdown lives in ls_sales.calc_discount and ls_sale_lines.calc_line_discount + calc_transaction_discount, which also include automatic price rules and manual overrides that carry NO discount_id — so summing discount value grouped by rule always under-attributes.

The ground-truth extract documents this object under the Sale-SaleLine endpoint page (its GET is listed as Sale/{saleID}/SaleLine.json) and inherits that page's sortable-fields list. The queryable rule catalogue is the account-level Discount.json collection; treat the published sortable fields here as unreliable.

columns.name: discount_id
columns.description: Unique numeric identifier for the discount rule. Both ls_sales.discount_id (deprecated, sale-level) and ls_sale_lines.discount_id (line-level) point here.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The description/name staff see when applying the rule (e.g. 'ARC Riders 20% SERVICE DISCOUNT'). VERIFIED LIVE: names can carry trailing whitespace — TRIM before grouping or the same rule splits into two rows in every report.

columns.name: discount_amount
columns.description: Dollar amount off, in store currency. A rule is EITHER an amount or a percentage, never both — the unused side sits at 0. Documented as required to be > 0.00 when this is the active side.

columns.name: discount_percent
columns.description: Percentage off stored as a FRACTION of 1 — the docs cap it at <= 1.00 (100%), and VERIFIED LIVE every 20% rule at the reference store stores 0.2. Multiply by 100 for display. Reading 0.2 as 0.2% is the single easiest 100x error in this domain.

columns.name: require_customer
columns.description: True when a customer must be attached to the sale before the rule can be applied (club, trade and loyalty rules). Explains why these discounts never appear on walk-in tickets, which otherwise looks like staff ignoring them.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the rule is retired. VERIFIED LIVE: DELETE archives rather than deletes, and Discount.json accepts archived=true to retrieve them. Historical sales keep referencing archived rules, so an INNER join filtered to archived = false silently drops old markdowns from reports.

columns.name: source_id
columns.description: What KIND of discount this is. Mislabelling a loyalty redemption (1) as a promotional markdown (2) misstates both gross margin and the cost of the loyalty programme, because loyalty is a redemption of a previously accrued liability rather than a price concession.
columns.enums: 0 = price rule (automatic pricing), 1 = loyalty (points/reward redemption), 2 = discount rule (manual/named discount)

columns.name: time_stamp
columns.description: When the rule record was last modified, store-local. It moves on every edit, so it is NOT 'when the discount was introduced' — and at the reference store record dates were bulk-set during a platform migration, making them useless for rule-age analysis.

tables.grain: one catalogue item — a single sellable SKU. Every colour/size variant of a matrix product is its own row here; the matrix itself is a row in ls_item_matrices.
tables.description: The product master: identity, SKUs/barcodes, categorisation, current price levels, cost basis and the flags that govern tax, discounting and stock behaviour. It answers what the store sells today and at what price and margin. It is NOT a sales ledger (units sold and revenue live on sale lines) and NOT stock (quantities live in ls_item_shops). The 1:1 ItemAttributes and itemECommerce sub-objects are folded in here because they share this grain.
gotchas: Archiving is the only delete. A DELETE request archives the item, and archiving an item WITH inventory zeroes that inventory irreversibly (it cannot be undone except by re-entering every inventory record). You also cannot archive by setting the archived flag on an update.

VERIFIED LIVE: Lightspeed writes 0, not null, into unset integer FKs and numerics — categoryID, manufacturerID, itemMatrixID, taxClassID, departmentID, seasonID, modelYear. Map 0 to NULL on load or 'uncategorised' counts are wrong and joins silently match a non-existent id 0.

VERIFIED LIVE: prices arrive inline on EVERY Item response under the response key Prices.ItemPrice[] even though the documented load_relations name is 'ItemPrices'. You do not need to request the relation. Likewise 'Vendor' is NOT a loadable relation — defaultVendorID is a plain field.

VERIFIED LIVE: selling prices follow the store's tax-inclusive setting (AU stores: price includes 10% GST) while defaultCost/avgCost are always ex-tax. Margin at a 10% GST store is (price/1.1 - avg_cost)/(price/1.1); comparing price to avg_cost raw overstates margin by the tax rate.
VERIFIED LIVE: msrp is 0 on most items because the level was never set. Filter msrp > 0 before any RRP comparison.
VERIFIED LIVE: manufacturer name casing is inconsistent in real data (VITTORIA vs Elite, ZEFAL vs Shimano). UPPER() before grouping or one brand becomes several.

VERIFIED LIVE: live Item responses also carry laborDurationMinutes (workshop labour minutes per service item, 0 when not a labour item). It is absent from the published field table so it is not staged here; add it if workshop capacity is in scope.
Every colour/size variant is a separate row. 'How many products do we sell' almost never means COUNT(*): it means COUNT(*) WHERE item_matrix_id IS NULL plus COUNT(DISTINCT item_matrix_id).

updated_at does not move when related records change (documented). Stock movements, ItemShop edits and related-record changes leave it untouched, so it cannot answer 'what changed recently' for anything but the item record itself.

Single reads support a special itemCode query that matches an Item's itemID, upc OR ean — one parameter, three namespaces. Only '=', 'or' and 'IN' operators are supported on it; ranges and LIKE are rejected.
modelYear, departmentID and seasonID only exist on older Retail POS accounts (Department and Season were removed as organisers). Treat any analysis built on them as account-specific.
Exclude item_type = 'non_inventory' from anything counting units or valuing stock — labour and service SKUs carry meaningless quantities.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: Stable primary key of the SKU across the whole account; the join target for sale lines, stock rows, images, serial numbers and order lines. Survives archiving (items are never hard-deleted), so historical sale lines always resolve.

columns.name: system_sku
columns.description: The barcode Lightspeed generates and prints on shelf labels (e.g. 210000000004). Documented as an integer but it is an identifier, never a quantity — store and compare as text or leading zeros and precision are lost. Read-only; distinct from custom_sku (the shop's own code) and upc/ean (the manufacturer's barcodes).

columns.name: default_cost
columns.description: Expected per-unit reorder cost from the supplier, EXCLUSIVE of tax. Used to seed the inventory record cost when stock is received without a stated cost. It is an intention, not what was actually paid — avg_cost is the realised figure. 0 means never set, not free.

columns.name: avg_cost
columns.description: Weighted average unit cost of ALL purchases of this item ever, including stock already sold, EXCLUSIVE of tax. This is the cost basis for margin maths at account level. Commonly confused with default_cost (a forward-looking reorder price) and with the FIFO cost the next sale will actually consume.

columns.name: taxable
columns.description: True when sales tax/GST is charged on this item at the register. Governs whether the price already carries tax in a tax-inclusive jurisdiction; get it wrong and margin on zero-rated goods is understated by the tax rate.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the item has been retired. The published doc text for this field reads 'Whether this discount is archived' — a copy-paste error in the Lightspeed docs; it refers to the item. Archiving is the ONLY form of delete (a DELETE request archives) and it irreversibly zeroes the item's inventory. Cannot be set via update. Filter false for the live range.

columns.name: discountable
columns.description: True when cashiers may apply a discount to this line at the register. False on fixed-price or contract lines; explains why some items never appear in discount analysis.
columns.enums: true = discounts permitted; false = register blocks discounting

columns.name: item_type
columns.description: What kind of thing the SKU is, which decides whether its stock number means anything. non_inventory rows (labour, services, fees) carry stock quantities that are noise and must be excluded from unit and value totals. box/assembly rows are built from ls_item_components children.
columns.enums: default = normal stocked product; non_inventory = no stock tracking (labour, services, misc charges); serialized = each unit carries a serial number; box = sold as a box/case that breaks down into components; serialized_assembly = serialized item built from components; assembly = built up from component items

columns.name: serialized
columns.description: True when every unit gets a serial number captured at sale. Independent of item_type — it may be true on any type — but must be true before item_type can be set to serialized or serialized_assembly. Serial records live in ls_serialized.

columns.name: description
columns.description: The product name printed on receipts and labels. For matrix variants Lightspeed composes it as '<matrix description> <attribute1> <attribute2> <attribute3>', so a LIKE on the family name catches every size/colour. Not a long marketing description — that is ecom_long_description.

columns.name: model_year
columns.description: Model year of the product (e.g. 2008, 2024). Stored as 0 when unset — map 0 to NULL or year filters silently include everything unset.

columns.name: upc
columns.description: UPC barcode, 11-14 digits. Text, not a number: leading zeros are significant. Also one of the three values the itemCode single-read query matches against.

columns.name: ean
columns.description: EAN barcode, 11-14 digits — the international sibling of upc, usually empty when upc is populated. Also matched by the itemCode query.

columns.name: custom_sku
columns.description: The shop's own internal SKU, entered by staff. Frequently empty and free-text, so never assume uniqueness or a format.

columns.name: manufacturer_sku
columns.description: The manufacturer's own part number. The most reliable key for matching against supplier catalogues and price lists — join it to ls_catalog_vendor_items.manufacturer_number.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When the item RECORD was last edited. Documented to exclude changes to related records, so it does not move when stock, ItemShops or related prices change. Using it to find 'recently received' or 'recently sold' products is the classic wrong answer here — use the inventory movement log instead.

columns.name: created_at
columns.description: When the SKU was first created in the catalogue. A good proxy for when the shop began ranging the product; unaffected by later edits.

columns.name: publish_to_ecom
columns.description: Flag requesting publication to Lightspeed eCom. A catalogue intent flag only — it is not proof the item is live on a webstore, and it is independent of ecom_list_on_store.

columns.name: category_id
columns.description: The single category node this item hangs off, at any depth of the tree. 0 is written when uncategorised — map to NULL, otherwise uncategorised items join a non-existent category 0.

columns.name: tax_class_id
columns.description: Which tax class governs the item's rate. 0 when unset. Together with taxable it decides the effective rate; a wrong reading silently shifts tax-exclusive margin.

columns.name: department_id
columns.description: Legacy department grouping. Only populated on older Retail POS accounts — the Department organiser was removed in favour of categories, manufacturers and tags. Expect 0/NULL on modern accounts.

columns.name: item_matrix_id
columns.description: The variant family this SKU belongs to: all sizes/colours of one product share it. 0 (map to NULL) means a standalone item, not a variant. The key to collapsing variant rows into products.

columns.name: manufacturer_id
columns.description: Who MAKES the product (brand). Not the supplier the shop buys from — that is default_vendor_id. 0 when unset.

columns.name: season_id
columns.description: Legacy season grouping. Lightspeed has deprecated Seasons; only older accounts populate it. 0/NULL in practice.

columns.name: default_vendor_id
columns.description: The supplier the shop reorders this item from by default. A plain scalar field, NOT a loadable relation — there is no 'Vendor' load_relations name on Item. An item may have many vendor SKUs (ls_item_vendor_nums) but only one default vendor. 0 when unset.

columns.name: category_name
columns.description: Denormalised leaf name of the category only (e.g. 'Service'). Ambiguous across branches — two different branches can both have a 'Parts'. Prefer category_full_path_name for grouping.

columns.name: category_full_path_name
columns.description: Denormalised slash-delimited path from the tree root (e.g. 'Accessories/Bottles & Cages'). LIKE 'Bikes%' rolls up an entire department, which plain category_id cannot do because items attach at any depth. NULL when uncategorised.

columns.name: manufacturer_name
columns.description: Denormalised brand name. Real data has inconsistent casing and near-duplicate spellings, so UPPER()/TRIM() before grouping across brands or the same brand splits into several rows.

columns.name: tax_class_json
columns.description: Raw tax-class object as returned. Kept as JSON because the ground truth publishes no field table for TaxClass, so no sub-field can be traced to a documented column. Read the rate/name out of it only after probing a live response.

columns.name: note_json
columns.description: Raw note object attached to the item (staff notes; public notes also print on receipts). JSON because Note has no published field table. Usually absent.

columns.name: custom_field_values_json
columns.description: Raw account-defined custom field values. Shape is account-specific and has no published field table, so it stays JSON — treat any key you find as unstable across accounts.

columns.name: attribute_1
columns.description: First variant axis VALUE for a matrix item, conventionally the colour. Meaningless without attribute_name_1, which names the axis. NULL for standalone items (the ItemAttributes subtree is absent).

columns.name: attribute_2
columns.description: Second variant axis value, conventionally the size. NULL for standalone items and for single-axis matrices.

columns.name: attribute_3
columns.description: Third variant axis value; only used by the '3 Attributes' attribute set. Almost always NULL.

columns.name: item_attribute_set_id
columns.description: Which attribute-set definition explains this item's attribute_1/2/3. Documented as a string but it is a numeric FK to ls_item_attribute_sets. NULL/absent for non-variant items.

columns.name: attribute_set_name
columns.description: Denormalised name of the attribute set — one of 'Color/Size', 'Size', 'Color', '3 Attributes'. Tells you how many of the attribute_N columns are meaningful.

columns.name: attribute_name_1
columns.description: Label for variant axis 1 (typically 'Color'). Pair with attribute_1 to render 'Color: Black'. Empty when the set does not use axis 1.
