columns.name: attribute_name_2
columns.description: Label for variant axis 2 (typically 'Size').

columns.name: attribute_name_3
columns.description: Label for variant axis 3 ('Attribute 3'). Rarely populated.

columns.name: ecom_item_ecommerce_id
columns.description: Id of the item's eCommerce info record. Its presence means an eCom record exists at all; NULL means the item was never given web content or dimensions.

columns.name: ecom_long_description
columns.description: Long-form marketing copy for the item. The docs explicitly note the itemECommerce fields are NOT used by Lightspeed eCommerce, so treat this as free-text storage, not as what a webstore renders.

columns.name: ecom_short_description
columns.description: Short marketing blurb. Same caveat: not consumed by Lightspeed eCommerce.

columns.name: weight
columns.description: Item weight. The API publishes no unit — it follows whatever the account entered (lb or kg), so never aggregate weights across an account without confirming the unit. 0 means unset.

columns.name: width
columns.description: Item width, unitless per the API — same unit caveat as weight. 0 means unset, not zero-width.

columns.name: height
columns.description: Item height, unitless per the API. 0 means unset.

columns.name: length
columns.description: Item length, unitless per the API. 0 means unset. This plus width/height/weight is the only place shipping dimensions exist in the catalogue.

columns.name: ecom_list_on_store
columns.description: Whether the item is flagged to be sold online. Documented as not settable in the user interface, so it is often stale or false even on items that are for sale online. Distinct from publish_to_ecom.

columns.name: price
columns.description: TODAY's shelf/register selling price at the Default price level. In a tax-inclusive jurisdiction this INCLUDES tax while default_cost/avg_cost exclude it — mixing them raw inflates apparent margin by the tax rate. This is not what past customers paid; historical prices live on sale lines.

columns.name: msrp
columns.description: Manufacturer's suggested retail price level. 0 means the level was never set (very common), NOT that the item is free — filter msrp > 0 before any discount-versus-RRP comparison or the average collapses.

tables.grain: one item's stock record in one shop. The row with shop_id = 0 is not a shop: it is Lightspeed's account-wide aggregate record for that item.
tables.description: The current stock position per item per shop: quantity on hand, what is sellable, what is on order, and the reorder thresholds. This is a point-in-time snapshot that the API overwrites in place — it is the source of truth for 'how much do we have RIGHT NOW'. It is NOT a history: 'how much stock did we hold in March' cannot be answered here and belongs to the inventory movement log.
tables.additivityAxis: time — qoh/sellable/backorder are levels, never flows, so they must never be summed across dates; additionally never sum real shop rows together with the shop_id = 0 aggregate row, which already contains them
gotchas: shop_id = 0 is documented as an all-shops summary record that Lightspeed maintains per item. VERIFIED LIVE: summing real shop rows AND the 0 row double counts every unit in the account. Whole business: WHERE shop_id = 0. Per shop: WHERE shop_id > 0. Never both in one aggregate.

VERIFIED LIVE: ItemShop responses carry substantial UNDOCUMENTED fields absent from the published field table — averageCost, totalValueFifo, totalValueAvgCost, totalValueNegativeInventory, onLayaway, onSpecialOrder, onWorkorder (the docs spell it onWorkOrder; live responses use onWorkorder), onTransferIn, onTransferOut, lastReceivedCost, lastReceivedLotID, nextFifoLotCost, nextFifoLotID. They are not staged here because they cannot be traced to the ground truth, but stock VALUATION and reservation questions need them: extend this table first if valuation is in scope.
VERIFIED LIVE: averageCost only populates on the shop_id = 0 row; per-shop rows return 0. Use the parent item's avg_cost when you need a cost on every row.
This is a snapshot, not a ledger. There is no as-at date and no history — 'stock on hand last quarter' is unanswerable from this table.
Negative qoh rows are oversells. They subtract from any SUM(qoh * avg_cost), quietly understating stock value; count and report them separately as a hygiene metric.
qoh already includes units reserved against layaways, special orders and workshop jobs, so 'available to promise' is lower than qoh even when sellable is positive.
Archiving an item zeroes its inventory irreversibly, so archived rows showing stock predate a restore or a data import.
reorder_point = 0 means unconfigured. Always add reorder_point > 0 to a reorder list or every zero-stock SKU in the account appears.

columns.name: item_shop_id
columns.description: Primary key of this item-in-shop stock record. Either this or shopID must be supplied when writing an update, which is why it exists at all — analytically it is just a surrogate.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: The item this stock row belongs to. Also available on the parent Item envelope when exploding; joins ls_items.item_id.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: The shop holding the stock — EXCEPT 0, which is documented as a summary record containing the QOH for all shops combined. 0 is a sentinel, not a location and not a null. Whole-business questions use shop_id = 0; per-shop breakdowns use shop_id > 0; using both double counts every unit in the account.

columns.name: qoh
columns.description: Units physically on hand. Positive means stock is available; NEGATIVE is legal and means the shop oversold (sold stock the system did not have) — a data-hygiene signal, not an error to filter away silently. Already includes units promised to layaways, special orders and workshop jobs.

columns.name: sellable
columns.description: Units the POS will let you sell: identical to qoh except it clamps at 0 when qoh is negative. The gap (sellable - qoh) is therefore exactly the size of the negative-inventory problem for that item.

columns.name: backorder
columns.description: Units already committed on a purchase order but not yet received — 'on order' in shop language. Zero or positive only. Incoming stock, so it must not be added to qoh when reporting what is physically present.

columns.name: component_qoh
columns.description: Additional units of this item that could be produced by breaking down or building up boxes/assemblies that are themselves in stock. Zero or positive. It is potential, not physical stock — adding it to qoh double counts the box.

columns.name: component_backorder
columns.description: Additional units obtainable from boxes/assemblies that are currently on order rather than in stock. Doubly notional: potential units from stock that has not arrived. 0 for normal items.

columns.name: reorder_point
columns.description: Threshold: when qoh is at or below this, the item is considered due for reorder in this shop. 0 means no reorder point was configured, NOT 'reorder at zero' — an unfiltered qoh <= reorder_point flags every out-of-stock item in the account.

columns.name: reorder_level
columns.description: Target stock level to reach when reordering: an automatic reorder adds (reorder_level - qoh) units. Suggested order quantity is derived, never stored.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When this stock record last changed. Unlike ls_items.updated_at this DOES move on stock movements, making it the only freshness signal in the catalogue for inventory. It cannot be pushed down when scanning via the Item endpoint, whose timeStamp filter applies to the item record.

columns.name: item_description
columns.description: Denormalised product name from the parent item, so stock rows are readable without a join.

columns.name: item_archived
columns.description: Parent item's archived flag. Archived items were inventory-zeroed at archive time, so any non-zero stock on an archived row is historical noise.

columns.name: item_type
columns.description: Parent item type, carried here because non_inventory rows must be excluded from every stock count and valuation — their quantities are meaningless.
columns.enums: default, non_inventory, serialized, box, serialized_assembly, assembly

columns.name: avg_cost
columns.description: Parent item's account-wide weighted average unit cost, ex tax. Present on every row, which makes qoh * avg_cost the workable stock valuation in this table.

columns.name: category_id
columns.description: Parent item's category. Pushing this down makes category-scoped stock scans dramatically cheaper than filtering after the fact.

columns.name: manufacturer_id
columns.description: Parent item's brand, for brand-level stock rollups without a join.

tables.grain: one price level amount on one item — the unique key is (item_id, use_type_id), not item_id alone.
tables.description: Every configured price level for every item: Default, MSRP, Online and any account-defined level. ls_items.price/msrp cover the two everyday cases; this table exists for the rest and for level-versus-level comparisons. It holds CURRENT prices only — there is no price history and no record of what any customer actually paid.
gotchas: The unique key is (item_id, use_type_id). Joining this table to ls_items without pinning use_type multiplies every item row by the number of price levels and silently inflates every downstream SUM.

VERIFIED LIVE: prices arrive inline on every Item response under the key Prices.ItemPrice[] — the documented load_relations name is 'ItemPrices' but the response key is 'Prices', and no relation request is needed to get them.
VERIFIED LIVE: an amount of 0 means the level was never configured for that item (extremely common for MSRP and Online), not a zero price.
Amounts follow the account's tax-inclusive setting while all cost columns in this domain are ex tax. Never subtract a cost from an amount without dividing out tax first.
There is no price history: this is the current state only. 'When did we last change the price' is unanswerable from the catalogue.

VERIFIED LIVE: the same ItemPrice shape appears inline on ItemMatrix responses, but those family-level amounts are usually 0 because real prices sit on the child items — which is why matrix prices are not staged in this table.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: The item the price belongs to. NOT unique in this table — each item contributes one row per configured level, so an unpinned join to ls_items multiplies item rows by the number of levels.

columns.name: use_type_id
columns.description: Numeric FK to the pricing level definition (ls_price_levels.price_level_id). The stable half of the key: use it for grouping because use_type names can be renamed by the account at any time.

columns.name: use_type
columns.description: Human name of the price level, which also indicates how the level is applied. Documented behaviour: an amount set at this level OVERRIDES the amount that would otherwise be generated dynamically from cost via the level's calculation — so a stored row means someone pinned the price.
columns.enums: Default = the register/shelf selling price; MSRP = manufacturer's suggested retail; Online = eCom/webstore level; plus any account-defined and renameable levels

columns.name: amount
columns.description: The price at this level, in store currency, following the account's tax-inclusive setting (tax-inclusive jurisdictions: it INCLUDES tax, unlike costs which are ex tax). 0 means the level is not set for this item, NOT that it is free — filter amount > 0 before any AVG/MIN price maths.

columns.name: item_description
columns.description: Denormalised product name so price rows are readable without a join.

columns.name: item_archived
columns.description: Parent item's archived flag; filter false to price only the live range.

tables.grain: one component line: the link between one assembly/box item and one of the items it is made from.
tables.description: The bill of materials for box and assembly products — which single items make up a box, and how many of each. It explains where ls_item_shops.component_qoh comes from and lets you cost an assembly from its parts. It is NOT a stock table and NOT a sales table; quantity here is a recipe ratio, never a number of units held.
gotchas: component_group is the type discriminator, not a grouping convenience: 0 = assembly recipe, non-zero (unique per component) = box relationship. Aggregating without splitting on it mixes two different data models.
quantity is units-of-component per ONE parent. It is never a stock quantity and must never be summed as if it were.
Both id columns point at ls_items, so any readable report needs a self-join aliased twice; forgetting to alias silently joins the wrong end.

This table explains ls_item_shops.component_qoh / component_backorder — potential units obtainable by building up or breaking down. Those are potential, not physical, and adding them to qoh double counts the box.
There is no direction flag: whether stock is currently assembled or broken down is not recorded here, only the recipe.

columns.name: item_component_id
columns.description: Primary key of the component line. Surrogate — the meaningful identity is (assembly_item_id, component_item_id, component_group).

columns.name: assembly_item_id
columns.description: The parent: the box or assembly item being built. Joins ls_items.item_id. Its item_type will be box, assembly or serialized_assembly.

columns.name: component_item_id
columns.description: The child: the single item consumed to build the parent. Joins ls_items.item_id. Also the row you would deduct stock from when a box is broken down.

columns.name: quantity
columns.description: How many units of component_item_id it takes to build ONE assembly_item_id. A ratio, not an inventory figure — summing it across rows produces a meaningless number. Divide a box's stock by it to get equivalent singles.

columns.name: component_group
columns.description: Discriminates the two relationship kinds that share this table. Assemblies always have componentGroup = 0; box relationships get a UNIQUE componentGroup per single component. So 0 vs non-zero is how you tell a multi-part assembly recipe from a box/case breakdown, and treating them alike mis-costs both.

tables.grain: one vendor-specific SKU: one item as catalogued by one vendor.
tables.description: The cross-reference between the shop's items and the part numbers its suppliers use, with the per-vendor buy cost when vendor-cost functionality is enabled. This is how you turn an item into something orderable from a specific supplier, and how you compare what different suppliers charge for the same item. An item may appear here many times (one row per vendor) even though it has only one default vendor.
gotchas: An item can have MULTIPLE vendors, so joining this table to ls_items without aggregating multiplies item rows and inflates any SUM over item-level measures.
cost = 0 means the vendor cost was never captured (the feature may be disabled account-wide), not that the item is free. Filter cost > 0 before comparing suppliers.

vendor_sku is the key for purchase orders and supplier price-list matching; it is NOT the same namespace as ls_items.manufacturer_sku, which is the maker's part number. A vendor may relabel a manufacturer part.
Only one vendor is the default (ls_items.default_vendor_id); presence in this table does not mean the shop currently orders from that supplier.

columns.name: item_vendor_num_id
columns.description: Primary key of the item-vendor cross-reference row.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: The shop's item this vendor SKU refers to. Joins ls_items.item_id. Not unique here — one item can be stocked by several vendors.

columns.name: vendor_id
columns.description: The supplier that uses this SKU. Joins the Vendor/supplier domain. Compare with ls_items.default_vendor_id to see whether the shop buys from the cheapest listed source.

columns.name: vendor_sku
columns.description: The vendor's own part number for the item — the string you put on a purchase order. Free text: formats differ per supplier and duplicates across vendors are normal.

columns.name: cost
columns.description: The buy cost from THIS vendor, ex tax. Documented as optional and only meaningful when vendor-cost functionality is enabled; when not supplied Lightspeed stores 0, so 0 means 'not captured', not 'free'. Distinct from ls_items.default_cost (a single item-level figure) and avg_cost (realised average).

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When this cross-reference row was last modified. The freshest available signal of when a supplier's price for the item was last touched.

tables.grain: one matrix — one variant family of items (e.g. one jersey that exists in five sizes).
tables.description: The product-family layer above ls_items: family-level identity, defaults and the attribute set that defines the variant axes. Nothing is ever sold, stocked or priced at this grain — the sellable units are the child rows in ls_items joined by item_matrix_id. Use it to collapse variants into products and to read what the colour/size axes mean.
gotchas: Nothing is sold, stocked or priced at matrix grain. Use this table to GROUP variants, never to MEASURE them — every quantity and amount lives on the child ls_items rows.

VERIFIED LIVE: ItemMatrix responses carry the same Prices.ItemPrice[] shape inline as Item does, but the family-level Default/MSRP amounts are usually 0 because real prices are maintained per variant. That is why matrix prices are not staged here — read prices from the children.
ItemMatrix has no createTime field (Item does). Family age must be approximated from MIN(ls_items.created_at) of its children.
Family-level defaults (default_cost, taxable, category_id, tax_class_id) are seeds, not authority. A child item can diverge from every one of them.

VERIFIED LIVE: the published attribute VALUE lists that appear on live matrix responses (attribute1Values/attribute2Values/attribute3Values) are absent from the ground-truth field table and are not staged; derive the value set with SELECT DISTINCT attribute_1 FROM ls_items instead, which is authoritative anyway.
Archiving a matrix does not guarantee its children are archived — check ls_items.archived when counting the live range.

columns.name: item_matrix_id
columns.description: Primary key of the variant family. ls_items.item_matrix_id points here; ls_images.item_matrix_id attaches family-level photos here.

columns.name: description
columns.description: Family-level product name. Documented composition rule: each child item's description is '<this description> <attribute1> <attribute2> <attribute3>', so this string is the stable prefix for matching every variant.

columns.name: item_type
columns.description: Type default inherited by the family's items. Same enumeration as ls_items.item_type; the authoritative value for stock logic is on the child item, not here.
columns.enums: default, non_inventory, serialized, box, serialized_assembly, assembly

columns.name: serialized
columns.description: True when units in this family carry serial numbers (typical for bike model families). Must be true before item_type can be serialized or serialized_assembly.

columns.name: taxable
columns.description: Whether tax is charged on this family's items. A default; the child item's own flag is what the register applies.

columns.name: default_cost
columns.description: Family-level reorder cost, ex tax, used to seed inventory cost. Frequently 0 because real costs are maintained per variant on the child items.

columns.name: model_year
columns.description: Model year of the family (e.g. 2024). Stored as 0 when unset — map to NULL before filtering by year.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the family is retired. The published doc text says 'Whether this discount is archived', a copy-paste error — it refers to the matrix. Archiving the family does not by itself guarantee every child item is archived; check ls_items too.

columns.name: category_id
columns.description: Category default for the family. 0 when unset. Children may sit in a different category, so category rollups should use the item rows.

columns.name: tax_class_id
columns.description: Tax class default for the family. 0 when unset.

columns.name: department_id
columns.description: Legacy department grouping. Departments were removed as an item organiser; expect 0/NULL on modern accounts.

columns.name: manufacturer_id
columns.description: Brand of the family (who makes it), not the supplier. 0 when unset.

columns.name: season_id
columns.description: Legacy season grouping; Seasons are deprecated by Lightspeed. 0/NULL in practice.

columns.name: default_vendor_id
columns.description: Default supplier for the family. 0 when unset.

columns.name: item_attribute_set_id
columns.description: Which attribute-set definition shapes the family's variant axes (Color/Size, Size, Color, 3 Attributes). Documented as a string but it is a numeric FK to ls_item_attribute_sets. Tells you how many axes the children actually use.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When the matrix record was last modified. There is NO createTime on ItemMatrix (unlike Item), so family age is not directly knowable — approximate it with MIN(created_at) of the child items.

columns.name: category_name
columns.description: Denormalised leaf category name for the family. Ambiguous across branches — prefer the full path.

columns.name: category_full_path_name
columns.description: Denormalised slash-delimited category path for the family; LIKE 'Bikes%' rolls up a department.

columns.name: manufacturer_name
columns.description: Denormalised brand name for the family; same inconsistent-casing caveat as on items.

columns.name: season_name
columns.description: Denormalised season label. Season is a loadable relation on ItemMatrix (unlike on Item) but the feature is deprecated, so expect NULL.

columns.name: attribute_set_name
columns.description: Denormalised attribute-set name: 'Color/Size', 'Size', 'Color' or '3 Attributes'. The quickest way to know whether this family varies on one axis or two.

columns.name: attribute_name_1
columns.description: Label of the family's first variant axis (typically 'Color'); pairs with ls_items.attribute_1 on the children.

columns.name: attribute_name_2
columns.description: Label of the second variant axis (typically 'Size').

columns.name: attribute_name_3
columns.description: Label of the third variant axis; only meaningful for the '3 Attributes' set.

columns.name: tax_class_json
columns.description: Raw tax-class object. JSON because the ground truth publishes no field table for TaxClass — no sub-field can be traced to a documented column.

columns.name: department_json
columns.description: Raw department object for the family. JSON because Department has no published field table, and the organiser itself is deprecated. Expect absent.

columns.name: custom_field_values_json
columns.description: Raw account-defined custom field values on the matrix. Shape is account-specific with no published field table, so it stays JSON.

tables.grain: one attribute-set definition (the schema of a matrix's variant axes).
tables.description: Tiny lookup that names what the attribute1/2/3 slots on items and matrices MEAN — e.g. attribute1 = Color, attribute2 = Size. Without it the variant values are unlabelled strings. Lightspeed restricts the vocabulary to four sets; there are no measures here.
gotchas: A handful of rows at most — join it freely, never push it down.
The set names the AXES, never the values. Which colours and sizes actually exist is only discoverable from DISTINCT attribute_1/attribute_2 on ls_items.
The docs list only 'itemAttributeSetID' as sortable and publish no createTime/timeStamp, so there is no change history for these definitions.
Both referencing fields (Item.ItemAttributes.itemAttributeSetID and ItemMatrix.itemAttributeSetID) are documented with type string; cast before joining or the join silently fails.

columns.name: item_attribute_set_id
columns.description: Primary key. ls_items.item_attribute_set_id and ls_item_matrices.item_attribute_set_id point here (both are documented as strings on those objects but are numeric ids).

columns.name: name
columns.description: Name of the set. Documented as a closed vocabulary — 'Color/Size', 'Size', 'Color', '3 Attributes' are the only allowed values for now, so it is safe to branch on but not to treat as extensible.
columns.enums: Color/Size; Size; Color; 3 Attributes

columns.name: attribute_name_1
columns.description: Label for the first axis — documented as 'Color' or the generic 'Attribute 1'. Read alongside an item's attribute_1 value to render a variant properly.

columns.name: attribute_name_2
columns.description: Label for the second axis — documented as 'Size' or 'Attribute 2'. Empty for single-axis sets such as 'Color'.

columns.name: attribute_name_3
columns.description: Label for the third axis — 'Attribute 3'. Only populated for the '3 Attributes' set.

tables.grain: one configured item fee definition.
tables.description: The configuration list of fixed-amount surcharges that attach to item categories — tyre recycling levies, e-bike environmental fees and similar. It is CONFIGURATION ONLY: money actually charged appears as its own sale line with lineType 'item_fee' (or 'item_fee_refund'), parented to the item's line via parentSaleLineID. Fee revenue questions belong on sale lines, never here.
gotchas: This is configuration, not revenue. A fee that was actually charged is a SALE LINE with lineType 'item_fee' (refunds: 'item_fee_refund') whose parentSaleLineID points at the item's line — so fee income is measured on sale lines, and this table only tells you what the fee is called and what it should cost.

Documented disambiguation rule: to tell an item being refunded from a fee attached to a refunded item, check for a NON-ZERO parentSaleLineID together with a lineType that is not 'item_fee'. Getting this backwards double counts refunds.
VERIFIED LIVE: the modified timestamp really is lowercase 'timestamp' on this endpoint, unlike 'timeStamp' everywhere else in the domain.
discountable and nonRefundable are documented as providing no functionality today. Treat them as reserved, not as behaviour.
calculationMethod has exactly one legal value (fixed_amount); a percentage fee cannot be represented.
VERIFIED LIVE: a real store may have zero fees configured — an empty result is normal, not a failed extract.

columns.name: item_fee_id
columns.description: Primary key of the fee definition.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Fee name as shown at the register and on the receipt line. The only way to recognise the fee's sale lines, since sale lines carry no itemFeeID.

columns.name: calculation_method
columns.description: How the fee amount is derived. Currently only fixed_amount exists, so fee_value is always a flat per-item charge — do not build percentage logic against this field.
columns.enums: fixed_amount = a flat monetary amount per item (the only method Lightspeed currently supports)

columns.name: fee_value
columns.description: The monetary amount of the fee in store currency. Whether it is tax-inclusive follows the account's tax setting and the taxable flag below.

columns.name: taxable
columns.description: True when tax is charged ON the fee itself. Misreading it shifts the tax base on every transaction that carries the fee, which is why it is load bearing despite being configuration.

columns.name: discountable
columns.description: Nominally whether the fee can be discounted, but documented as currently providing NO extra functionality. Do not build logic on it — it does not affect what the register does.

columns.name: non_refundable
columns.description: Nominally whether the fee can be refunded; documented as currently not in use. Note the inverted naming: true would mean NOT refundable. Non-functional today.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the fee is retired and can no longer be used within a transaction. Historical sale lines from before archiving still exist, so archived fees still appear in past revenue.

columns.name: created_at
columns.description: When the fee was configured — the earliest date its sale lines can appear.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When the fee was last updated. Note the raw API field is lowercase 'timestamp' on this endpoint alone; every other object in this domain uses 'timeStamp'. A case-sensitive extractor written for the rest of the domain silently returns NULL here.

columns.name: item_fee_categories_json
columns.description: Raw list of the item categories the fee attaches to. Kept as JSON because the ground truth publishes no field table for ItemFeeCategories; the category ids inside can be matched against ls_categories only after probing a live response.

tables.grain: one product image, attached to EITHER an item or a matrix (exactly one of the two).
tables.description: Product photo metadata hosted on Lightspeed's Cloudinary account. Answers image-coverage questions (which products have no photo) and supplies the pieces needed to build a display URL. It stores metadata, not image bytes, and the docs warn the endpoint must not be used as an image host for external websites — traffic is monitored and may be billed.
gotchas: Matrix-level images cover every variant in the family. 'Products without a photo' must check for an image on the item AND on its item_matrix_id, or every matrix product is wrongly reported as imageless.

VERIFIED LIVE: responses carry undocumented fields absent from the published field table — baseImageURL, size (bytes), originalFilename, createTime and timeStamp. They are not staged here, but baseImageURL matters: the working URL is baseImageURL || publicID || '.jpg' (base observed as https://res.cloudinary.com/lightspeed-retail/image/upload/), and a Cloudinary transform segment may be inserted between 'upload/' and the public id, e.g. .../upload/w_300/<publicID>.jpg.
Because createTime/timeStamp are not in the published field table, this table has no timestamps at all — image freshness is not answerable from the documented surface.

The docs explicitly warn this endpoint is not an alternative to image hosting for external sites; traffic is monitored and additional charges may apply. Build URLs for display, never proxy bulk traffic.
For item/matrix work the docs point to the dedicated Item Image and ItemMatrix Image endpoints; this generic controller handles both data and metadata.

columns.name: image_id
columns.description: Primary key of the image record.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: The single item this photo belongs to, or NULL/0 when the photo is attached at matrix level instead. Exactly one of item_id and item_matrix_id is meaningful on any row.

columns.name: item_matrix_id
columns.description: The variant family this photo belongs to, or NULL/0 when it is attached to a single item. A matrix-level photo implicitly covers every variant in the family, which is why coverage checks must test both columns.

columns.name: description
columns.description: Caption or alt text for the image. Usually empty in real data; do not rely on it for search.

columns.name: filename
columns.description: Original filename of the upload. Its extension indicates the source format, which is not necessarily the format Cloudinary serves.

columns.name: ordering
columns.description: Display sequence among a product's images. The lowest ordering is the primary/hero photo — ties are possible, so break them with image_id for determinism.

columns.name: public_id
columns.description: The Cloudinary public id used to retrieve the image. It is not a URL by itself: it must be concatenated onto the Cloudinary base URL with a file extension to resolve.

tables.grain: one serial-number record — one physical serialized unit, whether it came from stock or was logged as a customer's own property.
tables.description: The register of serialized units: bikes, frames, e-bikes and anything else tracked by serial number. It is the place to answer 'what units does this customer own' and 'who owns serial X'. Rows either link to a catalogue item (sold from stock) or stand alone with a free-text description (a customer's own machine logged at the service desk).
gotchas: Serials are owned by items OR customers (documented). A NULL item_id with a populated customer_id is a customer's own machine, not a data error, and it is the normal case at a service-led store.
VERIFIED LIVE: serial is very often an empty string; identity lives in description. Never require a non-empty serial when listing a customer's units.

VERIFIED LIVE: one customer can accumulate junk placeholder rows ('Service', 'Gen Serv') left by old workflows, so COUNT(*) per customer overstates units owned — eyeball descriptions before quoting a number.
No server-side filters are documented for this endpoint, so customer and serial lookups scan pages. Acceptable at small-store volume; plan differently for large accounts.
The record does not track possession or status — there is no 'sold', 'in for service' or 'returned' flag. sale_line_id being NULL is the only hint the unit never went through the POS.

columns.name: serialized_id
columns.description: Primary key of the serial record.

columns.name: serial
columns.description: The serial number stamped on the unit. Frequently an EMPTY STRING in real data because staff logged the machine without reading the number — filtering serial <> '' silently drops most of a customer's units. Match case-insensitively and trimmed.

columns.name: description
columns.description: Free-text identity used when the record is NOT connected to a catalogue item — typically a customer's own bike ('black planet x'). For service-heavy stores this is the only identity most rows have.

columns.name: color_name
columns.description: Colour of the unit as typed by staff. Free text, often empty, unrelated to the matrix attribute vocabulary.

columns.name: size_name
columns.description: Size of the unit (frame size for bikes) as typed by staff. Free text, often empty; not the matrix Size attribute.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: The catalogue item this serial is an instance of, when the unit was sold from stock. Stored as 0 (map to NULL) for customer-owned units logged free-text — which is the MAJORITY of rows in service-heavy stores, so an inner join to ls_items quietly hides most customer machines.

columns.name: sale_line_id
columns.description: The sale line where this unit was sold, or 0/NULL if it never went through the POS. Join it to recover the sale date, price and salesperson for the specific physical unit.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: The customer who owns this unit. The key for 'what bikes does customer X own'. Personal data — treat under the same handling rules as the customer record.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When the record last changed. A rough proxy for when the unit was last touched in the system (sold, serviced, re-tagged), not when it was manufactured or acquired.

tables.grain: one tag in the account's tag vocabulary.
tables.description: The list of tags staff can attach to items and matrices for ad-hoc grouping. It is the VOCABULARY only — which items carry which tag is not modellable from the documented surface, because the linking object (TagRelations) has no published field table. Use it to see what labelling conventions the account uses, not to segment products.
gotchas: The item-to-tag EDGE is not modelled. Item exposes TagRelations / TagRelations.Tag as load_relations but the ground truth publishes no field table for TagRelation, so 'which items are tagged X' is unanswerable from this layer — only 'what tags exist'.
VERIFIED LIVE: the tag relation on Item returns a denormalised shape unsuited to columns, which is the practical reason the edge is not staged.
VERIFIED LIVE: live Tag responses also carry an undocumented readOnly flag (system-managed tags); it is absent from the published field table so it is not staged.
VERIFIED LIVE: tag names contain staff typos ('size:universall'); match loosely and never treat the vocabulary as controlled.
The docs publish no timestamps on Tag, so there is no way to tell when a tag was created or last used.

columns.name: tag_id
columns.description: Primary key of the tag.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The tag text itself. Free text entered by staff, so typos and near-duplicates are normal; VERIFIED LIVE stores often adopt a 'group:value' convention (color:black, size:318mm, year:2018) that the API does not enforce or parse.

tables.grain: one tag group name for the account.
tables.description: Helper list of the tag groups configured on the account. The docs publish NO field table for this object — the two keys here were harvested from the documented example payload — so it should be treated as low-confidence until probed live. Useful only for interpreting the 'group:value' convention seen in tag names.
gotchas: This object has NO published field table. Both keys come from the documented example payload only — verify the real shape against a live response before depending on it.
No id field is published, so the name is the primary key and is inherently unstable across renames.
The docs' 'sortable fields' line for this endpoint is a scrape of the page footer (logo/copyright/privacy links), not a real field list — ignore it entirely.
This is a read helper: it lists groups for the current account and carries no counts, no timestamps and no membership.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The tag group's name. The only usable key: no numeric id is published for tag groups, so renaming a group breaks any stored reference. Undocumented type — inferred as a string from the example payload.

tables.grain: one season label.
tables.description: Legacy organiser: season labels that older accounts used to group items. Lightspeed has DEPRECATED seasons — the documentation states items are now organised with Categories, Manufacturers and Tags only, with Season and Department removed. Staged solely because ls_items.season_id and ls_item_matrices.season_id still exist and must resolve to something.
gotchas: Deprecated feature. VERIFIED LIVE: a modern account returns ZERO rows — an empty result is the expected outcome, not a failed extract or a reason to retry.
Season is not a valid load_relations name on Item (though it is on ItemMatrix), so an item's season can only be resolved through this table by id.
Any analysis segmented by season is account-specific and will not port; use categories, manufacturers or tags instead.

columns.name: season_id
columns.description: Primary key of the season label. ls_items.season_id and ls_item_matrices.season_id point here; on modern accounts they are 0 and this table is empty.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The season's label text. The published description reads 'The name/description of the department' — a copy-paste error in the docs; it is the season's name.

tables.grain: one manufacturer (brand).
tables.description: The brand list: who MAKES the products. Explicitly distinct from vendors/suppliers, who are who the shop BUYS from — the docs note every item can have one manufacturer but multiple vendors. A dimension table with no measures; brand performance is computed by joining items to sale lines.
gotchas: Manufacturer is NOT supplier. The docs are explicit: manufacturers are separate from vendors, an item has one manufacturer but can have many vendors (see ls_item_vendor_nums). Reporting 'spend by brand' as if it were 'spend by supplier' is a common and invisible error.

VERIFIED LIVE: duplicate/near-duplicate brand rows exist (same brand entered twice with different casing or spelling). Sanity-check COUNT(DISTINCT UPPER(TRIM(name))) against COUNT(*) before quoting a brand count.
This table has no measures at all — every brand ranking requires joining through ls_items to the sales domain.

columns.name: manufacturer_id
columns.description: Primary key of the brand. ls_items.manufacturer_id and ls_item_matrices.manufacturer_id point here.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Brand name. VERIFIED LIVE: real accounts have inconsistent casing (VITTORIA vs Elite) and occasional duplicate rows for the same brand — group on UPPER(TRIM(name)) or a single brand splits across several ids.

columns.name: created_at
columns.description: When the brand was added to the account. A reasonable proxy for when the shop started ranging that brand — earlier than any of its items' created_at.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When the brand record was last modified (typically a rename). Does not move when the brand's items change.

tables.grain: one category node in the item category tree.
tables.description: The hierarchical category tree used to organise items, structured like a directory. Items attach to exactly one node at ANY depth, and the tree is stored as a nested set (leftNode/rightNode) with a precomputed slash-delimited path. Use full_path_name for rollups; it is the only reliable way to aggregate a whole branch.
gotchas: Items attach to ONE node at any depth. Grouping items by a parent category id misses everything filed on its children — roll up with full_path_name LIKE 'Parent/%' OR full_path_name = 'Parent', or with the nested-set bounds.
name alone is ambiguous across branches; group and display by full_path_name.
nodeDepth is documented as a string type even though it holds an integer. Cast it or ordering is lexicographic (10 before 2).
left_node/right_node are renumbered whenever the tree is edited. They are correct for subtree queries at read time but must never be cached as identifiers.
The tree is small (tens of rows). Join it freely; there is no benefit to pushdown here.
Only the Parent relation is loadable, so a full ancestor chain needs either a recursive CTE on parent_id or string work on full_path_name.

columns.name: category_id
columns.description: Primary key of the node. ls_items.category_id and ls_item_matrices.category_id point here.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The node's OWN name only, not its path (e.g. 'Service'). Ambiguous across branches — several branches can each contain a 'Parts' — so grouping by name silently merges unrelated categories.

columns.name: full_path_name
columns.description: Slash-delimited path from the root to this node (e.g. 'Workshop/Service'). The standard rollup key: LIKE 'Bikes%' selects an entire subtree, which category_id alone cannot do because items attach at any depth. Precomputed by Lightspeed, so it goes stale only when the tree is reshuffled.

columns.name: parent_id
columns.description: The node directly above this one. 0 (map to NULL) marks a top-level category. Recursive CTEs walk this; for a single-query subtree filter, full_path_name is cheaper.

columns.name: node_depth
columns.description: How many ancestors the node has: 0 = top level, 1 = one parent, and so on. Documented with type string — cast before numeric comparison. Equals the number of '/' separators in full_path_name.

columns.name: left_node
columns.description: Nested-set left bound. A node's descendants all have left_node strictly between this node's left_node and right_node — the O(1) subtree test. Renumbered wholesale when the tree is edited, so never persist it as a key.

columns.name: right_node
columns.description: Nested-set right bound, the closing partner of left_node. (right_node - left_node - 1) / 2 gives the descendant count without a join.

columns.name: created_at
columns.description: When the node was created.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When the node was last modified. Tree reshuffles renumber left/right bounds across MANY nodes at once, so a burst of identical updated_at values means a restructure, not real editing.

tables.grain: one account option: a name/value pair the account has turned on.
tables.description: The account's feature switches as name/value strings. It matters to this domain because account-level settings — not the item record — decide how catalogue numbers must be read (for example whether prices carry tax, or whether vendor-cost functionality is enabled at all). The docs enumerate no option names or values, so any specific key must be discovered from a live response.
gotchas: The docs list 'optionID' as a sortable field but publish NO optionID in the field table. Do not assume such a column exists; key on name.
Values are strings regardless of their semantic type. Comparing value directly in a boolean context is always true.

The docs describe this only as 'options that the account has turned on' and enumerate no names or values — every option key you depend on must be confirmed against a live account, and may differ between accounts.

This table is the documented home of account-level behaviour switches. Behaviour that changes how catalogue money must be read (tax-inclusive pricing, vendor cost functionality) is account-level, but the ground truth does not name the specific options that control it — do not guess key names.
No timestamps are published, so option changes cannot be dated.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The option's identifier. The only available key: no numeric id is published for Option, so a renamed option breaks any stored reference. The set of legal names is not documented anywhere in the ground truth.

columns.name: value
columns.description: The option's value, always delivered as a string even when it represents a boolean or a number. Cast explicitly and never rely on truthiness — '0' and 'false' are both non-empty strings.

tables.grain: one price level definition on the account.
tables.description: The definitions behind the price levels that ls_item_prices rows reference: their names, whether they are archived, their type, and the calculation parameters used to derive prices from cost. Configuration only — no amounts live here; the per-item amounts are in ls_item_prices.
gotchas: The docs' sortable-fields line for this endpoint reads 'orderLineID, name' — orderLineID is not a PriceLevel field, so that is a documentation copy-paste error. Do not attempt to sort by it.
The endpoint path in the docs is misspelt for the single read ('/PriceLeve/{priceLevelID}'); use the plural collection endpoint and filter, or expect a 404.
VERIFIED LIVE: on a real account the level ids ran 1 = Default, 2 = MSRP, 3 = Online. These are ACCOUNT-SPECIFIC — never hardcode them; resolve names through this table.
canBeArchived is documented as having no effect when set; it describes a constraint, it does not enforce one.

No amounts here. A price level with a calculation but no per-item override still produces a price at the register — absence of a row in ls_item_prices does not mean the item is unpriced at that level.

columns.name: price_level_id
columns.description: Primary key of the price level. ls_item_prices.use_type_id is documented as the foreign key for the pricing level and resolves here.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Display name of the level (Default, MSRP, Online, or an account-defined label). Renameable, so never key logic on the string — use price_level_id.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the level is retired. Archived levels can still appear on existing ls_item_prices rows, so an archived level does not mean the amounts vanished.

columns.name: can_be_archived
columns.description: Whether Lightspeed permits archiving this level — false on built-in levels such as Default. Documented as having NO effect when set, so it is a read-only capability hint, not a control.

columns.name: type
columns.description: The kind of price level. Documented as an enumeration but the ground truth publishes no member list, so treat observed values as account-specific until confirmed against a live response.
columns.enums: documented as an enum with no published members

columns.name: calculation_json
columns.description: Raw parameters used to derive a price from cost (markup/margin rules). Kept as JSON because the ground truth publishes no field table for Calculation. It explains the documented ItemPrice behaviour: a stored amount OVERRIDES the amount this calculation would otherwise generate — so an item with no explicit amount is priced by these rules, not by a NULL.

tables.grain: one product entry in one configured vendor catalogue.
tables.description: What the shop's suppliers say is available to ORDER: supplier part numbers, tiered costs, bulk price breaks, MSRPs, availability status and supersession. This is the supplier's world, not the shop's — it is neither inventory nor sales, and there is no item_id. Match to the shop's catalogue by barcode or manufacturer part number. A POST here imports an entry and creates a real Item.
gotchas: This is what COULD be ordered, not what the shop owns or sold. There is no item_id and no sales measure — link to the shop's catalogue by upc/ean/ean2 or manufacturer_number, compared AS TEXT so leading zeros survive.
Costs and MSRPs are in the CATALOGUE's own currency, which is frequently not the store's. Never combine them with store revenue or cost without stating the conversion.
cost is per ORDER UNIT. Divide by retail_unit to get a per-sellable-unit cost, or pack items look far more expensive than they are.
0 in any cost tier, break price or msrp means 'not published', not free. Filter > 0 before averaging or ranking.

Vendor catalogues are large (tens of thousands of rows). Only catalogVendorID is a documented server-side filter; targeted text search lives on the separate Catalog/Search.json endpoint, which is not modelled here. Keep queries narrow or expect long scans.

Queries are limited to the account's currently configured catalogues unless catalogVendorID is specified explicitly — an empty result may mean the catalogue is not configured, not that the product does not exist.
POST is destructive-adjacent: creating against a catalogVendorItemID IMPORTS the entry and creates a real Item in the account. This table must be treated as read-only in any analytic pipeline.

VERIFIED LIVE: live responses also carry timeStamp and catalogMasterID, which are absent from the published field table (the docs even list timeStamp as sortable while publishing no such field). They are not staged here for that reason — so this table has no freshness column other than last_price_change.
last_qoh is the VENDOR's stock, with no as-at date. It answers 'can I get it', never 'do I have it'.

columns.name: catalog_vendor_item_id
columns.description: Primary key of the catalogue entry. Also the id you POST to import the entry and create an Item in the account — so it is a write handle, not just an analytic key.

columns.name: catalog_vendor_id
columns.description: Which vendor CATALOGUE the entry belongs to. This is a catalogue-service id, NOT the account's own vendor/supplier id — joining it to the supplier domain produces silently wrong attributions. Unless specified, queries are limited to the catalogues currently configured for the account.

columns.name: vendor_number
columns.description: The part number the VENDOR assigns — what goes on a purchase order to that supplier. Join it to ls_item_vendor_nums.vendor_sku.

columns.name: manufacturer_number
columns.description: The part number the MANUFACTURER assigns. The most reliable key for matching a catalogue entry to ls_items.manufacturer_sku, because it survives changing supplier.

columns.name: description
columns.description: Name/description of the product as the vendor writes it. Will not match the shop's own item description; do not use it as a join key.

columns.name: category
columns.description: The VENDOR's suggested category as free text (e.g. 'Trunk Racks'). It is not a node in the shop's tree and does not join ls_categories.

columns.name: brand
columns.description: Brand of the product per the catalogue. Compare against ls_manufacturers.name for range-gap analysis, with the same casing caveats.

columns.name: model
columns.description: Model designation; the docs note it is usually a year. Overlaps confusingly with the separate 'year' field, which is also a model year — expect one or the other to be populated, not both.

columns.name: year
columns.description: Model year of the item as text (not a number, so no arithmetic or range filters without casting). Often empty; see also 'model'.

columns.name: upc
columns.description: Universal Product Code. The other reliable join key to ls_items.upc — compare as TEXT, since leading zeros are significant and numeric casting corrupts the match.

columns.name: ean
columns.description: International Article Number for the entry; the international counterpart of upc.

columns.name: ean2
columns.description: An alternate EAN. Its existence means a barcode match must test upc, ean AND ean2 before concluding the shop does not stock the product.

columns.name: color_name
columns.description: Colour as published by the vendor. Free text — unrelated to matrix attribute vocabularies, so do not expect it to match ls_items.attribute_1.

columns.name: size_name
columns.description: Size as published by the vendor. Same caveat: free text, not the matrix Size attribute.

columns.name: retail_unit
columns.description: How many SELLABLE units come per order unit (e.g. inner tubes supplied in boxes of 50). Unit cost per sellable item is cost / retail_unit — ignoring it overstates unit cost by the pack size, which is the single most expensive mistake in this table.

columns.name: unit_of_measurement
columns.description: How multiple quantities are grouped for ordering — EA, box, pair. The label that explains retail_unit.

columns.name: cost
columns.description: Base cost per ORDER UNIT from the vendor, in the CATALOGUE's own currency (which may not be the store's). Never compare it to store costs or revenue without both converting currency and dividing by retail_unit.

columns.name: cost_level_2
columns.description: First discounted cost tier (a dealer-terms tier, not a volume break). 0 means no tier published, not free.

columns.name: cost_level_3
columns.description: Second discounted cost tier. 0 means not published.

columns.name: cost_level_4
columns.description: Final discounted cost tier — the best published terms. 0 means not published.

columns.name: msrp
columns.description: Manufacturer's suggested retail price per the catalogue, in the catalogue's currency. Compare to ls_items.price only after currency conversion and after accounting for tax-inclusive store pricing.

columns.name: break_qty
columns.description: Order quantity at which the first bulk price break applies. 0 = no break published.

columns.name: break_price
columns.description: Unit price once at least break_qty is ordered. Documented as the price for items ABOVE breakQty — a step function, not a discount percentage.

columns.name: break_qty_2
columns.description: Second bulk break quantity. 0 = none published.

columns.name: break_price_2
columns.description: Unit cost at the second break quantity. The docs call it the 'cost of breakQty2' — it is a per-unit figure at that tier, not a line total.

columns.name: break_qty_3
columns.description: Third bulk break quantity. 0 = none published.

columns.name: break_price_3
columns.description: Unit cost at the third break quantity.

columns.name: status
columns.description: The vendor's lifecycle status for the entry. VERIFIED LIVE: 'current' is the common value; anything else generally signals a discontinued or superseded line, which is when replacement becomes meaningful.

columns.name: replacement
columns.description: Vendor part number of the suggested successor when this entry is superseded. A pointer into vendor_number within the same catalogue — the supersession chain can be walked by self-joining.

columns.name: replacement_description
columns.description: Description of the suggested replacement. VERIFIED LIVE: often a terse marker such as 'SUBSTITUTE' rather than a product name, so it is not a substitute for looking the replacement part number up.

columns.name: last_price_change
columns.description: When the vendor last changed pricing on this entry. Documented as a date, but VERIFIED LIVE the API sends a full datetime — parse as a timestamp. The freshest signal of supplier cost inflation.

columns.name: last_qoh
columns.description: Last reported quantity on hand AT THE VENDOR's warehouse — not in the shop. Staleness is not published and there is no as-at date, so treat it as a hint about availability, never as a stock figure.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the catalogue entry itself is archived. Independent of ls_items.archived — the shop may still stock a product the vendor has retired.

columns.name: catalog_vendor_json
columns.description: Raw catalogue-owner object. Kept as JSON because the ground truth publishes no field table for CatalogVendor. VERIFIED LIVE: it arrives inline without requesting the relation and carries a human-readable catalogue name.

tables.grain: one inventory change event — one item's stock level changing in one shop, for one reason, at one moment
tables.description: The inventory movement ledger: every stock change with why it happened (sale, purchase-order receive, transfer, manual adjustment, stocktake correction, refund, auto-add, bulk import) and who caused it. This is the ONLY dated, historical view of stock movement in the R-Series API and the table to reach for when reconciling 'where did the stock go'. It is read-only and it is NOT a stock-level table: current on-hand lives on ItemShop (ls_inventory in the catalogue domain), and units-sold questions belong on sale lines.
gotchas: cost_change is the item's NEW unit cost after the event, not a delta, despite the name. qoh_change is the only column in this table you may sum.

VERIFIED LIVE: enormous volume — roughly one row per unit movement since the store opened. Never scan unfiltered; push down itemID, shopID or a createTime range. The bike deployment pushes createTime/itemID/shopID successfully even though the docs advertise only inventoryLogID and itemID as sortable.
VERIFIED LIVE: item_id and shop_id come back as 0, not null, on events with no item/shop (cancelled special orders observed). Treat 0 as NULL or inner joins silently drop those rows.

VERIFIED LIVE: reason values are internal method names ('createAndRemoveInventoryForTransaction' is an ordinary sale). Classify movements on the document FK columns (sale_id / order_id / transfer_id / inventory_count_id / vendor_return_id / item_import_id), which are effectively mutually exclusive, and use reason only as a sub-label.

Units-sold and revenue questions belong on sale lines. A single sale's deduction can be split across several rows here, and non_inventory items (labour, services) never appear at all, so this table under-reports 'what we sold'.
Stocktake shrinkage = rows where inventory_count_id IS NOT NULL AND qoh_change < 0. Manual shrinkage = automated = false with all document FKs null.

There is no balance column. Running stock = SUM(qoh_change) OVER (ORDER BY created_at, inventory_log_id) per item+shop, and it will NOT tie back to today's on-hand if items were archived (archiving zeroes inventory) or if a bulk import reset levels.
Read-only endpoint: Lightspeed writes these rows, no client ever can. An event missing from here did not happen through a documented inventory path.
This log has no aggregate row per item. Unlike ItemShop where shopID 0 is the all-shops total, here shop_id 0 means unattributed — do not filter it out of whole-business totals.

columns.name: inventory_log_id
columns.description: Unique id of the movement event. Monotonically ascending with time, so it is the correct tiebreaker when two movements share a created_at to the second.

columns.name: created_at
columns.description: When the stock change happened, store-local time. The real event clock of this table — always range-filter on it. VERIFIED LIVE: usable as a server-side pushdown filter even though the docs list only inventoryLogID and itemID as sortable.

columns.name: qoh_change
columns.description: Units added (positive) or removed (negative) by this event. The ONLY summable measure in this table. Rows with qoh_change = 0 exist (cost-only corrections, cancelled reservations) so filter qoh_change <> 0 when counting real movements.

columns.name: cost_change
columns.description: Despite the '-Change' name this is NOT a delta: documented as 'the updated unit cost for the Item', i.e. the item's unit cost AFTER this event, ex tax, in store currency. SUM() of it is meaningless. Contrast ls_inventory_count_reconciles.cost_change, which uses the same name for a genuine value delta.

columns.name: automated
columns.description: true when Lightspeed itself made the change (a sale deducting stock, a PO receive posting); false when a human typed an adjustment. automated = false with every document FK null is the signature of 'someone edited stock by hand' — the first place to look for shrinkage.

columns.name: reason
columns.description: Machine-named cause of the change. These are internal method names, not a tidy business enum, and the vocabulary differs by account — GROUP BY reason to discover what exists before hard-coding a filter. Classify movements on the document FK columns first and use reason only to sub-classify.
columns.enums: Documented families: transfers, manual adjustments, purchase orders, refunds, auto-adds, inventory-count. VERIFIED LIVE values include 'createAndRemoveInventoryForTransaction' (a sale consuming stock) and 'cancelSpecialOrder' (a reservation released, usually qoh_change = 0).

columns.name: caused_negative
columns.description: true when this specific event pushed the item's on-hand below zero in that shop — the exact moment an oversell happened. A data-hygiene flag, not a movement measure: never sum or net it against qoh_change.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Employee who made or triggered the change. The accountability column for adjustment and shrinkage questions. 0/NULL on purely system-generated rows, so absence does not mean 'unknown staff member', it means 'no staff member'.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: Item whose stock changed. Joins the catalogue item table. VERIFIED LIVE: arrives as 0 rather than null on non-item events (cancelled special orders observed) — normalise 0 to NULL or an inner join to the catalogue silently deletes those rows from your result.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: Shop where the change happened; 0/NULL means unattributed. Do NOT carry over the ItemShop convention where shopID 0 is the account-wide aggregate row — this log has no aggregate rows, so summing every row here is correct whereas summing every ItemShop row double counts.

columns.name: order_id
columns.description: Purchase order whose receiving caused the change. A supplier PO id from the purchasing domain — never a sale id, despite 'order' being the retail word for a customer order in other systems. Non-null with positive qoh_change = goods inwards.

columns.name: transfer_id
columns.description: Inter-shop transfer that caused the change. One transfer produces at least two rows at different times: a negative at the origin shop when sent and a positive at the destination when received. Netting them to zero across shops is expected, not an error.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: Sale that caused the change. Set for both directions — a sale consuming stock (negative) and a refund returning it (positive) — so read the sign of qoh_change, not the presence of this id, to tell them apart.

columns.name: inventory_count_id
columns.description: Stocktake that caused the change. Non-null rows are count corrections and are the raw material of a shrinkage report. There is no InventoryCount header object anywhere in the R-Series inventory docs, so this id is groupable but not resolvable to a count's name, shop or date.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: Customer associated with the change — set on special-order and layaway reservation movements. Joins the customer table; personal data, so treat aggregate-only unless the question is explicitly about one named customer.

columns.name: vendor_return_id
columns.description: Vendor return (RMA) that caused the change: stock sent back to a supplier, so qoh_change is normally negative. No VendorReturn object is documented in this domain, so treat it as an opaque grouping id rather than a joinable key.

columns.name: item_import_id
columns.description: Bulk item import that caused the change — a spreadsheet load setting stock levels. Big clusters of rows sharing one item_import_id are data migrations, not trading activity; exclude them from shrinkage, receiving and movement analysis or a single import will dwarf a year of real movement.

tables.grain: one item within one inventory count (the system-vs-physical rollup for that item/count pair)
tables.description: The scoreboard of a stocktake: for each item in a count, what the system thought was on hand (calc_qoh) versus what people physically found (counted_qoh). This is where variance and count-accuracy questions are answered. It is auto-maintained and read-only, it is NOT the individual count entries (ls_inventory_count_items) and it is NOT proof the books were adjusted — only a reconcile moves stock.
tables.additivityAxis: inventory_count_id / time — calc_qoh and counted_qoh are stock LEVELS restated by each count, so never sum them across counts for the same item. Their difference (counted_qoh - calc_qoh) is a delta and may be summed freely.
gotchas: Two lookalike quantities with opposite meanings: calc_qoh is what the SYSTEM thought, counted_qoh is what HUMANS found. Variance = counted_qoh - calc_qoh; negative is shrinkage. Getting them the wrong way round flips every shrinkage report's sign.
calc_qoh is frozen at the last count entry for that item, not at reconcile time and not now. A count left open for weeks accumulates drift, so a large variance can be timing rather than loss.
counted_qoh is already the SUM of the count-item entries. Joining ls_inventory_count_items and summing qty alongside counted_qoh double counts the physical side.
Never sum calc_qoh or counted_qoh across counts for the same item — each count restates a level. Summing the variance across counts IS valid, because a difference of two levels is a delta.
A row here does not mean the books moved. Variance becomes real stock and real money only when a reconcile posts (ls_inventory_count_reconciles); calc rows for un-reconciled counts are open findings.

There is no InventoryCount header object in the R-Series inventory documentation, so inventory_count_id cannot be resolved to a count name, shop or date. If you need the shop, get it from the resulting ls_inventory_logs rows for the same inventory_count_id.

columns.name: inventory_count_calc_id
columns.description: Unique id of this item's rollup within a count. Surrogate only — the meaningful key is (inventory_count_id, item_id).

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Modified date/time of this rollup: the last time a count entry was recorded for THIS item in THIS count. A per-item watermark inside the count, not the count's start date, not its end date and not the reconcile date.

columns.name: calc_qoh
columns.description: What the system believed the business should have in stock — the 'book' side of the variance. Frozen at the moment the last count entry landed for this item, so stock that moved between counting and reading this number is not reflected. Can be negative if the item was already oversold.

columns.name: counted_qoh
columns.description: The physical amount counted — the sum of every ls_inventory_count_items.qty entry for this item in this count. The 'physical' side of the variance. Zero here means counted-and-found-none only if a count entry exists; an item never scanned may still show 0.

columns.name: inventory_count_id
columns.description: The stocktake this rollup belongs to. Groupable but not resolvable: no InventoryCount header object is documented, so the count's name, shop, status and date are unavailable in this domain.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: The item this rollup is for. Joins the catalogue item table for description, category and cost so variance can be valued.

tables.grain: one physical counting act — one item counted once by one employee at one moment (counting the same item three times creates three rows)
tables.description: The keystroke-level record of a stocktake: each quantity an employee entered, when, for which item. This is the audit trail behind a count and the only place with a real per-entry event time and a named counter. It is NOT the per-item total (that is ls_inventory_count_calcs.counted_qoh) and its quantities are observations, never stock movements.
gotchas: One row per counting ACT, not per item. An item counted at three shelf locations has three rows; the item's total for the count is SUM(qty), which is exactly what ls_inventory_count_calcs.counted_qoh already holds.
qty is an observation, not a delta. It never belongs in an inventory-movement sum and it is not comparable with ls_inventory_logs.qoh_change.

No shop column: the shop is a property of the count, and no InventoryCount header object is documented. If you need the location, resolve it from the ls_inventory_logs rows carrying the same inventory_count_id.

Duplicate entries for the same item are normal (recount, second aisle) — but a duplicate entered by mistake silently inflates counted_qoh and therefore manufactures a positive variance. GROUP BY item with COUNT(*) > 1 to review them before trusting a count.
counted_at is entry time, not reconcile time; stock keeps moving after an item is counted, which is the main source of 'phantom' variance in long-running counts.

columns.name: inventory_count_item_id
columns.description: Unique id of this single count entry.

columns.name: qty
columns.description: The quantity found in this one counting act. An absolute observation of what was on the shelf at that spot, NOT a change — it must never enter a stock-movement sum. Multiple entries for one item accumulate to ls_inventory_count_calcs.counted_qoh.

columns.name: counted_at
columns.description: The date/time at which the count was made. The only genuine event clock in the count tables (the calc table's timestamp is a rollup watermark), so use it to measure how long a stocktake took and when each aisle was walked.

columns.name: inventory_count_id
columns.description: The stocktake this entry belongs to. No count header object exists in the docs, so this is a grouping id only.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: The item that was counted. Joins the catalogue item table.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Employee who physically made this count entry. The accountability trail: pair it with the resulting reconcile variance to find who is counting badly or who was on the floor when a discrepancy appeared.

tables.grain: one reconcile posting — one item's stock and cost adjustment applied when a count was reconciled
tables.description: The posted result of a stocktake: the adjustment actually written to the books for each item, in units and in cost value. This is the financial shrinkage record and the only count table that changes stock. It is NOT the variance measurement (ls_inventory_count_calcs) — a variance can exist forever without a reconcile — and it is irreversible once created.
gotchas: This is the only count table that MOVES THE BOOKS. Calc and Item rows are observations; a reconcile row is the posted adjustment and the number finance cares about.

Same field name, opposite meaning: cost_change HERE is a value delta you may sum ('the amount lost or gained in the reconcile to the books'), while InventoryLog.costChange is an updated unit cost you must not sum.
Reconciling is irreversible — the docs warn it cannot be undone without manually adjusting the inventory levels of every affected item. Treat these rows as immutable financial postings.
The same adjustment also appears in ls_inventory_logs with the same inventory_count_id. Summing shrinkage from both tables double counts it. Prefer this table for value, the log for shop attribution.
A whole-count reconcile (POST with no itemID) creates a burst of rows sharing a reconciled_at, while per-item reconciles dribble in. Row counts are therefore not a count of 'reconcile events'.
No shop column. If you need shrinkage by shop, join through ls_inventory_logs on (inventory_count_id, item_id) and read shop_id there.

columns.name: inventory_count_reconcile_id
columns.description: Unique id of this reconcile posting.

columns.name: reconciled_at
columns.description: When the reconcile was performed — the moment the books actually moved. This is the event date for shrinkage reporting; the counting itself happened earlier (ls_inventory_count_items.counted_at), sometimes much earlier.

columns.name: cost_change
columns.description: The cost VALUE of the adjustment: the amount lost (negative) or gained (positive) to the books for this item, ex tax, in store currency. Unlike InventoryLog.costChange — same field name, different object — this really is a delta and really is summable. It is a total for the adjustment, not a unit cost.

columns.name: qoh_change
columns.description: The stock-level change applied by the reconcile: negative means the count found FEWER units than the books claimed (shrinkage written off), positive means it found more (stock found). A genuine, summable delta.

columns.name: inventory_count_id
columns.description: The stocktake being reconciled. Group by it to price a whole count's shrinkage. No count header object is documented, so the id is not resolvable to a count name or shop.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: The item adjusted. Note the write-side asymmetry: a POST WITH itemID reconciles only that item, a POST WITHOUT itemID reconciles the entire count and produces a row per item.

tables.grain: one inter-shop transfer document (header), with its origin-side and destination-side records flattened in
tables.description: Transfers of stock between shops: one row per transfer document, carrying whether it has been sent and received, which shops and staff were on each end, and the send/receive dates. TransferFrom and TransferTo are one-to-one sub-records of the same document, so they are flattened here rather than split out. This is the document header only — the items and quantities live on ls_transfer_items, and the actual stock movement lands in ls_inventory_logs.
gotchas: Adding items to a transfer does NOT move stock (documented). Nothing changes until the receiving shop checks it in, so a transfer with is_sent = true and is_received = false is stock in limbo that still counts against the origin shop's on-hand.

Field naming trap: Transfer.sent/received are booleans (modelled here as is_sent/is_received) while TransferItem.sent/received are quantities. Mixing them produces silently wrong 'units transferred' numbers.
need_by is two different dates depending on is_received: a deadline while pending, the actual receipt date once received. Never treat it as a due date unconditionally.

Two shop columns and two employee columns, both derived from sub-records that each name their field 'shopID'/'employeeID'. from_shop_id/sent_by_employee_id come from TransferFrom, to_shop_id/received_by_employee_id from TransferTo — get them backwards and every flow direction reverses.
The docs type note as integer and archived as integer; both are documentation errors (note is text, archived is a flag). Cast defensively.
archived means done/filed, not cancelled. There is no documented cancelled state, so abandoned transfers look identical to fresh unsent ones — age them with updated_at to find the stale ones.

updated_at is last-modified on the header, not a movement date. Period reporting on transfers must use sent_on (outbound) or need_by-with-is_received (inbound), or better, ls_inventory_logs.created_at.

VERIFIED LIVE (bike repo, ItemMatrix.attribute1Values): Lightspeed's JSON collapses single-element arrays into a bare object, so TransferItems.TransferItem can arrive as an object rather than a list. Normalise to an array when exploding or every single-line transfer silently loses its line.
Origin and destination are reached through TransferFrom/TransferTo records rather than direct shop ids. A one-hop join to ls_shops will silently return nothing.

columns.name: transfer_id
columns.description: Unique id of the transfer document. Joins ls_transfer_items.transfer_id and ls_inventory_logs.transfer_id.

columns.name: is_sent
columns.description: true once the origin store has dispatched the transfer. Renamed from the API's plain 'sent' to avoid a dangerous collision: TransferItem.sent is a QUANTITY while this is a flag. is_sent AND NOT is_received = stock in transit, sitting on nobody's shelf.

columns.name: is_received
columns.description: true once the receiving store has checked the transfer in. Stock levels do not change until this happens — an unreceived transfer's units are still counted at the origin shop's on-hand, which is why unreceived transfers make two shops' stock look wrong at once.

columns.name: note
columns.description: Free-text note for the store. The docs type this field 'integer', which is a documentation error — the same docs describe it as 'Text notes for the store'. Treat as text and cast defensively.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: true when the transfer is filed away as done. Documented as 'integer' but behaves as a 0/1 flag. Means finished/hidden, NOT cancelled — there is no cancelled state, so an abandoned transfer is indistinguishable from one that was never started. Filter archived = false for the live worklist.

columns.name: transfer_from_id
columns.description: Key of the origin-side sub-record whose three payload fields are flattened onto this row as sent_on, sent_by_employee_id and from_shop_id. Rarely useful directly; kept so the API shape is traceable.

columns.name: transfer_to_id
columns.description: Key of the destination-side sub-record, flattened onto this row as need_by, received_by_employee_id and to_shop_id. Rarely useful directly.

columns.name: order_id
columns.description: Purchase Order this transfer was attached to for centralized ordering (head office buys once, then transfers stock out to shops). A supplier purchase order id from the purchasing domain, never a sale. NULL for ordinary shop-to-shop transfers, and non-null rows should not be double counted as separate procurement.

columns.name: sent_on
columns.description: Date/time the transfer left the origin shop. The genuine event date for outbound flow — bucket transfers by this, never by updated_at. NULL while the transfer is still being picked.

columns.name: sent_by_employee_id
columns.description: Employee who sent the transfer from the origin shop. Distinct from received_by_employee_id; the pair is the chain of custody for stock lost in transit.

columns.name: from_shop_id
columns.description: Origin shop — where the stock leaves. Swapping this with to_shop_id inverts every inbound/outbound flow report, which is easy to do because both sub-records call the field simply 'shopID'.

columns.name: need_by
