columns.description: OVERLOADED, exactly as documented: while pending it is the date the transfer must be received BY; once received it is the date it WAS received. Always read it together with is_received or you will report completed receipts as future deadlines and vice versa.

columns.name: received_by_employee_id
columns.description: Employee who received/checked in the transfer at the destination shop. NULL until receipt.

columns.name: to_shop_id
columns.description: Destination shop — where the stock is being sent. Pairs with from_shop_id to give the flow direction.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification to the transfer record, store-local. Moves whenever anything on the document changes, including line edits, so it is a staleness signal only: it is NOT the send date (sent_on) and NOT the receive date (need_by once received).

tables.grain: one line on one transfer — one item on one inter-shop transfer document
tables.description: The lines of an inter-shop transfer: which item, how many were meant to go, how many actually left, how many the destination counted, how many landed, and the cost value on each side. This is where transfer discrepancies and stock-lost-in-transit are found. These are mutable current-state quantities on an open document, not dated movements — the dated version is ls_inventory_logs filtered on transfer_id.
tables.additivityAxis: time — to_send/sent/to_receive/received are the line's CURRENT state, restated in place on every edit, so never bucket them by updated_at and sum. Summing across lines and across transfers within one snapshot is fine.
gotchas: Four quantity columns with four different meanings: to_send is the origin's intent, sent is what actually left, to_receive is the destination's count at check-in, received is what actually landed. Documented: in transit = sent - received.

sent_value and received_value are TOTALS for the line's quantity, ex tax — not unit costs. Dividing by the quantity is the only way to get a unit cost, and a gap between the two totals on a fully received line means the cost basis changed in transit.

Do not bucket these quantities by updated_at and sum them: updated_at is last-modified, so a line touched today would report its full history as today's movement. Dated transfer movement lives in ls_inventory_logs WHERE transfer_id IS NOT NULL.
Adding a line moves no stock (documented). Quantities here are promises until the parent transfer is received.
No shop columns on the line — origin and destination are on the parent transfer, so any per-shop transfer report must join ls_transfers.

VERIFIED LIVE (bike repo, ItemMatrix.attribute1Values): Lightspeed collapses single-element relation arrays into a bare object, so TransferItems.TransferItem is sometimes an object, not a list. Normalise to an array or one-line transfers vanish from the exploded table.

There is no account-wide TransferItem list endpoint: the standalone path is per transfer (Inventory/Transfer/{transferID}/TransferItems.json). Scan Transfer.json with load_relations=["TransferItems"] instead of issuing one request per transfer.

columns.name: transfer_item_id
columns.description: Unique id of this transfer line. Also the target of ls_special_orders.transfer_item_id when a special order is fulfilled from another shop.

columns.name: transfer_id
columns.description: The transfer document this line belongs to. Origin shop, destination shop and all dates live on the parent, not here.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: The item being transferred. Joins the catalogue item table.

columns.name: to_send
columns.description: The quantity the origin shop INTENDS to send — the picking instruction. Aspirational: to_send > sent on a dispatched transfer means the picker could not find them all.

columns.name: to_receive
columns.description: The quantity the receiving shop has counted as received during check-in. The destination's claim, which is what you compare against sent to catch a discrepancy before it is posted.

columns.name: sent
columns.description: The actual number dispatched from the origin shop. A QUANTITY — not the boolean ls_transfers.is_sent. Documented: sent - received is the number still in transit.

columns.name: received
columns.description: The actual number that landed at the destination. sent - received > 0 on an old, supposedly-complete transfer is stock that left one shop and never arrived: the classic in-transit shrinkage signal.

columns.name: sent_value
columns.description: TOTAL inventory cost value of the quantity sent, ex tax, in store currency — not a unit cost. Implied unit cost = sent_value / NULLIF(sent, 0). This is the cost basis leaving the origin shop's balance sheet.

columns.name: received_value
columns.description: TOTAL inventory cost value of the quantity received, ex tax. Diverges from sent_value when quantities differ or the cost basis moved in transit; sent_value - received_value on a closed transfer is the dollar value of the loss.

columns.name: comment
columns.description: Free-text note on the line — usually where staff explain a short shipment or damage. Worth reading whenever sent <> received.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification to this line, store-local. Not a send or receive date: an old line edited today would count its whole quantity as today's movement if you bucket by it.

tables.grain: one special order — one item a named customer asked the shop to bring in, tracked from the sale line it was raised on to the purchase order line or transfer that fulfils it
tables.description: Customer special orders: a customer wants something the shop does not stock, the shop optionally takes a deposit and orders it in. Each row bridges the customer side (sale_line_id) with the supply side (order_line_id for a supplier PO, or transfer_item_id when another shop supplies it), plus the contacted/completed workflow flags. It is NOT a sale (no money or price here) and NOT a purchase order — it is the link record that makes 'who is waiting for what' answerable.
tables.additivityAxis: time — unit_quantity is the currently requested quantity, restated in place as staff edit the order, and this object exposes no event date at all, so never bucket or sum it by period.
gotchas: A special order is neither a sale nor a purchase order — it is the bridge. sale_line_id is where the customer asked, order_line_id is where it was bought. Counting rows here as sales or as procurement double counts both.
completed = true means fulfilled/closed, not paid. contacted = true means only that somebody rang the customer. NOT completed AND NOT contacted is the shelf-of-shame report this table exists for.

Fulfilment can come from another shop: transfer_item_id set with order_line_id NULL is a legitimate, fully-sourced special order. Filtering on order_line_id IS NULL alone mislabels those as never ordered.
unit_quantity is demand restated in place, not a flow measure. It is not units sold and it must not be trended.

The endpoint advertises timeStamp as a sortable/filterable field but the documented field list contains NO timestamp, so this table has no date column. Age a special order through its sale line's date; you can still sort/filter server-side by timeStamp when scanning.

Special-order reservations already show up as ItemShop.onSpecialOrder in the catalogue domain and those units are inside qoh. Adding special-order quantities on top of on-hand double counts reserved stock.
customer_id makes every row personal data — one row tells you what a named person is waiting for, and the linked sale line tells you what they paid.

columns.name: special_order_id
columns.description: Unique id of the special order.

columns.name: unit_quantity
columns.description: How many units the customer asked the shop to bring in. Current requested quantity, restated when staff edit the order — this is customer DEMAND, not units sold. What was actually sold lives on the linked sale line.

columns.name: contacted
columns.description: true once someone has told the customer their special order has arrived. contacted = false with the goods already in is the 'the customer does not know it is here' backlog — the single most valuable operational query on this table.

columns.name: completed
columns.description: true when the special order has been closed out (collected and rung up on the originating sale line). This is the filter that separates the live backlog from history. It does not by itself mean the customer paid — payment lives on the sale.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: The customer waiting for the item. Joins the customer table. Personal data: a row here reveals what a named individual is waiting on, so keep it aggregate unless the question is explicitly about one customer.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: Shop where the special order was raised and where the customer will collect. The only location column on this table — the supplying shop, when a transfer fulfils it, is on the parent transfer of transfer_item_id.

columns.name: sale_line_id
columns.description: The sale line the special order was started from and where it will be completed — the customer's side of the deal, carrying the price, deposit and sale date. Joins the sales domain's sale-line table; it is also the only way to date a special order, since this object has no timestamp field.

columns.name: order_line_id
columns.description: The purchase order line where the item is being bought from the supplier — the supply side. NULL when the item has not been ordered yet OR when it is being fulfilled by an inter-shop transfer instead. Joins the purchasing domain's order-line table.

columns.name: transfer_item_id
columns.description: The transfer line fulfilling this special order when another shop supplies it rather than a supplier. NULL on the normal supplier route. Reports that only look at order_line_id classify these as unsourced and generate false 'we never ordered it' alarms.

tables.grain: one origin record for one stock transfer
tables.description: The sending side of a stock transfer. Lightspeed models the two ends of a transfer as separate records rather than as two columns, so this table resolves a transfer to the shop the stock left. It exists purely to complete that join and carries no quantities of its own.
gotchas: Thinly documented: the reference publishes only the primary key. Any shop linkage must be confirmed from a live payload before use.

columns.name: transfer_from_id
columns.description: Primary key of the origin record. Referenced by ls_transfers.transfer_from_id.

tables.grain: one destination record for one stock transfer
tables.description: The receiving side of a stock transfer, mirroring ls_transfer_from. Resolves a transfer to the shop that received the stock. Reference-only; quantities live on the transfer item lines.
gotchas: Thinly documented: the reference publishes only the primary key.

columns.name: transfer_to_id
columns.description: Primary key of the destination record. Referenced by ls_transfers.transfer_to_id.

tables.grain: one purchase order raised with one vendor for one shop (Lightspeed resource `Order`)
tables.description: One row per PURCHASE ORDER: stock the business is buying from a supplier, with the header-level costs, discounts, currency and lifecycle flags. This is the document the shop sends to a vendor and later checks in against. It is NOT a customer order — customer purchases live in the sales domain (Sale/SaleLine); a customer waiting on an item is a SpecialOrder. It is also NOT a receipt: what physically arrived is in ls_order_shipments / ls_order_shipment_items and in the per-line counters on ls_purchase_order_lines.
gotchas: 'Order' in Lightspeed means a PURCHASE order raised with a supplier. It is never a customer order. Answering 'how many orders did we take last month?' from this table is the single most common wrong answer in the whole R-Series API — customer demand lives in Sale/SaleLine, and a customer waiting on an item is a SpecialOrder.

VERIFIED LIVE: legacy/imported POs carry vendorID = 0 instead of null, and the Vendor relation does not embed for them, so vendor_name is null. Per-vendor spend built with an inner join silently drops those orders; always LEFT JOIN and report the unattributed bucket.

VERIFIED LIVE: the Order payload also returns subTotalCost and totalCost, which are absent from the documented field table and therefore deliberately NOT columns here. If your loader retains the raw payload you may read them; otherwise derive PO value as SUM(line_total) over the lines, plus ship_cost and other_cost, less total_discount.

Open on-order stock requires BOTH is_complete = false AND is_archived = false. Lightspeed itself drops archived orders from backorder totals (stated on the archived field), and is_complete = true does not prove full receipt — POs get closed short.

Two generations of discount fields coexist on the same record: the legacy percentage discount_percent_legacy, and discount_method / discount_is_percent / discount_percent_value / discount_money_value. Applying both double-discounts the cost of goods. Prefer discount_money_value as the resolved money figure.

shipping_cost_method and discount_method = 'total' means the amount is held at ORDER level and never allocated to lines. Landed cost assembled purely from ls_purchase_order_lines understates by the entire freight bill on those POs.
costs_modified_after_shipment = true invalidates the freight/discount splits already stored on the shipments and shipment items for that PO. Treat landed cost on those orders as approximate.

All money on this table is COST — what the shop pays the supplier — and is exclusive of retail markup and (per the docs' silence) says nothing about tax treatment. Never line total-cost figures up against sales revenue without labelling the comparison.
VERIFIED LIVE: vendor_currency_rate is 0 or 1 for domestic suppliers. 0 means 'not applicable', so any conversion that divides by it produces infinity or a silent NULL.
received_at is a single header stamp on a document that can arrive in many deliveries. Use ls_order_shipments.received_at for real goods-inwards timing and lead-time work.
created_at can be the migration timestamp on imported accounts, bunching years of history onto one date. Date supplier spend with ordered_at.
Only orderID and timeStamp are documented as sortable, so incremental syncs must page on timeStamp; there is no server-side ordering by orderedDate.

columns.name: order_id
columns.description: Unique id of the purchase order and the join key for every child table (lines, shipments). Lightspeed exposes no separate human-facing PO number — this integer IS the PO number staff see; ref_number is the VENDOR's number, not ours.

columns.name: ordered_at
columns.description: When the order was placed WITH the vendor. This is the business date for supplier-spend and commitment reporting. Empty/null on drafts that were never sent, so a spend report keyed on this date silently excludes drafts (correctly) but also excludes any PO where the buyer never filled it in.

columns.name: received_at
columns.description: The date the order actually arrived. A single header stamp: for a PO that arrived in several deliveries the docs do not say whether this is the first or the last, so use ls_order_shipments.received_at for real goods-inwards timing. Null while nothing has been received.

columns.name: expected_arrival_at
columns.description: The date the order is EXPECTED to arrive — a promise/ETA typed by staff, not a system-computed date and not evidence anything arrived. Null unless someone entered it, so 'late orders' queries must handle nulls explicitly rather than treating them as on time.

columns.name: ref_number
columns.description: Free-text external reference — in practice the vendor's own order or invoice number (VERIFIED LIVE: values like '87344', 'WEB5730'). Not unique, not validated, frequently blank. Never use as a key.

columns.name: ship_instructions
columns.description: Free-text instructions for the VENDOR or shipper about how to ship the order (carrier, consolidation, drop-ship address). Outbound-facing prose; carries no structured meaning.

columns.name: stock_instructions
columns.description: Free-text instructions for the RECEIVING employees about how to stock the goods once they land (which bay, label runs, hold for customer). Internal-facing counterpart to ship_instructions; easily confused with it.

columns.name: ship_cost
columns.description: Freight the vendor added to the order, in the MERCHANT's default currency. Order-level: whether it is spread down to the lines depends on shipping_cost_method. Part of landed cost, not of goods cost.

columns.name: ship_cost_vendor_currency
columns.description: The same freight expressed in the VENDOR's currency. Equals ship_cost for domestic suppliers; for import POs the pair differs by vendor_currency_rate. Adding it to ship_cost mixes currencies and doubles the freight.

columns.name: other_cost
columns.description: Other vendor-added costs (handling, surcharges, duty recharges) in merchant currency. CAN BE NEGATIVE, in which case it is a discount — so it must be added, never ABS()'d or summed as a cost-only bucket.

columns.name: other_cost_vendor_currency
columns.description: Other vendor-added costs in the vendor's currency; same negative-means-discount convention as other_cost. The vendor-currency twin, not an additional charge.

columns.name: is_complete
columns.description: True once the order is marked complete, which usually happens after check-in finishes. It is a workflow flag, NOT proof that every unit arrived: buyers routinely close POs short. Open on-order stock = is_complete = false AND is_archived = false.

columns.name: is_archived
columns.description: True when the PO is archived. Lightspeed itself excludes archived orders from backorder/on-order totals, so any 'what is on order' answer that ignores this flag overstates incoming stock. Archived POs remain valid history for spend reporting.

columns.name: discount_percent_legacy
columns.description: Legacy order-level PERCENTAGE discount applied to each line's unit cost (5 = 5%, not 0.05). Superseded on current accounts by the discount_method / discount_is_percent / discount_percent_value / discount_money_value family, which expresses the same intent. Never apply both families — the discount exists once and double-applying it silently understates cost of goods.

columns.name: total_discount
columns.description: Total MONEY value of all discounts on the order, merchant currency — the realised sum, whichever discount family produced it. It is a rollup, so adding it to the per-line discount_money_value allocations double counts the same money.

columns.name: total_quantity
columns.description: Total units ORDERED across all lines — a header rollup of ls_purchase_order_lines.quantity, and never units received. Summing this alongside line quantities in the same query double counts.

columns.name: vendor_id
columns.description: Supplier the PO is for; joins ls_vendors.vendor_id. VERIFIED LIVE: legacy/imported POs carry 0 rather than null and the Vendor relation does not embed for them, so treat 0 as NULL — otherwise per-vendor spend quietly drops those orders and a phantom 'vendor 0' appears in group-bys.

columns.name: vendor_name
columns.description: Denormalised supplier name from the embedded Vendor relation, for readable grouping without a join. VERIFIED LIVE: null whenever vendor_id is 0/absent because the relation does not embed. Group by vendor_id AND this column, never by name alone — the same brand can exist under several vendor_id values.

columns.name: note_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the Note record holding the PO's free-text note. Only the id is exposed; the note body requires load_relations=Note and is not modelled here. 0 means no note.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: The shop (location) the stock is being ordered FOR, i.e. where it will be checked in — not necessarily where the buyer sits. Joins the locations domain (ls_shops.shop_id / canonical `location`). 0 behaves as null.

columns.name: created_by_employee_id
columns.description: Employee who CREATED the PO — the buyer, not the person who later received it (that is ls_order_shipments.employee_id). Joins the workforce domain (canonical `worker`). 0/null on migrated or API-created orders.

columns.name: custom_field_values
columns.description: Raw JSON of the account-defined custom fields attached to this PO. Kept as JSON because the field set is defined per merchant and the ground-truth documentation exposes no member-field table to model — so there are no stable column names to promise. Empty/absent on accounts that define no PO custom fields.

columns.name: created_at
columns.description: When the PO RECORD was created. On migrated accounts this is the data-import timestamp, not when the buyer raised the order, so it can cluster thousands of historic POs on one day. Prefer ordered_at for business dating and keep this for record-level auditing.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of the record — the correct high-water mark for incremental syncs, and meaningless as a business date (a PO from 2019 touched yesterday shows yesterday). One of only two documented sort keys on this endpoint.

columns.name: vendor_currency_rate
columns.description: Exchange rate captured on the PO, defaulting to the vendor's rate: multiply vendor-currency amounts by this to reach merchant currency. VERIFIED LIVE: domestic suppliers show 0 or 1 — a 0 here means 'not applicable', NOT a zero-valued currency, so guard every division and never revalue an old PO at today's rate.

columns.name: vendor_currency_code
columns.description: Currency code of the purchase order, defaulting to the vendor's currency (e.g. 'USD'). Tells you which of each *_vendor_currency column pair is meaningful; absent on legacy rows with no vendor. Never assume it equals the merchant currency.

columns.name: shipping_cost_method
columns.description: How ship_cost is distributed to the lines. 'total' means the freight stays at ORDER level and is NOT allocated down, so ls_purchase_order_lines.shipping_cost will be empty and any landed-cost-per-line built from the lines alone understates by the whole freight bill.
columns.enums: evenly = split equally across lines; proportionally = split by line value; total = held at order level as a single amount, not pushed to lines

columns.name: has_shipments
columns.description: True when the PO has any shipment records. False does NOT mean nothing arrived — POs received before the shipments workflow existed have no shipment rows at all (VERIFIED LIVE: shipment history on the probed store only begins March 2023), and their receiving lives solely in the line-level check-in counters.

columns.name: discount_method
columns.description: How the order-level discount is distributed to the lines, mirroring shipping_cost_method. 'total' means the discount is held at order level and the per-line discount_money_value allocations are not populated.
columns.enums: evenly = split equally across lines; proportionally = split by line value; total = held at order level as a single amount, not pushed to lines

columns.name: discount_money_value
columns.description: The order-level discount expressed as MONEY in the merchant's currency. Populated regardless of how it was entered (Lightspeed resolves a percentage into money here), so this is the field to sum for 'discount received from suppliers'. Do not also subtract discount_percent_value.

columns.name: discount_money_vendor_value
columns.description: The same order-level discount in the VENDOR's currency. The twin of discount_money_value, not an extra discount; summing both double counts across two currencies.

columns.name: discount_is_percent
columns.description: True when the buyer typed the order discount as a percentage, false when as a fixed amount. Tells you which of discount_percent_value / discount_money_value was the INPUT — both may still be populated as derived values, which is exactly how double-discount bugs start.

columns.name: discount_percent_value
columns.description: Order-level discount percentage in whole-percent units (5 = 5%, not 0.05). Applies to the goods cost of the lines, not to freight or other costs.

columns.name: costs_modified_after_shipment
columns.description: True when the shipping cost or discount changed AFTER the first shipment was created. That means the per-shipment freight/discount splits already written into ls_order_shipments and ls_order_shipment_items are stale relative to this header — landed-cost answers for those POs need a caveat or a recompute.

columns.name: b2b_order_uid
columns.description: Opaque unique identifier of this order in NuORDER (Lightspeed's B2B wholesale platform). Populated only for POs that originated in NuORDER; empty everywhere else, which makes non-empty a decent proxy for 'ordered through B2B'.

columns.name: b2b_order_number
columns.description: Human-readable order number in NuORDER, the display counterpart to b2b_order_uid. Empty unless the PO came through NuORDER; it is the vendor-platform number, not our order_id and not ref_number.

tables.grain: one product line on one purchase order (one row per OrderLine)
tables.description: One row per item line on a purchase order: which product, how many units were ordered, at what unit cost, and how many of them have physically landed. This is the line-level truth for 'how many X are on order' and for per-product buying history and cost trends. It is NOT a receipt log — the two receiving columns are running counters that are overwritten in place, with no history of when units arrived; dated receipts live in ls_order_shipment_items.
tables.additivityAxis: time — qty_checked_in and qty_received_not_checked_in are in-place running counters with no history, so they may be summed ACROSS lines but never across dates or snapshots of the same line; quantity, unit costs and line_total are static once set and are safe to sum either way
gotchas: Units still to arrive on a line = quantity - qty_checked_in - qty_received_not_checked_in. qty_checked_in is IN stock; qty_received_not_checked_in is at the door but invisible to stock-on-hand. Conflating the two either overstates sellable stock or double counts arrivals.

The receiving counters are mutated in place and keep no history, so this table cannot answer 'what did we receive in March'. Dated receiving lives in ls_order_shipments (header) and ls_order_shipment_items (per item).
The line has no open/complete/archived flag. Every 'on order right now' query must join ls_purchase_orders and filter is_complete = false AND is_archived = false.

Three cost columns, two currencies, two discount states: unit_cost = discounted merchant currency, unit_cost_original = pre-discount merchant currency, unit_cost_vendor_currency = pre-discount VENDOR currency. The docs say vendorCost should be used instead of originalPrice, never both. VERIFIED LIVE: unit_cost_vendor_currency is 0 on domestic suppliers, and a naive COALESCE onto it prices those lines at zero.
line_total excludes allocated freight. Landed cost per line = line_total + shipping_cost, and shipping_cost is itself empty when the header's shipping_cost_method is 'total'.
discount_money_value is already baked into unit_cost and line_total; subtracting it again is the most common double-discount error in this domain.

VERIFIED LIVE: the account-level OrderLine collection covers every line of every PO ever placed on the account, so unfiltered scans walk the entire purchasing history. Push orderID or itemID down; only orderLineID, timeStamp and orderID are documented sort keys.
The same item can legitimately appear on several lines of one PO (different costs, different destinations), so per-item aggregates must SUM rather than assume one row.

columns.name: order_line_id
columns.description: Unique id of the PO line. Stable across edits to the line, and the target of SpecialOrder.orderLineID in the sales domain — that is how 'this customer's item is on PO 4821' is expressed.

columns.name: order_id
columns.description: Parent purchase order; joins ls_purchase_orders.order_id. The line carries no open/complete/archived state of its own, so every 'is this still on order' question has to reach the header through this key.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: The product being ordered; joins the products domain (canonical `product_variant`, since a Lightspeed Item is the sellable variant). 0 behaves as null. The same item can appear on several lines of one PO, which breaks naive one-line-per-item assumptions.

columns.name: quantity
columns.description: Units ORDERED on this line. Not units received and not units still to come: outstanding = quantity - qty_checked_in - qty_received_not_checked_in. Editing a PO changes this in place, so it is the current ask, not the original ask.

columns.name: unit_cost
columns.description: Unit COST in the merchant's default currency, ALREADY adjusted for any order-level discount. Despite the API name 'price' this is what we pay the supplier, never what the customer pays; pairing it with retail price from the products domain is how margin is computed, and confusing the two inverts margin entirely.

columns.name: unit_cost_original
columns.description: Unit cost in merchant currency BEFORE any order-level discount. unit_cost_original - unit_cost is the per-unit discount the supplier gave. Using this as cost of goods overstates cost by the whole discount.

columns.name: unit_cost_vendor_currency
columns.description: Unit cost BEFORE order discount in the VENDOR's currency — the vendor-currency counterpart of unit_cost_original, and per the docs it should be used instead of, not alongside, that field. VERIFIED LIVE: 0 for domestic suppliers, where 0 means 'not applicable', not free.

columns.name: qty_checked_in
columns.description: Units checked in, meaning ADDED TO INVENTORY — the stock is on the shelf and counted in quantity-on-hand. A cumulative running counter overwritten on every receipt, so it answers 'how many have landed in total', never 'how many landed in June'.

columns.name: qty_received_not_checked_in
columns.description: Units received at the door but NOT yet added to inventory — physically present, invisible to stock-on-hand. Usually 0 on finished POs. Adding it to qty_checked_in gives units physically arrived; treating it as available stock overstates what staff can sell.

columns.name: line_total
columns.description: Documented as quantity x price, so it is the discounted goods cost of the line in merchant currency and EXCLUDES the allocated shipping_cost. Landed cost of the line = line_total + shipping_cost (the discount is already inside line_total via unit_cost).

columns.name: shipping_cost
columns.description: This line's share of the PO-level freight, calculated down from the header in merchant currency. Empty/zero when the order's shipping_cost_method is 'total' (freight stays at header level), which is the usual reason per-line landed cost looks too cheap.

columns.name: shipping_cost_vendor_currency
columns.description: The same allocated freight share expressed in the vendor's currency. A currency twin of shipping_cost, not an additional charge.

columns.name: discount_money_value
columns.description: This line's share of the order-level discount as money in merchant currency. Already reflected in unit_cost and line_total, so subtracting it again from line_total double-discounts the line.

columns.name: discount_money_vendor_value
columns.description: This line's allocated discount share in the vendor's currency — the currency twin of discount_money_value, not a second discount.

columns.name: discount_percent_value
columns.description: The order-level discount percentage as it lands on this line, in whole-percent units (5 = 5%). Derived from the header, not a line-specific negotiation.

columns.name: created_at
columns.description: When the line was added to the PO — which can be later than the order's own created_at when a buyer appends items, and can be the migration timestamp on imported history.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of the line and the sync high-water mark. In practice this is when receiving last touched the line (check-in mutates the counters), which makes it a rough but unreliable proxy for receipt date — use the shipment tables when the date matters.

tables.grain: one shipment (receiving event) against one purchase order
tables.description: One row per delivery received against a purchase order: how many units landed, the landed cost of that delivery, the freight and discount allocated to it, and who received it when. A PO can arrive in several shipments, each with its own sequence number and invoice due date. This is the DATED receiving fact for the purchasing domain; it is NOT the purchase order's own totals (those are on ls_purchase_orders) and it is NOT per-item detail (that is ls_order_shipment_items). The Order-scoped OrderShipment endpoint and the account-wide Shipment endpoint are documented as identical, so they are one table here.
tables.endpoint: Order/{orderID}/Shipment.json (account-wide alias: Shipment.json — documented as identical but not constrained to one Order)
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: the account-wide Shipment endpoint returns its records under an `OrderShipment` envelope key, not `Shipment`. A loader that keys the envelope off the endpoint name silently returns zero rows.

OrderShipment (scoped as /Order/{orderID}/Shipment) and Shipment (account-wide) are documented as identical objects — same grain, same fields, different URL scope. Modelling them as two tables would duplicate every receipt.

shipping_cost_order_full_value, shipping_cost_order_full_vendor_value, discount_order_full_money_value and discount_order_full_money_vendor_value are WHOLE-PO figures repeated on every shipment of that order. Sum the per-shipment shipping_cost / discount_money_value instead, or freight and discounts inflate by the number of deliveries.

cost/vendor_cost are pre-freight, pre-discount goods; total_cost/total_vendor_cost are landed. Picking the wrong pair shifts gross margin by the entire freight bill in whichever direction flatters the report.
received_at (receptionDate) is the goods-inwards date; created_at is when the record was keyed. Use received_at for any period, lead-time or ageing calculation.

VERIFIED LIVE: shipment history on the probed store only starts around March 2023 — purchase orders received before the shipments workflow have NO rows here at all even though the goods arrived. Pre-workflow receiving exists only as ls_purchase_order_lines.qty_checked_in, so a receiving time series built from this table shows a false zero for earlier years.
One PO, many shipments: SUM(total_qty_received) GROUP BY order_id is what has arrived; COUNT(*) is how many times the supplier split the delivery.
payment_due_date is a bare date and only present when someone typed the invoice terms, so 'payables due' reports systematically miss the deliveries where it was skipped.
If the parent order has costs_modified_after_shipment = true, the freight and discount splits stored on these rows predate the change and no longer reconcile to the header.
Only orderShipmentID, paymentDueDate and sequenceNumber are documented sort keys — you cannot ask the API for shipments ordered by receptionDate.

columns.name: order_shipment_id
columns.description: Unique id of the shipment across the whole account (not per order — that is sequence_number). Join key for ls_order_shipment_items.

columns.name: order_id
columns.description: The purchase order this delivery was received against; joins ls_purchase_orders.order_id. Every vendor, shop and ordered-date attribute of the receipt has to be reached through this key — the shipment itself carries no vendor or shop.

columns.name: sequence_number
columns.description: The delivery's number WITHIN its purchase order (1 = first delivery, 2 = second). Unique only relative to the order, so it is never a global key; sequence_number > 1 identifies split/backordered deliveries.

columns.name: total_qty_received
columns.description: Total units received in THIS delivery, summing its items. SUM over an order_id gives what has arrived so far on that PO; comparing that against ls_purchase_orders.total_quantity gives true fill rate.

columns.name: total_vendor_cost
columns.description: Total LANDED cost of everything in this shipment expressed in the VENDOR's currency — goods plus allocated freight, net of allocated discount. The vendor-currency twin of total_cost; adding both mixes currencies.

columns.name: total_cost
columns.description: Total LANDED cost of this shipment in the merchant's default currency — goods plus allocated freight, net of allocated discount. This, not `cost`, is what the inventory was actually valued at on arrival; choosing `cost` instead moves gross margin by the entire freight bill.

columns.name: currency_code
columns.description: The merchant's DEFAULT currency code at the time this shipment was created (e.g. 'AUD') — the unit for every non-vendor money column here. Frozen at creation, so it does not follow later account changes.

columns.name: vendor_currency_code
columns.description: The vendor's currency code, the unit for every *_vendor_cost / *_vendor_value column on this row. Equal to currency_code for domestic suppliers, which is why the two column families look redundant until an import PO appears.

columns.name: vendor_currency_rate
columns.description: Exchange rate from vendor currency to merchant currency CAPTURED AT SHIPMENT CREATION. Multiply vendor-currency amounts by it to reach merchant currency; it is frozen history, so revaluing an old receipt at today's rate is wrong. VERIFIED LIVE (on the Order twin of this field): domestic suppliers can carry 0 or 1, and 0 means 'not applicable' — guard against dividing by it.

columns.name: created_at
columns.description: When the shipment RECORD was created (keyed by staff). Frequently close to but not equal to received_at, and it is the wrong column for goods-inwards periods — a delivery keyed a week late lands in the wrong month.

columns.name: payment_due_date
columns.description: Date the supplier's invoice for this delivery falls due — a DATE with no time component, populated only when the receiver entered the invoice terms. This is the domain's only accounts-payable signal; null means 'unknown', never 'due now'.

columns.name: shipment_packing_ref_num
columns.description: Reference number for the shipment as typed by staff — in practice the packing slip or supplier invoice number. Free text, not unique, often blank; it is how a receipt gets matched to a paper invoice, not a key.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last update of the shipment record and the incremental-sync high-water mark. Changes when costs are re-split after the fact, so it is not a receiving date.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Employee who received/checked in this delivery; joins the workforce domain (canonical `worker`). Distinct from ls_purchase_orders.created_by_employee_id, which is the buyer — attributing receiving errors to the buyer is a classic mix-up.

columns.name: received_at
columns.description: When the goods were actually received. THE date for goods-inwards volume, lead time and receiving-by-period reporting — preferred over both created_at here and the header stamp on ls_purchase_orders.

columns.name: shipping_cost_method
columns.description: How the freight charged to this shipment was spread across its items. 'total' means it stayed at shipment level and the per-item shipping_cost values are not populated, so per-item landed cost built from the items alone understates.
columns.enums: evenly = split equally across the shipment's items; proportionally = split by item value; total = held at shipment level as a single amount

columns.name: shipping_cost_vendor_currency
columns.description: Freight allocated to THIS shipment, in the vendor's currency. The per-delivery share, not the PO's total freight — that is shipping_cost_order_full_vendor_value.

columns.name: shipping_cost
columns.description: Freight allocated to THIS shipment, in merchant currency, and already included inside total_cost. This is the column to SUM for freight spend by period; summing the *_order_full_* columns instead multiplies the bill by the number of deliveries.

columns.name: shipping_cost_order_full_value
columns.description: The FULL freight applied to the whole purchase order, in merchant currency, repeated on every shipment row of that order as context. It is not this delivery's share — SUM()ing it across shipments multiplies the PO's freight by the number of deliveries. The biggest double-count trap in this domain.

columns.name: shipping_cost_order_full_vendor_value
columns.description: The full whole-PO freight in the vendor's currency, repeated on every shipment row. Same double-count hazard as shipping_cost_order_full_value, in the other currency.

columns.name: discount_method
columns.description: How the discount charged to this shipment was spread across its items, mirroring shipping_cost_method. 'total' leaves it at shipment level with no per-item allocation.
columns.enums: evenly = split equally across the shipment's items; proportionally = split by item value; total = held at shipment level as a single amount

columns.name: discount_money_vendor_value
columns.description: Discount allocated to THIS shipment in the vendor's currency. Already netted off total_vendor_cost.

columns.name: discount_money_value
columns.description: Discount allocated to THIS shipment in merchant currency, already netted off total_cost. Subtracting it from total_cost double-discounts the delivery.

columns.name: discount_percent_value
columns.description: Discount percentage applied on the shipment, in whole-percent units (5 = 5%). Documented on this object as 'the discount percent value of the item', but it sits on the shipment header — the per-item figure is the same-named column on ls_order_shipment_items.

columns.name: discount_order_full_money_value
columns.description: The FULL discount applied to the whole purchase order in merchant currency, repeated on every shipment row as context. Not this delivery's share; SUM()ing it across shipments inflates supplier discounts by the number of deliveries.

columns.name: discount_order_full_money_vendor_value
columns.description: The full whole-PO discount in the vendor's currency, repeated on every shipment row. Same double-count hazard, other currency.

columns.name: cost
columns.description: Goods cost of the items in this shipment BEFORE freight and discount, merchant currency. The pre-landed figure: total_cost - cost is roughly the net freight/discount effect. Reporting `cost` as cost of goods received omits freight entirely.

columns.name: vendor_cost
columns.description: Goods cost of the items in this shipment before freight and discount, in the VENDOR's currency. Note the name collision: on ls_purchase_order_lines `vendorCost` is a UNIT cost, here it is a shipment total.

columns.name: status
columns.description: Lifecycle state of the shipment, constrained by the docs to two values. 'received' does not mean the PO is fully satisfied — more deliveries may follow; 'finished' closes receiving for it. Neither value means the shipment was cancelled: there is no cancelled state.
columns.enums: received = goods received, the order may still expect further shipments; finished = receiving complete for this shipment

tables.grain: one product's receipt within one shipment (one row per ShipmentItem)
tables.description: One row per item received in a shipment: how many units of that product landed in that delivery, its cost before freight, its allocated freight and discount, and its final landed cost. This is the finest-grained, dated goods-receipt fact in the purchasing domain and the correct basis for actual landed unit cost. It is NOT the ordered quantity (that is ls_purchase_order_lines.quantity) and it carries no link to the PO line it satisfies — only the item id.
tables.endpoint: Shipment/{orderShipmentID}/Item.json (documented as identical to the OrderShipmentItem endpoint, without the Order constraint)
gotchas: The documented field table has NO orderLineID. Shipment items link to the ITEM, not to the PO line they satisfy (an OrderLine load_relation exists but no scalar FK is published), so 'which line did this receipt close' is inference by order + item and is ambiguous when a PO carries the same item on two lines.

cost and vendor_cost are documented only as 'item cost ... before applying shipping cost & discounts' — the docs never say whether they are per unit or extended for qty_received. Verify against total_cost / qty_received on real data before publishing either as a unit cost; guessing wrong scales cost of goods by the order quantity.

total_cost and total_vendor_cost are landed for this item within this shipment. They already roll up into ls_order_shipments.total_cost, so joining header to items and summing both counts the same money twice.
item_vendor_id is a vendor SKU STRING, not an id and not a key. Joining on it will either error on type or match garbage.
item_description is frozen at receipt time; grouping a multi-year cost history by it splits one product into several rows after a rename. Group by item_id.
The currency triplet is frozen at shipment creation. Historic landed costs must be read at the rate that was captured, never re-converted at today's rate.

Sort keys documented here are description, orderShipmentItemID, qtyReceived and vendorCost — note that `description` is the sort name for the itemDescription field, and there is no sort by date at all.

VERIFIED LIVE (parent table): no rows exist for purchase orders received before the shipments workflow (~March 2023 on the probed store), so landed-cost analysis has a hard historical floor and earlier receipts must fall back to ls_purchase_order_lines.

columns.name: order_shipment_item_id
columns.description: Unique id of this item-within-shipment row. Unique account-wide despite the nested URL, so it is a safe primary key.

columns.name: order_shipment_id
columns.description: Parent shipment; joins ls_order_shipments.order_shipment_id. This is the ONLY route from an item receipt to its purchase order, vendor, receive date and receiving employee — none of those exist on this row.

columns.name: qty_received
columns.description: Units of this item received in THIS delivery — a per-delivery event quantity, safe to sum over time, unlike the running counters on ls_purchase_order_lines. The denominator for landed unit cost.

columns.name: vendor_cost
columns.description: Item cost in the VENDOR's currency before freight and discount. The docs say only 'item cost' and do not state whether it is per unit or extended for qty_received — verify against total_vendor_cost / qty_received on live data before treating it as a unit cost. Note the collision: the same API name on OrderLine is definitively a unit cost.

columns.name: cost
columns.description: Item cost in the merchant's default currency before freight and discount. Same documented ambiguity as vendor_cost about per-unit vs extended; resolve it empirically against total_cost before publishing any unit-cost figure.

columns.name: total_vendor_cost
columns.description: Total LANDED cost of this item within this shipment, in the vendor's currency — goods plus allocated freight, net of allocated discount. Vendor-currency twin of total_cost, not an additional amount.

columns.name: total_cost
columns.description: Total LANDED cost of this item within this shipment in merchant currency — the true inventory value added by this receipt, and the numerator for real landed unit cost (total_cost / qty_received). Summing this across a shipment reproduces the shipment header's total_cost, so never add the two.

columns.name: shipping_cost
columns.description: Freight allocated to this item in merchant currency, already included in total_cost. Zero when the parent shipment's shipping_cost_method is 'total' — the freight then exists only at shipment level.

columns.name: shipping_cost_vendor_currency
columns.description: Freight allocated to this item in the vendor's currency; the currency twin of shipping_cost, not an extra charge.

columns.name: discount_money_value
columns.description: Discount allocated to this item in merchant currency, already netted off total_cost. Subtracting it again double-discounts the receipt.

columns.name: discount_money_vendor_value
columns.description: Discount allocated to this item in the vendor's currency — currency twin of discount_money_value.

columns.name: discount_percent_value
columns.description: Discount percentage applied to this item, in whole-percent units (5 = 5%). Inherited from the shipment/PO allocation rather than negotiated per item.

columns.name: currency_code
columns.description: The merchant's default currency code for this row's non-vendor money columns, frozen when the shipment was created. Repeated from the parent shipment for self-containment.

columns.name: vendor_currency_code
columns.description: The vendor's currency code — the unit for every *_vendor_* money column on this row. Identical to currency_code for domestic suppliers, which hides the distinction until an import receipt appears.

columns.name: vendor_currency_rate
columns.description: Exchange rate from vendor to merchant currency captured AT SHIPMENT CREATION — historic and frozen, so re-converting old receipts at a current rate is wrong. Can be 0 or 1 for domestic suppliers, where 0 means 'not applicable' rather than a real rate.

columns.name: created_at
columns.description: When this item row was created, i.e. when the line was keyed during check-in. The actual goods-inwards date lives on the parent shipment (received_at); use this only for record auditing.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last update of this item row and the sync high-water mark. Moves when costs are re-split after the fact, so it is not a receipt date.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: The product received; joins the products domain (canonical `product_variant`). This is the only product key on the row — there is no orderLineID, so attribution back to a specific PO line is inferred, not given.

columns.name: item_vendor_id
columns.description: The VENDOR's own SKU for this item — a STRING despite the '...ID' name, and not a foreign key to anything in Lightspeed. Never join on it; it is for matching supplier paperwork and can be blank or duplicated across items.

columns.name: item_description
columns.description: The item's description as captured on this receipt — a point-in-time snapshot, so it can differ from the product's current name after a rename. This is the field the API exposes for sorting under the key `description`.

tables.grain: one supplier the account buys from
tables.description: One row per supplier: the party that fulfils purchase orders and receives vendor returns, with the trading terms the shop holds with them (account number, price level, purchasing currency) and the catalogue-sync behaviour switches. This is a small reference list, NOT a spend table — order counts, spend and lead times all come from ls_purchase_orders. It is also not a contacts table: people, addresses and reps sit behind relations.
gotchas: This is a lookup list with no measures. Every 'how much do we spend with X' question is answered on ls_purchase_orders; the only numeric column here is an exchange rate.

VERIFIED LIVE: the same brand can exist as two or more vendor records (direct vs distributor), so grouping spend by name merges genuinely different trading relationships while grouping by vendor_id splits one brand. Say which you did.
Archived vendors still own their historical POs. Filtering archived = false in a spend report deletes that history rather than excluding inactive suppliers from a shortlist.
account_number is the shop's confidential account WITH the supplier. It is not an internal key and should be redacted by default.

update_price / update_cost / update_description are forward-looking behaviour switches for what happens when a catalogue item is added to a PO. They are not data-quality indicators and they do not describe existing items.
purchasing_currency_rate is today's default, not the rate any historical PO used. Use ls_purchase_orders.vendor_currency_rate (or the shipment's) for anything historical.

Contact people, addresses, phones and rep names live behind the Contact reference and the Reps collection. Contact is carried here as raw JSON; Reps has no documented member fields at all and is therefore not modelled.
Only vendorID, timeStamp and name are documented sort keys.

columns.name: vendor_id
columns.description: Unique supplier id; the target of ls_purchase_orders.vendor_id and ls_vendor_returns.vendor_id. Note that 0 is used as an 'absent vendor' sentinel on those tables and will never match a row here.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Supplier name exactly as the shop typed it — a brand or a distributor. Not normalised and not unique: VERIFIED LIVE, the same brand can exist as several vendor records (bought direct and through a distributor), so summing spend by name silently merges or splits suppliers.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the supplier is retired from the picker. Archived vendors still own all their historical purchase orders, so filtering them out of a spend report deletes real history — filter them only from 'who can we order from today' questions.

columns.name: account_number
columns.description: The shop's own account number WITH this supplier (our customer number at their end), not an internal id. Commercially confidential — redact by default and never surface in shared output unless explicitly asked.

columns.name: price_level
columns.description: Name of the pricing tier the business trades on with this supplier — usually '1','2','3' running from HIGHEST price to lowest, so a numerically larger level is normally the better deal. A free-text label, not an enforced enum, and it does not by itself price anything.

columns.name: update_price
columns.description: Behaviour switch: when true, adding a catalogue item to a purchase order refreshes the item's RETAIL price from the catalogue MSRP. It changes future data, it is not a description of past orders.

columns.name: update_cost
columns.description: Behaviour switch: when true, adding a catalogue item to a purchase order refreshes the item's COST from the catalogue entry. Vendors with this off are where stale item costs (and therefore wrong margins) accumulate.

columns.name: update_description
columns.description: Behaviour switch: when true, adding a catalogue item to a purchase order overwrites the item's description from the catalogue entry — which is how carefully edited local descriptions get reverted.

columns.name: share_sell_through
columns.description: True when the shop has agreed that this vendor may receive sell-through data. A data-sharing consent flag with commercial consequences; it says nothing about how much is bought from them.

columns.name: b2b_seller_uid
columns.description: The vendor's unique identifier in NuORDER (Lightspeed's B2B platform). Non-empty is a reliable marker that this supplier is wired for B2B ordering; it pairs with ls_purchase_orders.b2b_order_uid on the resulting orders.

columns.name: contact
columns.description: Raw JSON of the supplier's contact record — addresses, phone numbers, emails, websites. Kept as JSON because the Contact object's own field table is documented in the contacts domain, not in this domain's ground truth, so no column names can be promised here. Contains named individuals: treat as personal data.

columns.name: purchasing_currency_code
columns.description: Currency the shop buys from this supplier in (e.g. 'USD'). It seeds ls_purchase_orders.vendor_currency_code but does not override it — an existing PO keeps the code it was raised with.

columns.name: purchasing_currency_symbol
columns.description: Display symbol for the purchasing currency (e.g. '$'). Presentation only, and ambiguous across currencies that share a glyph — never use it to identify a currency; use purchasing_currency_code.

columns.name: purchasing_currency_rate
columns.description: The vendor's CURRENT default exchange rate, used to seed new purchase orders. It is a live default, not history: the rate that priced any given PO is ls_purchase_orders.vendor_currency_rate, captured at order time. Restating past spend with this rate silently rewrites history.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of the vendor record and the incremental-sync high-water mark. Not a trading date — it moves when someone edits an address, not when an order is placed.

tables.grain: one vendor return document raised at one shop for one vendor
tables.description: One row per return of stock BACK TO a supplier — warranty batches, faulty goods, agreed stock swaps — with the cost value the shop expects to be credited. Header only. It is NOT a customer refund (those are negative sales in the commerce domain) and it is NOT itemised here: the ground-truth documentation exposes the VendorReturnItems relation but none of its member fields, so per-item return quantities are not queryable from this layer.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: the probed store has ZERO vendor returns, so an empty result set here is normal and not a broken query or a permissions problem. Say 'no vendor returns recorded' rather than reporting an error.
Money on this table is inventory COST credited back by a supplier. It is not a customer refund — customer refunds are negative sales in the commerce domain — and it is not retail value.

The line items are NOT modelled: the ground truth documents the VendorReturnItems relation (and VendorReturnItems.Item / VendorReturnItems.VendorReturnItemReason) but no member fields, so per-item quantities, costs and return reasons cannot be queried. Only header subtotal/total are available, which means 'why are we returning stock' is unanswerable from this layer.
status is documented by example only ('open', 'sent'), not as a closed enum. Do not assume a completed/credited state exists, and do not treat an unexpected value as an error.
There is no createTime on this object. sent_at is null until dispatch, so returns in progress have only updated_at as a date — period reports must declare which date they used.
total already includes the ship_cost and other_cost adjustments; subtotal is goods only. Adding the cost columns to total double counts them.
Nothing here records whether the supplier actually issued the credit. A 'sent' return with no matching credit is invisible to this API and has to be reconciled outside it.
Only vendorReturnID and timeStamp are documented sort keys.

columns.name: vendor_return_id
columns.description: Unique id of the vendor return document. There is no separate human-facing RMA number in Lightspeed — the supplier's RMA is typed into ref_number.

columns.name: vendor_id
columns.description: Supplier the stock is being sent back TO; joins ls_vendors.vendor_id. As on purchase orders, treat 0 as null so a supplier-less legacy record does not appear as a phantom 'vendor 0'.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: The shop the stock is LEAVING — the location that loses the inventory, not the vendor's address. Joins the locations domain (canonical `location` / `stock_location`).

columns.name: ref_number
columns.description: Free-text external reference, in practice the supplier's RMA or credit-note number. Not unique, not validated, often blank; a blank one on a sent return usually means nobody has chased the credit.

columns.name: status
columns.description: Lifecycle state of the return. The docs give only examples ('open', 'sent') rather than a closed set, so unseen values are possible and must not be treated as errors. There is no documented 'credited' state — receipt of the supplier credit is not tracked on this object at all.
columns.enums: open = still being assembled in the shop, stock not yet dispatched; sent = dispatched to the vendor (documented as examples, not an exhaustive list)

columns.name: sent_at
columns.description: When the return was dispatched to the vendor. NULL while the return is still open, so any 'returns this quarter' figure must state whether it counts dispatch date (this) or last activity (updated_at) — the two give different answers for returns still being assembled.

columns.name: ship_cost
columns.description: Shipping cost incurred on the return, in the shop's currency. A cost to us that reduces the net benefit of the return; per the total field's definition it is an adjustment already reflected in total, so do not add it again.

columns.name: other_cost
columns.description: Other costs on the return (restocking fees, handling). Treated as an adjustment inside total; by analogy with the Order object a negative value would be a credit rather than a charge.

columns.name: hide_vendor_details
columns.description: True when the vendor's details are suppressed on the printed return document. A presentation switch only — it has no effect on the data returned by the API and none on the value of the return.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the return has been archived. Archived returns are settled or abandoned paperwork; leaving them in an 'outstanding credits' report overstates what is owed to the shop.

columns.name: subtotal
columns.description: Cost value of the goods being returned, before ship_cost/other_cost adjustments. This is inventory COST leaving the building, never retail value and never a customer refund.

columns.name: total
columns.description: Total cost value of the return INCLUDING adjustments — the credit the shop expects from the supplier. total minus subtotal is the adjustment effect; adding ship_cost or other_cost on top double counts them.

columns.name: vendor_name
columns.description: Denormalised supplier name from the embedded Vendor relation for readable grouping. Null when vendor_id is absent or 0, exactly as on purchase orders.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of the record and the incremental-sync high-water mark. This object documents no createTime, so updated_at and sent_at are the ONLY timestamps available — there is no way to know when a return was first raised.

tables.grain: one row per Customer record (one POS customer identity, account-wide, not one human being)
tables.description: The CRM master record: names, company/tax identifiers, date of birth, archive state, and the foreign keys that drive register behaviour (customer type, discount, tax category, store credit account). It is NOT a de-duplicated person table and NOT a purchase-history table: one human commonly owns several customer rows, and walk-in sales carry no customer at all. Contact details (email/phone/address/opt-outs) live in ls_contacts and its child tables, reached via contact_id.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: duplicate POS identities are the norm — the register, webstore and workshop each create their own customer row, so one human owns several customer_ids. Before computing lifetime value, visit counts or 'how many customers do we have', resolve identities by fuzzy-matching first_name/last_name (both push down as server-side LIKE) plus email, and treat the whole matching id set as one person.

VERIFIED LIVE: walk-in sales reference no customer at all, so every 'revenue per customer' or 'repeat rate' built from sales covers identified customers only and understates volume. State that caveat in the answer.

VERIFIED LIVE: dob's date part is the real birthday but the YEAR frequently equals the year the record was created (observed dob years matching createTime). Use month/day for birthday campaigns; never publish an age distribution from this column without checking the year spread.

VERIFIED LIVE: deleting a customer archives it (and cascades archived = true to its credit account) instead of removing it, and plain listings return unarchived customers only. archived pushes down, so decide the scope explicitly rather than inheriting the default.

VERIFIED LIVE: the API returns 0 rather than null for creditAccountID, customerTypeID, discountID and taxCategoryID. Load them as NULL or every 'has a discount / has store credit' count is wrong by the size of the whole table.
VERIFIED LIVE: updated_at moves on bulk and integration edits, so it is not a proxy for last activity. Last-visit questions must come from the sales domain.
There is no shop/location field on Customer: customers are account-wide, shared across every shop. 'Customers per store' can only be derived from where they transacted, not from this table.
Marketing opt-outs (noEmail/noPhone/noMail) live on the Contact relation, not on Customer. A campaign audience built from this table alone silently ignores opt-outs — always join ls_contacts.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of this POS customer identity. Load-bearing distinction: it identifies a RECORD, not a person — the register, webstore and workshop each mint their own record, so one human often owns several customer_ids. Never null, never reused. Join target for ls_credit_accounts.customer_id, ls_ship_tos.customer_id and (sales domain) sale.customerID.

columns.name: first_name
columns.description: Customer's given name. Free text, unnormalised (case and whitespace vary by who typed it). Blank on business accounts where only company is filled. Pushes down as a fuzzy server-side LIKE match, which makes it the main tool for finding duplicate identities.

columns.name: last_name
columns.description: Customer's family name. Same unnormalised free text as first_name and blank on company-only records. Pushes down as a fuzzy server-side LIKE match.

columns.name: full_name
columns.description: Convenience display name derived by concatenating first_name and last_name, falling back to company when both person names are blank. Presentation only — never group by it for identity, since duplicates differ by spacing and case.

columns.name: dob
columns.description: Documented as the customer's date of birth, stored as a datetime at store-local midnight, so only the date part is meaningful. Null/absent for most customers. Treat the YEAR as unreliable: it is frequently the year the record was keyed rather than a birth year, so use the month/day for birthday campaigns and sanity-check before computing ages.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the customer has been archived. Deleting a customer in the POS archives it (and its credit account) rather than removing it, and plain list responses exclude archived rows unless you ask for them. Any all-time customer count must decide explicitly whether archived rows are in scope.

columns.name: title
columns.description: The customer's JOB title (e.g. Purchasing Manager) — not an honorific like Mr/Ms, and not a record label. Free text, almost always empty outside B2B accounts.

columns.name: company
columns.description: Name of the company this customer belongs to. Populated for clubs, schools, fleet and wholesale buyers; it is the display fallback when person names are blank. Free text with no company master behind it, so the same business appears under several spellings.

columns.name: company_registration_number
columns.description: The customer's company registration number (ABN/company number depending on locale). Stored as text — never coerce to a number, leading zeros are significant. Rarely filled.

columns.name: vat_number
columns.description: The customer's VAT/GST registration number, as text. Presence does NOT make the customer tax exempt — exemption comes from tax_category_id; the two are commonly confused.

columns.name: create_time
columns.description: When the customer record was created, i.e. when this identity first entered the system. The correct basis for new-customer counts, but because duplicates exist it counts new RECORDS, not new humans. Immutable.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of the record. Bumps on any edit including bulk/integration updates, so it is NOT a last-visit or last-purchase proxy — deriving recency from it silently overstates engagement. Use it only for incremental sync and change detection.

columns.name: credit_account_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the customer's store credit account in ls_credit_accounts. Sentinel: the API returns 0 when the customer has no account — normalise 0 to NULL, otherwise counts of 'customers with store credit' include everyone.

columns.name: customer_type_id
columns.description: Foreign key to ls_customer_types (the segment: VIP, Club, Wholesale, Staff...). Sentinel: 0 means untyped and must be normalised to NULL. In most stores the majority of customers are untyped, so any segmentation report needs an explicit 'No type' bucket or it silently drops most of the base.

columns.name: discount_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the Discount (pricing domain) auto-applied at the register for this customer. Sentinel 0 = no discount, normalise to NULL. Load-bearing for margin analysis: these customers' sale totals are systematically lower with no manual discount ever recorded on the sale.

columns.name: tax_category_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the TaxCategory (tax domain, canonical tax_code) that overrides normal tax for this customer, e.g. tax-exempt bodies or export customers. Sentinel 0 = standard tax applies, normalise to NULL. Misreading this makes tax-collected reconciliations plausible but wrong.

columns.name: contact_id
columns.description: Id of the Contact block carrying this customer's emails, phones, postal address and marketing opt-outs. Join key to ls_contacts.contact_id. Only present when the Contact relation was requested; live responses also echo a top-level customerID-adjacent contactID.

columns.name: contact_json
columns.description: Raw Contact subtree kept verbatim for anything the normalised tables do not flatten. Shape warning: Emails.ContactEmail, Phones.ContactPhone, Addresses.ContactAddress and Websites.ContactWebsite are a plain OBJECT when there is one entry, an ARRAY when there are several, and an empty STRING when there are none, so any extractor must try both $.Emails.ContactEmail.address and $.Emails.ContactEmail[0].address.

columns.name: custom_field_values_json
columns.description: Raw CustomFieldValues subtree, NULL when the customer has none. Same object-vs-array polymorphism: one value arrives as {CustomFieldValue:{...}}, several as an array under the same key. The normalised, queryable form is ls_customer_custom_field_values; this column exists for fields added after the loader shipped.

tables.grain: one row per Contact record (the single contact block attached to a Customer, CreditAccount or ShipTo)
tables.description: The shared contact block: exactly one postal address plus the three marketing opt-out flags, and the parent of the multi-valued email, phone and website child tables. Documented as at most one address per contact, so address lines are flattened here legitimately. This is NOT a per-person table — the same human's several customer records each carry their own contact block, and a ShipTo contact is a delivery destination that may name someone else entirely.
tables.endpoint: Customer.json (load_relations=Contact); same object also arrives on CreditAccount.json and ShipTo.json
gotchas: The Contact object is published on the Employee endpoint page, so that page's endpoint description, GET paths, load_relations (EmployeeRole, EmployeeRights) and sortable fields (employeeID) belong to Employee and NOT to Contact. Contact is never fetched on its own — it only ever arrives embedded in a parent via load_relations=Contact.

Documented limitation: only ONE address can be stored per contact, which is why address lines are columns here rather than a child table. Emails, phones and websites are genuinely multi-valued and are normalised out.

VERIFIED LIVE: the containers are polymorphic — Emails.ContactEmail (and Phones/Addresses/Websites) is an OBJECT for a single entry, an ARRAY for several, and an empty STRING when absent. A loader that assumes arrays drops every single-entry contact, which is most of them.
The three opt-out flags are negatives. Reading no_email = true as 'has email' inverts the entire campaign audience — this is the single most damaging misreading in this domain.
zip and country_code are documented as possibly empty; geographic roll-ups should fall back city -> state_code -> state and report an 'unknown' bucket rather than silently dropping rows.

Opt-outs are stored per contact block, not per person. A customer with duplicate records can be opted out on one and contactable on another; resolve to the strictest flag across the identity set before mailing.

columns.name: contact_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the contact block. Join key from ls_customers.contact_id, ls_credit_accounts.contact_id and ls_ship_tos.contact_id, and the parent key of ls_contact_emails / ls_contact_phones / ls_contact_websites.

columns.name: owner_object
columns.description: Which parent the contact block hung off: 'Customer', 'CreditAccount' or 'ShipTo'. Load-bearing because the three populations are different kinds of thing — a ShipTo contact is a delivery address for one parcel, not the customer's address on file. Any mailing-list query must filter owner_object = 'Customer'.
columns.enums: Customer | CreditAccount | ShipTo

columns.name: owner_id
columns.description: Primary key of the parent record the contact block came from, interpreted according to owner_object. Denormalised so the contact can be traced back without three outer joins.

columns.name: address1
columns.description: The contact's street address, first line. Free text, frequently empty unless the store ships or delivers to the customer. Not validated against any address service.

columns.name: address2
columns.description: Second address line: apartment, suite, unit, care-of. Often empty even when address1 is filled; do not treat emptiness as a bad address.

columns.name: city
columns.description: Postal address city or suburb, free text and unnormalised (spelling and case vary), so group with lower(trim(city)) for catchment analysis.

columns.name: state
columns.description: Postal address state/province as free text, e.g. 'Victoria'. Use state_code when you need a stable key — this column mixes full names and abbreviations.

columns.name: state_code
columns.description: ISO code for the state/province, e.g. 'VIC'. The stable grouping key when populated; falls back to empty on hand-typed addresses.

columns.name: zip
columns.description: Postal/zip code. Documented as possibly empty even on otherwise complete addresses. Always text — leading zeros are significant and numeric casting corrupts US and European codes.

columns.name: country
columns.description: Postal address country as free text; often the store's own country by default rather than a deliberate entry.

columns.name: country_code
columns.description: ISO code for the country. Documented as possibly empty even when country is filled, so never use it alone to split domestic from export customers.

columns.name: no_email
columns.description: True when the contact has opted OUT of email messages. Note the negative sense: no_email = false means emailable. Every outbound email audience must filter no_email = false or the store sends to people who unsubscribed.

columns.name: no_mail
columns.description: True when the contact has opted OUT of postal mail. Independent of no_email — a customer can accept post and refuse email.

columns.name: no_phone
columns.description: True when the contact has opted OUT of phone calls. Apply to call and SMS lists; the API has no separate SMS flag.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of the contact block. Changes when any email, phone, address or opt-out changes, so it is useful for consent-change auditing but says nothing about customer activity.

tables.grain: one row per email address held on a contact
tables.description: The multi-valued email addresses of a contact, one row each, with the documented Primary/Secondary use type. Exists as its own table because a contact can hold several addresses; flattening them onto the customer would silently pick one and hide the rest. It is NOT a consent table — the opt-out flag lives on ls_contacts.no_email.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: single-entry contacts return Emails.ContactEmail as a plain object and empty ones return an empty string, not an empty array — the exploder must normalise all three shapes or most contacts produce zero email rows.
Selecting an email without filtering use_type = 'Primary' (or MIN(entry_index)) fans the join out and double-counts customers in any audience count.

The same address recurs across many contacts because duplicate customer records share it. Email is therefore the best available identity-resolution key in this domain, but grouping by it merges genuine household sharers too.
This table records addresses on file, not permission. Always join ls_contacts and filter no_email = false before building a send list.

columns.name: contact_id
columns.description: Owning contact block. Join to ls_contacts.contact_id, and through it to the customer.

columns.name: entry_index
columns.description: Zero-based position of this address inside the parent's email container, needed only because the API gives email entries no id of their own. Position is not stable across syncs — never store it as a durable key outside a single load.

columns.name: email_address
columns.description: The email address itself. Note the API field is literally called 'address' inside the email container, which is easily confused with the postal address1/address2 fields on the same Contact object. Unvalidated free text: typos, duplicates across customers and role addresses (info@) all occur.

columns.name: use_type
columns.description: Which slot this address occupies: Primary or Secondary. Distinct from the phone useType enum on the same object. Treat 'Primary' as the send-to address; when absent, fall back to the lowest entry_index.
columns.enums: Primary | Secondary

tables.grain: one row per phone number held on a contact
tables.description: The multi-valued phone numbers of a contact, one row each, tagged with the documented Home/Work/Mobile/Pager/Fax use type. Its own table because contacts routinely hold two or three numbers. It carries no consent: call/SMS permission is ls_contacts.no_phone.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: single-entry contacts return Phones.ContactPhone as a plain object, several as an array and none as an empty string; the first listed number is in practice the mobile, but that is a convention, not a guarantee.
Do not build SMS lists with 'the first phone number' — filter use_type = 'Mobile', or Fax and Pager numbers end up in the send.
Numbers are unnormalised free text, so joining customers on raw phone_number finds far fewer duplicates than it should. Strip non-digits and compare the trailing 9-10 digits.
Permission still lives on the parent: filter ls_contacts.no_phone = false for calls and SMS.

columns.name: contact_id
columns.description: Owning contact block. Join to ls_contacts.contact_id.
