columns.name: entry_index
columns.description: Zero-based position within the parent's phone container; phone entries carry no id of their own. Not stable across reloads — use it for ordering within a single snapshot only.

columns.name: phone_number
columns.description: The phone number exactly as typed: spaces, dashes, brackets and missing country codes all occur. Always text — leading zeros and '+' are significant. Normalise to digits before matching numbers across records.

columns.name: use_type
columns.description: What kind of number this is: Home, Work, Mobile, Pager or Fax. Distinct enum from the email useType on the same Contact object. Mobile is the SMS-capable slot; Fax and Pager rows must be excluded from any contact campaign.
columns.enums: Home | Work | Mobile | Pager | Fax

tables.grain: one row per website URL held on a contact
tables.description: The multi-valued website URLs attached to a contact. Almost always empty for retail consumers and populated only for business accounts. Separate table purely because the container is an array; there is no use-type or label on a website entry.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: the Websites container comes back as an empty STRING for the overwhelming majority of contacts, so this table is typically near-empty. An empty result means 'nobody filled it in', not a load failure.
The docs list only a bare 'url' field for this container — there is no use type, no primary flag and no ordering guarantee, so 'the customer's website' is whatever entry_index 0 happens to be.

columns.name: contact_id
columns.description: Owning contact block. Join to ls_contacts.contact_id.

columns.name: entry_index
columns.description: Zero-based position within the parent's website container; website entries carry no id. Snapshot-local only.

columns.name: url
columns.description: The URL as typed. Often missing its scheme (www.example.com rather than https://www.example.com), so prepend a scheme before rendering it as a link. Not validated or reachable-checked.

tables.grain: one row per customer type (segment definition)
tables.description: Lookup of customer segments such as VIP, Club, Wholesale or Staff. Attaching a customer of a given type at the register automatically applies that type's discount and tax category, which is how club and staff pricing is actually implemented. It is a definition table only: it holds no customer counts and no revenue.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: most customers in a typical store are untyped (customerTypeID = 0 -> NULL), so segment reports must LEFT JOIN and carry an explicit 'No type' bucket or they quietly describe a small minority of the base.

A type's discount is applied automatically at the register, so typed customers show systematically lower sale totals with no manual discount recorded. Comparing average order value across segments without this in mind attributes a pricing rule to customer behaviour.

The type applies at the time of sale by whoever attached the customer. Retyping a customer today does not retroactively change historic sales, so segment revenue reports built by joining today's type onto old sales are approximate.
The table is tiny (usually under twenty rows) and has no timestamp field at all — there is no way to tell when a type was created or last changed.

columns.name: customer_type_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the segment. Referenced by ls_customers.customer_type_id, where 0 means untyped and must be read as NULL.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Description/name of the customer type as shown in the POS Type field. Free text that may carry stray leading or trailing whitespace, so trim before grouping or matching by name.

columns.name: tax_category_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the TaxCategory automatically applied at the register when a customer of this type is attached — the mechanism behind tax-exempt segments. Sentinel 0 = none, normalise to NULL. Canonical target tax_code.

columns.name: discount_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the Discount automatically applied at the register for this type. Sentinel 0 = none, normalise to NULL. Load-bearing for margin work: sales to these customers arrive already discounted with no per-sale discount record to explain the gap.

tables.grain: one row per credit account: either a customer store account or a gift card
tables.description: Two different instruments share this endpoint and this table. Customer accounts (gift_card = false) carry a running balance of money owed to the store or held on deposit for a customer. Gift cards (gift_card = true) are bearer instruments with a scannable code, remaining value and no customer link. The balance column is a CURRENT snapshot, not a transaction ledger — the movements themselves are SalePayment records in the payments domain.
tables.additivityAxis: time (updated_at): balance is a running current balance, so it may be summed ACROSS accounts at a single point in time but never summed across time or across successive syncs of the same account
gotchas: Sign convention, straight from the official reference: a NEGATIVE balance is a deposit made to the account (the store holds the customer's money) and a POSITIVE balance is an amount owed to the store. Accounts receivable = SUM(balance) over positive rows; deposits and gift value held = -SUM(balance) over negative rows. Never SUM(balance) across all rows — the two nets cancel and produce a meaningless number.

Gift cards and customer accounts share this endpoint and this table. Every query must state gift_card = true or gift_card = false; an unfiltered total mixes a customer liability with a store liability.

Documented: only the equals operator (=) works on query parameters at this endpoint. There is no server-side range filter on balance or updated_at, so anything beyond an id/code/flag lookup pulls the whole (usually small) table and filters locally.
VERIFIED LIVE: archiving a customer archives its credit account while the balance persists, so money-owed and money-held audits must deliberately include archived = true.

balance is a current snapshot with no history. 'How did the balance change last month' cannot be answered from this table — it needs the SalePayment records in the payments domain, joined on creditAccountID.
Documented: gift cards only appear in the POS UI once a completed Sale has loaded value onto them, so freshly created cards with zero balance can exist in the API and be invisible to staff.

VERIFIED LIVE: live responses also return an undocumented creditLimit field (maximum the customer may owe, 0 = no limit). It is absent from the published field reference, so it is deliberately not staged as a column here; add it only if the loader is permitted to carry undocumented fields.

columns.name: credit_account_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the credit account or gift card. Referenced by ls_customers.credit_account_id and by SalePayment.creditAccountID in the payments domain.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Label for the account. For customer accounts Lightspeed fills in the customer's name, which makes it look like a person field — it is a copy taken at creation and does not follow later customer renames. Usually blank for gift cards.

columns.name: code
columns.description: For gift cards, the barcode or numeric id scanned at the point of sale; documented as 8 to 32 characters and empty for customer credit accounts. Text, not a number — leading zeros matter. Effectively a bearer credential, so treat it as sensitive.

columns.name: description
columns.description: Free-text description of the account, typically empty. Occasionally used by staff to record why a deposit is being held; never structured enough to parse.

columns.name: gift_card
columns.description: True = a gift card (bearer code with monetary value, no customer), false = a customer store account. The single most load-bearing filter in this table: gift card float and accounts receivable are different money and summing them together produces a plausible, wrong liability figure.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the account is archived. Archiving cascades from the owning customer being archived (i.e. deleted in the POS), and the balance survives archiving. An accounts-receivable or gift-card-liability audit that filters archived = false can therefore miss real outstanding money.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the owning customer. Sentinel 0 (read as NULL) for gift cards, which by design belong to nobody. Join to ls_customers.customer_id.

columns.name: balance
columns.description: Current balance in store currency, signed from the STORE'S receivable viewpoint per the official reference: POSITIVE = the customer owes the store (on-account purchases, accounts receivable); NEGATIVE = a deposit has been made, i.e. the store holds the customer's money (prepayment, or remaining value on a gift card); 0 = settled. Getting the sign backwards inverts every liability and receivable figure in the store.

columns.name: contact_id
columns.description: Contact block attached to the account, available only when the Contact relation is requested. Rarely useful for customer accounts (the customer already has one) and normally absent on gift cards. Joins ls_contacts.contact_id.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of the record, which in practice means the last time the balance moved. The nearest thing to a 'last activity' date for an account, but it cannot distinguish a payment from a metadata edit.

tables.grain: one row per ShipTo record (one shipment destination created for a sale that needs sending)
tables.description: The store's shipping queue and history: a record is created when a sale has to be shipped to the customer, carrying the recipient name, a free-text note, the shipped flag and the destination address via the Contact relation. It is a fulfilment tracker, not a carrier integration — there is no tracking number, carrier, cost or dispatch timestamp anywhere in the object.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: live rows anchor to the SALE LINE, not the sale — an undocumented saleLineID is populated while saleID and customerID both come back as 0. Because saleLineID is absent from the published field reference it is not staged as a column here; if the loader may carry undocumented fields, add it, because it is the only reliable route from a shipment to its sale, customer and item.
VERIFIED LIVE: recipient first_name/last_name are frequently blank on integration-created rows. Identify a shipment by ship_to_id and its sale line, never by the recipient name.

There is no shipped-at timestamp, no carrier, no tracking number and no shipping cost in this object. Fulfilment-time and delivery-performance questions cannot be answered from this domain; updated_at is the only available approximation.
Counting shipments is not counting parcels: several ShipTo rows can exist for one sale when different lines ship separately, so 'shipments per sale' is really 'shipment records per sale'.

The recipient name and the destination address belong to the parcel, not the customer. Never backfill a customer's address on file from a ShipTo contact — one-off delivery addresses will pollute the CRM.

columns.name: ship_to_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the shipment record. The only reliably populated key on the row.

columns.name: shipped
columns.description: True once the parcel has gone out, false while it still needs to ship. shipped = false IS the open shipping queue. Beware: there is no dispatch timestamp, so 'when did it ship' can only be approximated by updated_at.

columns.name: ship_note
columns.description: Free-text delivery instructions for the parcel (leave at door, call on arrival, gift message). Unstructured and sometimes contains customer-supplied personal detail.

columns.name: first_name
columns.description: Recipient's first name for this shipment. May legitimately differ from the buying customer (gifts, deliveries to a workplace) and is frequently blank on rows created by integrations.

columns.name: last_name
columns.description: Recipient's last name for this shipment. Same caveats as first_name — blank on integration-created rows, so never use the name as the row identifier.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the customer this shipment is for. Sentinel 0 (read as NULL) is extremely common on live data, so this is NOT a dependable path back to the customer — reach the customer through the sale instead.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the sale being shipped. Sentinel 0 (read as NULL) on rows that anchor to an individual sale line instead, which is the live norm. A shipping report joined only on sale_id silently loses most of its rows.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of the shipment record. There is no dedicated shipped-at field, so for rows with shipped = true this is the closest available proxy for the dispatch date — it is a proxy, not a fact, and later edits move it.

columns.name: contact_json
columns.description: The destination address, i.e. where the parcel is going, taken from the Contact relation. Addresses.ContactAddress holds the ship-to address with the same object-or-array-or-empty-string polymorphism as the customer contact. This is the delivery address for this parcel and may differ from the customer's address on file.

columns.name: contact_id
columns.description: Id of the destination contact block; join to ls_contacts.contact_id where owner_object = 'ShipTo' for a normalised address. Only present when the Contact relation was requested.

tables.grain: one row per custom field definition available on customers
tables.description: The schema for store-defined customer attributes: name, data type, units, rounding precision, archive state and default value. It defines what CAN be recorded; the values actually recorded live in ls_customer_custom_field_values and the picklist options in ls_custom_field_choices. Reading a value without its definition here is how numbers get misparsed.
gotchas: The published field reference for this object sits on the Order-CustomField page (GET /Order/CustomField.json), but the same object shape serves customer custom fields at GET /Account/{accountID}/Customer/CustomField.json. Point the loader at the Customer path for this domain — the Order path returns order field definitions instead.

Type drives parsing. single_choice and multi_choice values are CustomFieldChoice objects with a customFieldChoiceID, not literals, so they must be resolved through ls_custom_field_choices; treating the id as the answer yields numeric garbage.

Documented: single_choice and multi_choice fields must have at least one choice and can hold at most 64, and the last remaining choice cannot be deleted. A choice-typed field therefore always has options even if none are in use.
name is editable on the definition; only custom_field_id is stable. Any saved query filtering on the field label breaks silently the day someone fixes a typo.

No timeStamp is published on the CustomField object itself even though the endpoint advertises timeStamp as a sortable field, so there is no reliable change-detection column here — reload definitions in full.

columns.name: custom_field_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the custom field definition. Referenced by ls_customer_custom_field_values.custom_field_id and ls_custom_field_choices.custom_field_id.

columns.name: type
columns.description: The declared data type, which controls both the validation applied on write and how the stored value must be parsed on read. Load-bearing: a 'float' value and a 'single_choice' value both arrive as untyped JSON, and reading a choice id as a number produces a plausible but meaningless average.
columns.enums: string (up to 64 chars) | text (up to 4096 chars) | url | email | datetime | date | boolean | integer | float | single_choice | multi_choice. For single_choice and multi_choice the value is a CustomFieldChoice object carrying a pre-set customFieldChoiceID, not a literal.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The label staff see for the field. Free text and editable, so it is a display label, not a stable key — always key on custom_field_id, since renaming a field would silently break any name-based filter.

columns.name: uom
columns.description: Unit of measure for the field, up to four characters (e.g. 'kg', 'cm'). Purely descriptive — the API stores no conversion and applies no validation, so values are only comparable within one field.

columns.name: decimal_precision
columns.description: Number of decimal places floats are rounded to. Documented as settable only on float-typed fields, so it is null or meaningless for every other type. Aggregations should round to this precision to match what staff see in the POS.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the field definition is archived. Archived definitions keep their historic values, so a field can disappear from the POS while its values still populate ls_customer_custom_field_values — exclude archived definitions from 'what can we record' questions but not from historic analysis.

columns.name: default_value
columns.description: The default CustomFieldValue applied when the field is first set, typed according to type (so it may be a scalar or a CustomFieldChoice object — stored as JSON to preserve either). A value equal to the default may mean 'staff chose it' or 'nobody touched it'; the two are indistinguishable.

tables.grain: one row per selectable option on a single_choice or multi_choice custom field
tables.description: The picklist options behind choice-typed custom fields: the option's id, its display name, an optional distinct stored value, and whether it can still be deleted. Required to translate a stored customFieldChoiceID into something a human recognises. Only choice-typed fields have rows here.
gotchas: The object is published under the Item-CustomField-CustomFieldChoice page with a GET path under /Item/, and the customFieldID field's own doc link is malformed (/Customer/CustomField/{customFieldID}/{customFieldID}). The customer-scoped path is /Account/{accountID}/Customer/CustomField/{customFieldID}/CustomFieldChoice.json, and choices must be fetched per custom field — there is no account-wide list.
value is optional and often empty; the effective stored value is COALESCE(NULLIF(value,''), name). Reporting on value alone drops every choice that never got a distinct code.

Editing a choice's name rewrites history in effect: stored values reference only the id, so yesterday's reports re-label themselves. Snapshot the label alongside the id if labels must be stable over time.

Documented: at most 64 choices per field, at least one required, and the last remaining choice cannot be deleted — so an empty result for a choice-typed field means the fetch failed, not that there are no options.

columns.name: custom_field_choice_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the choice. This is the value that actually appears inside a stored single_choice/multi_choice CustomFieldValue, which is why this table is mandatory for reading those values.

columns.name: custom_field_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the owning custom field definition in ls_custom_fields. Choices are scoped to one field — the same option text under two different fields is two different ids.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The label shown to staff for this option. When no separate value is set, the name is also the stored value, and uniqueness within the field is enforced on the name in that case.

columns.name: value
columns.description: An optional stored string value that differs from the display name (e.g. name 'Gold Member', value 'GOLD'). Documented as optional, so it is frequently empty — read COALESCE(NULLIF(value,''), name) to get the effective value. Uniqueness is enforced on this field when it is set.

columns.name: can_be_deleted
columns.description: False when the choice is in use somewhere and therefore cannot be removed. A useful in-use signal: can_be_deleted = false implies at least one record currently references it, though it does not say how many or on which object type.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of the choice. Moves when the label or value is edited, which means historic values referencing this choice silently take on the new label.

tables.grain: one row per custom field value recorded on one customer
tables.description: The store-defined attributes actually recorded against customers: one row per (customer, custom field) pair, carrying the value plus a snapshot of the field's name and type at read time. This is where segmentation data that has no first-class API field lives (membership numbers, referral source, bike serial, club). Values are untyped in transport, so the type column governs how each one must be parsed.
gotchas: Values only arrive when the CustomFieldValues relation is requested, and the nested literals require CustomFieldValues.value as a second relation. Requesting only CustomFieldValues returns the wrappers without usable values.

VERIFIED LIVE: the container is polymorphic — one value arrives as {CustomFieldValue: {...}}, several as an array under the same key, and none as an empty string. A loader that assumes an array silently records zero custom fields for every single-value customer.

Absence is not a value. A customer with no row for a field has never been asked, which is different from an empty answer; LEFT JOIN and bucket the NULLs explicitly rather than reporting a percentage over rows that exist.
deleted = true rows are tombstones, not answers. Filter deleted = false in every aggregate.
name and type are copies of the definition, changeable only on the CustomField object. Filter on custom_field_id; a renamed field breaks name-based filters with no error.
Duplicate customer identities each carry their own answers, so the same human can be both 'Referral: Google' and 'Referral: Friend'. Resolve identity before profiling on custom fields.

columns.name: custom_field_value_id
columns.description: Primary key of this individual value record. Distinct from custom_field_id (the definition) — confusing the two collapses every customer's answers into one row.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: The customer this value belongs to, taken from the parent record the relation was loaded on. Join to ls_customers.customer_id. Because duplicate customer records exist, the same person can hold conflicting answers under different ids.

columns.name: custom_field_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the field definition in ls_custom_fields. The stable key for 'which question is this the answer to' — always filter on this rather than on name.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The field's name copied onto the value for convenience. Documented as updatable only on the CustomField object, so it is a read-time snapshot of the label — do not filter on it, since a rename changes it everywhere at once.

columns.name: type
columns.description: The field's type copied onto the value, also only updatable on the definition. Load-bearing: it is the only in-row signal telling you whether value_raw is a literal, a date, a boolean or a CustomFieldChoice object.
columns.enums: string | text | url | email | datetime | date | boolean | integer | float | single_choice | multi_choice

columns.name: value_raw
columns.description: The stored value, preserved as JSON because its shape depends on the field type: a scalar for string/text/url/email/integer/float/boolean/date/datetime, and a CustomFieldChoice object (or array of them for multi_choice) carrying a customFieldChoiceID otherwise. Casting blindly to text turns choice answers into JSON blobs.

columns.name: value_text
columns.description: Display rendering of value_raw: the literal for scalar types, and the resolved choice name for single_choice (choice names joined for multi_choice). Convenience only — numeric and date analysis must go back to value_raw with the type in hand.

columns.name: choice_id
columns.description: For single_choice fields, the selected choice id lifted out of value_raw so it can be joined to ls_custom_field_choices. NULL for every non-choice type and for multi_choice (which holds several, and must be read from value_raw).

columns.name: deleted
columns.description: The delete flag: setting it true on an update of the parent is how a value is removed. Rows seen with deleted = true are tombstones and must be excluded from every count, or answered questions look more complete than they are.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of this value. The only per-attribute audit trail available; it does not record the previous value, so attribute history cannot be reconstructed.

tables.grain: one row per note attached to a customer
tables.description: Free-text notes staff attach to a customer record, with a flag controlling whether the text is printed on receipts. Available on the Customer endpoint through the Note relation. Purely qualitative: it holds no structure, no author and no category, so it supports lookup and text search but not measurement.
gotchas: The Note object is published on the Order endpoint page, so that page's endpoint description, GET paths and load_relations (OrderLines, Vendor, Shop) describe Order and NOT Note. Notes are only ever retrieved embedded in a parent via load_relations=Note; there is no standalone Note endpoint.

The same Note shape attaches to several parent objects across the API. This table is scoped to notes loaded from the Customer endpoint — do not union it with order or item notes without keeping a parent discriminator.

is_public controls receipt printing. The documented example is an Item note marked public flowing through to fill the sale line note, so a public note is genuinely customer-visible; assume internal notes are candid and handle accordingly.
No author and no created-at. 'Who wrote this and when' is unanswerable from the API, and updated_at moves on every edit.

VERIFIED LIVE shape risk: like every other relation container in this domain, a single note arrives as an object and multiple notes as an array under the same key, with an empty string when there are none.

columns.name: note_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the note. The only stable handle on a note — the text itself is editable and duplicated freely between customers.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: The customer this note hangs off, taken from the parent record the relation was loaded on. Join to ls_customers.customer_id. The same Note object shape is reused on other endpoints (Order, Item, SaleLine), so a notes table without this parent key is ambiguous.

columns.name: note
columns.description: The note text. Unstructured staff free text that frequently contains personal or sensitive detail (health, disputes, payment arrangements) and sometimes replaces fields that should have been custom fields. Treat as sensitive and never expose in an aggregate export.

columns.name: is_public
columns.description: True when the note is shown on receipts and other customer-facing output; false when it is internal-only. Load-bearing for privacy: internal notes are written on the assumption the customer never sees them, so any customer-facing surface must filter is_public = true.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of the note. There is no created-at and no author field, so this is the only temporal signal and it overwrites itself on every edit — note history cannot be reconstructed.

tables.grain: one row per workorder — one service/repair ticket for one customer item (a Serialized entry) at one shop
tables.description: The header of a workshop job: who it is for, which item is being worked on, where it is in the shop's status pipeline, when it came in and when it was promised. It carries NO money of its own — every charge lives in ls_workorder_lines (labour/tasks) or ls_workorder_items (parts), and recognised revenue only exists once the job is checked out into a Sale (sale_id). This is NOT a sales table, NOT a time-clock table, and NOT a history table: status and archived are overwritten in place, so there is no record of what the board looked like last week.
tables.additivityAxis: time — workorder_status_id, status_name, archived, sale_id and eta_out are mutated in place with no history rows, so you may not sum or trend status/backlog counts across past periods; only the CURRENT board state is knowable. Counting jobs by time_in (an immutable intake event) is safe.
gotchas: NO REVENUE LIVES IN THIS DOMAIN. Prices on workorder lines and items are quoted charges on a job sheet. Recognised workshop revenue is on the Sale created at checkout (reachable via sale_id) — the Checkout endpoint copies every WorkorderItem and WorkorderLine into SaleLines. Summing workorder charges and sale lines together double-counts every completed job.
VERIFIED LIVE: eta_out is defaulted to time_in when staff never enter an ETA. Any due/overdue report must exclude eta_out = time_in or it invents overdue work that was never promised.
VERIFIED LIVE: the header-level tax flag can be false while all of the job's lines are taxed. Never read tax treatment from ls_workorders.tax.

VERIFIED LIVE: status names are store-configured — the reference store has 13 statuses including custom boards named TODAY, TO ORDER, VAN, Nest, Staff, Non-Bike and 'Finished + Text Sent'. Never hardcode a status name; resolve it through ls_workorder_statuses.system_value.

VERIFIED LIVE: unset foreign keys come back as 0, not null (customer_id, employee_id, sale_id, discount_id, serialized_id). Normalise 0 to NULL on ingest, otherwise 'jobs with no customer' all aggregate under a fictitious customer 0 and 'unbilled' tests written as sale_id IS NULL match nothing.

VERIFIED LIVE: live responses carry an undocumented systemSku field (e.g. 250000000022) — the job number printed on the tag and the number staff quote. It is absent from the published field reference so it is deliberately NOT a column here; if humans reference job numbers you will need to source it outside this spec.
archived = true is the store's 'done and filed' state, not deletion. Because Lightspeed itself excludes archived jobs from its totals, a dashboard that includes them will disagree with the POS.
There is no status history. The row shows only the current status, so 'how many jobs were open at the end of last month' is unanswerable from this table — it requires a snapshotting job downstream.

Turnaround time has no clean pair of timestamps: time_in is real, but there is no completed_at. The nearest proxies are updated_at (contaminated by any later edit) or the linked sale's completion timestamp, which is the more defensible choice.

Bulk loading: only nested endpoints are documented for lines/items/images (GET /Workorder/{workorderID}/WorkorderLine.json etc.). Scanning them one job at a time is N+1; load Workorder.json with load_relations and explode the embedded arrays instead.

columns.name: workorder_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the job, account-scoped. The join key for ls_workorder_lines.workorder_id, ls_workorder_items.workorder_id and ls_workorder_images.workorder_id. This is NOT the job number staff read off the tag (see gotchas re: the undocumented systemSku).

columns.name: time_in
columns.description: When the item was received/booked in. The immutable intake event date and the ONLY correct basis for 'how many jobs came in this month'. Store-local wall time with no reliable offset — do not convert timezones. Commonly confused with updated_at (last modification), which drifts every time anyone touches the job.

columns.name: eta_out
columns.description: The promise date: when the job is expected to be finished. Basis for 'due today / overdue' questions. VERIFIED LIVE: Lightspeed writes eta_out = time_in when staff never set an ETA, so equality with time_in is a 'no promise recorded' sentinel, not a same-day promise — treating it as real manufactures a mountain of fake overdue jobs.

columns.name: note
columns.description: Customer-facing notes for the whole job: what was asked for, what was quoted, what the customer reported. Frequently the richest free text on the record (multi-line). Distinct from the per-task note on ls_workorder_lines and the per-part note on ls_workorder_items.

columns.name: internal_note
columns.description: Staff-only notes never shown to the customer. Treat as internal commentary (diagnosis, do-not-serve flags, pricing rationale); never surface verbatim in customer-facing output.

columns.name: warranty
columns.description: True when the WHOLE job is warranty work and the customer will not be charged. Job-level override: quoted value of a warranty job is zero revenue no matter what prices sit on its lines. Individual lines carry their own warranty flag, so a non-warranty job can still contain free lines.

columns.name: tax
columns.description: Documented as 'does this workorder have tax charged on it'. VERIFIED LIVE: unreliable — jobs are seen with tax = false while every one of their item and labour lines carries tax = true. Never derive tax treatment from this column; use the line-level tax flags.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the job is archived: hidden in the POS and explicitly excluded from every total Lightspeed reports. Current-workload and open-board questions MUST filter archived = false; historical/lifetime questions must not, or they silently drop most of the store's history.

columns.name: hook_in
columns.description: Free-text storage location (hook/rack/bay number) where the item waits for work to START. VERIFIED LIVE: empty at stores that do not run a hook system, so blank means 'feature unused', not 'item missing'.
columns.enums: free text, store-defined

columns.name: hook_out
columns.description: Free-text storage location where the finished item waits for customer PICKUP. Same 'blank means unused' caveat as hook_in. A non-empty hook_out is a decent proxy for 'physically finished and racked' at stores that use it.
columns.enums: free text, store-defined

columns.name: save_parts
columns.description: True when the customer asked to keep the parts removed from the item, to be handed back with the job. A customer-service instruction only — it has no effect on pricing, stock or the charges on the job.

columns.name: assign_employee_to_all
columns.description: Admin behaviour flag: when true the job's employee_id is auto-stamped onto every line. Consequence for analysis — when true, the employee_id on lines is inherited rather than a real statement of who did that task, so per-mechanic productivity from lines is only trustworthy where this is false.

columns.name: customer_id
columns.description: FK to the customer the job is for. VERIFIED LIVE: R-Series returns 0 (not null) for unset FKs — normalise 0 to NULL on ingest or every 'unknown customer' job collides on id 0 and produces a giant phantom customer.

columns.name: discount_id
columns.description: FK to a job-level Discount applied to the whole workorder. 0/NULL means none. The discount's percentage/amount lives in the discounts reference table; nothing on this row tells you the discounted value.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: FK to the employee IN CHARGE of the job (service writer / owner), not necessarily the person who performed the tasks. Per-mechanic workload must come from ls_workorder_lines.employee_id; using this column instead silently attributes an entire job to one name. 0 means unassigned.

columns.name: serialized_id
columns.description: FK to the Serialized entry for the customer's item being worked on (the bike/machine, tracked by serial). This is a customer-owned item record, NOT a catalog product and NOT stock on hand. 0 when the job is not tied to a serialized item.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: FK to the Shop (physical location) where the work is to be performed. For multi-location accounts this is the correct location axis for workshop capacity questions; it is the job's shop, which can differ from the shop of the sale that eventually bills it.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: FK to the Sale this job was checked out and paid on. NULL/0 until checkout, which makes 'sale_id IS NULL' the cleanest test for an unbilled job. The money for the job lives on THAT sale's lines, not here; joining through it is the only way to get recognised workshop revenue.

columns.name: sale_line_id
columns.description: FK to the single SaleLine that represents this job on the register once billed. Note this is the job-level line; each labour task and part also carries its own sale_line_id, so do not assume one job equals one sale line.

columns.name: workorder_status_id
columns.description: FK to the store's current status for this job. The whole pipeline lives here — there are no separate opened/closed/completed booleans on a workorder. Join ls_workorder_statuses and filter on system_value for anything that must be correct across stores.

columns.name: customer_name
columns.description: Denormalised convenience: the customer's display name (first + last, falling back to company) taken from the embedded Customer relation. Present only when the scan requests load_relations=Customer; otherwise NULL even though customer_id is set. Authoritative customer attributes live in the customers table.

columns.name: status_name
columns.description: Denormalised current status display name. STORE-CONFIGURED free text: VERIFIED LIVE the reference store runs custom boards (TODAY, TO ORDER, VAN, Nest, Staff, Non-Bike, 'Finished + Text Sent') alongside the system ones, so filtering on a guessed name silently returns zero rows. Read ls_workorder_statuses first, or filter status_system_value.

columns.name: status_system_value
columns.description: Denormalised stable status identifier for system-defined statuses. The only cross-store-safe way to say 'finished' or 'paid'. VERIFIED LIVE: it is an EMPTY STRING (not NULL) for store-created statuses, so 'is a custom board' is status_system_value = '' — an IS NOT NULL test matches everything and quietly does nothing.
columns.enums: open = job open/in progress; estimate = awaiting customer approval; waiting = waiting on parts/customer; finished = work done, awaiting pickup/payment; paid = checked out and paid; '' = store-created custom status

columns.name: item_description
columns.description: Denormalised description of the customer's item being worked on (e.g. the bike make/model) from the Serialized relation. The everyday answer to 'what is this job on'. NULL unless the scan requests load_relations=Serialized.

columns.name: item_serial
columns.description: Denormalised serial/frame number of the customer's item. VERIFIED LIVE: frequently blank because staff skip it, so absence does not mean the item is unidentified.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: Last modification of the record, store-local. Moves whenever anyone edits the job, adds a line or changes status — so it is a change-feed cursor, NOT a completion date and NOT an intake date. Using it as 'when the job happened' produces plausible but wrong monthly volumes.

tables.grain: one row per labour task or misc (non-part) charge on one workorder
tables.description: The work itself: each task performed or to be performed on a job, with its price, time estimate, assigned employee and done flag. Lightspeed routes a charge here rather than to ls_workorder_items when the underlying Item is type Non-Inventory with TaxClass 'Labor' — that routing rule, not the user, decides which table a charge lands in. These are quoted charges on a job sheet, not recognised revenue, and the hours/minutes here are shop estimates, not a payroll time clock.
gotchas: There is NO amount/total column. Line value = unit_price_override * unit_quantity when the override is set; when it is 0 the intended charge is (hours * 60 + minutes) priced at the shop's hourly service rate, and that rate is NOT exposed by this API — such lines cannot be valued from this table alone.

VERIFIED LIVE: the reference store flat-prices every task through unit_price_override with hours and minutes at 0. Any 'labour hours booked' metric therefore returns zero there, and any 'shop rate x hours' formula returns zero everywhere it is used.

This table and ls_workorder_items use DIFFERENT price column names (unit_price_override vs unit_price) and ls_workorder_items has no cost column at all. A naive UNION ALL of the two for 'total job value' will null out one side — alias explicitly.
VERIFIED LIVE: approved is routinely left false on work that was completed and paid. Never treat approved = false as customer refusal.
Quoted, not recognised. Sums here are what the job sheet says; recognised labour revenue lives on the linked sale's lines. Never add these to sales figures.

hours/minutes look like a timesheet and are not one: they are a single mutable estimate/actual field with no start or stop time and no link to a shift. Do not feed them into workforce_time_entry style analysis or payroll.
done is per task. A job with all lines done is not necessarily finished, and a finished job often has lines left not-done.
VERIFIED LIVE: unset FKs arrive as 0 rather than null (employee_id, sale_id, item_id, discount_id) — normalise on ingest or NULL-based tests silently match nothing.

columns.name: workorder_line_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the task/charge, account-scoped (not per-workorder), so it is safe as a standalone primary key.

columns.name: workorder_id
columns.description: FK to the parent job. Always populated — a line cannot exist without a workorder.

columns.name: note
columns.description: Free text for the task. In practice this IS the task title — what the mechanic wrote ('tube change', 'gear index'). There is no separate description/name field on a workorder line, so any 'what work was done' question resolves to this column or to the linked labour item_id.

columns.name: hours
columns.description: Whole-hours component of the task's duration. Documented ambiguously as time the task 'took, or is expected to take' — it is a single mutable field serving as both estimate and actual, so it can never be treated as verified worked time. Total duration = hours * 60 + minutes. VERIFIED LIVE: left at 0 at the reference store, which flat-prices tasks instead — labour-utilisation maths built on it silently returns zero.

columns.name: minutes
columns.description: Minutes component of the task duration, complementing hours (a 90-minute task is hours=1, minutes=30). Never a standalone total-minutes figure. VERIFIED LIVE: usually 0, same caveat as hours.

columns.name: unit_price_override
columns.description: Per-unit retail price for this charge. When set (> 0) it OVERRIDES the shop's hourly service rate; when 0 the charge is meant to be hours/minutes priced at the shop rate, which is not stored on this row. VERIFIED LIVE: every priced task at the reference store uses this field as a flat price with hours/minutes at 0, so line value = unit_price_override * unit_quantity. Tax-exclusive or inclusive per the tax flag and the line's tax class — this is not a total and not a tax-resolved figure.

columns.name: unit_quantity
columns.description: Units of this charge, documented as integer and usually 1 for tasks. Stored numeric so line-value arithmetic does not truncate. Always multiply by it — assuming 1 quietly under-reports multi-unit charges.

columns.name: unit_cost
columns.description: Per-unit cost to the business for this task (internal labour cost basis). Any gross-margin calculation on workshop labour rests entirely on this column. VERIFIED LIVE: 0 in most rows because stores do not maintain a labour cost, which makes naive margin = 100% — verify it is populated before reporting labour margin.

columns.name: done
columns.description: True when this individual task is complete. Task-level only: a job is finished when its workorder status says so, not when every line is done, and jobs routinely ship with lines left false. Counting 'done = false' as outstanding work is fine; counting it as unfinished JOBS is not.

columns.name: approved
columns.description: True when the customer approved this charge. VERIFIED LIVE: stores commonly skip the approval workflow entirely and leave it false even on completed, billed work — so false means 'not recorded', never 'declined'. Filtering quoted value on approved = true can zero out a real backlog.

columns.name: warranty
columns.description: True when this task is covered by warranty and the customer will NOT be charged for it. Its price still appears in unit_price_override, so any quoted/expected-revenue sum must exclude warranty = true or it inflates by the whole warranty book.

columns.name: tax
columns.description: True when this charge is taxed. Line-level and more trustworthy than the header flag on ls_workorders (VERIFIED LIVE: they disagree). Says only WHETHER tax applies — the rate comes from tax_class_id and the store's tax configuration; no tax amount is stored on this row.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: FK to the employee responsible for this task — the correct grain for per-mechanic workload and throughput. Caveat: when the parent job has assign_employee_to_all = true this value is auto-stamped from the header and reflects assignment, not who turned the spanner. 0 means unassigned.

columns.name: sale_line_id
columns.description: FK to the SaleLine that represents this task on the register once checked out. NULL/0 before checkout. This is the bridge from a quoted task to its recognised revenue row.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: FK to the Sale where this task was billed and paid. NULL/0 = not yet billed. Denormalised from the parent job, but check it per line: lines added after a partial checkout can be unbilled on an otherwise billed job.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: FK to the Non-Inventory / TaxClass=Labor Item used to create this task — i.e. the store's service-menu entry ('Full Service', 'Puncture Repair'). NULL/0 for ad-hoc labour typed in free-form, so grouping by it silently drops bespoke work. It is a catalog item id, but it holds no stock and must never be counted as a product sale.

columns.name: discount_id
columns.description: FK to a Discount applied to this charge. 0/NULL means none. The discounted amount is not stored here — unit_price_override is the pre-discount price, so quoted sums overstate any discounted line.

columns.name: tax_class_id
columns.description: FK to the TaxClass governing this line — for genuine labour this is the store's 'Labor' class, which is also the routing signal that put the charge on this table rather than ls_workorder_items.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When this task/charge was last modified. The ONLY date on the row — there is no task start, completion or performed-on date anywhere in the API. Any time series of workshop labour must join ls_workorders.time_in; using this instead reports when records were touched, not when work happened.

tables.grain: one row per part/product charge on one workorder
tables.description: The physical goods consumed on a job: tubes, chains, cables, cassettes. One row per part line on the job sheet, with the quoted retail price, quantity and the special-order flag. Charges land here rather than on ls_workorder_lines whenever the underlying Item is a normal inventory product (labour is a Non-Inventory item with TaxClass 'Labor' and goes to the lines table). Quoted charges only — no cost, no tax amount, and no stock movement happens until checkout.
gotchas: ASYMMETRY WITH LABOUR: this table has unitPrice and NO unitCost; the labour table has unitCost and unitPriceOverride and no unitPrice. Parts margin on a job sheet is therefore not computable from this table at all — you must join the catalog item for cost, and that cost is today's cost, not the cost at the time of the job.

No inventory movement happens here. A part sitting on an open workorder has not left stock; it is deducted when the job is checked out and the sale line is created. Treating these rows as consumption will double-count against inventory movements from the sale.
Quoted, not recognised. Parts revenue is recognised on the linked sale's lines. 'What did the workshop sell' is a sales question; 'what parts are committed to open jobs' is this table.
warranty = true rows are given away free — always exclude them from quoted value, and include them when measuring warranty cost exposure.
is_special_order = true with sale_id IS NULL is the practical definition of 'job blocked awaiting a part', and is far more reliable than any status name for that question.
VERIFIED LIVE: notes on part lines sometimes contain labour/task text, so do not mine this column for product information.
VERIFIED LIVE: unset FKs arrive as 0 rather than null — normalise on ingest so IS NULL tests behave.
Joining a workorder to both this table and ls_workorder_lines in one query multiplies rows (parts x labour). Aggregate each side in its own subquery first.

columns.name: workorder_item_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the part line. Documented under the workorder path but unique account-wide, so it stands alone as a primary key.

columns.name: workorder_id
columns.description: FK to the parent job. Always populated. The only route to the job's date, customer, status and archived flag — none of which exist on this row.

columns.name: approved
columns.description: True when the customer has approved this part charge. VERIFIED LIVE: stores frequently skip the approval workflow, so false means 'never recorded', not 'customer declined'. Do not gate parts value on it.

columns.name: unit_price
columns.description: Per-unit RETAIL price the part is quoted at on the job sheet — a per-unit figure, not a line total, and not necessarily the catalog price (staff can override at the job). Line value = unit_price * unit_quantity. Note the name differs from the labour table's unit_price_override.

columns.name: unit_quantity
columns.description: Quantity of the part being used/sold on the job. Documented integer, stored numeric so value arithmetic is exact. This is quoted consumption, not a stock movement — inventory is not decremented until the job is checked out to a sale.

columns.name: warranty
columns.description: True when this part is supplied under warranty and the customer is NOT charged for it. The price still populates unit_price, so warranty rows must be excluded from any quoted-value or expected-revenue sum — the part is still consumed and still costs the business.

columns.name: tax
columns.description: True when this part line is taxed. Line-level and more reliable than the header flag on ls_workorders (VERIFIED LIVE: they disagree). Unlike the labour table there is no tax_class_id here, so the applicable rate must come from the underlying item's tax class.

columns.name: is_special_order
columns.description: True when the part is not in stock and is being special-ordered for this job; Lightspeed then creates a special order reached through the linked sale line. The operational meaning is 'this job is blocked waiting on a part', which is usually the real question behind 'what is waiting on parts'.

columns.name: note
columns.description: Free-text note on the part line. VERIFIED LIVE: staff sometimes type task descriptions here rather than on a labour line, so it is not safe to assume this text describes a product.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: FK to the employee responsible for this part line — usually whoever added the part rather than who fitted it. 0 means unassigned; inherited from the header when the job has assign_employee_to_all = true.

columns.name: sale_line_id
columns.description: FK to the SaleLine this part becomes on the register at checkout. NULL/0 until then. Also the route to the special order record when is_special_order is true.

columns.name: sale_id
columns.description: FK to the Sale where the part was billed. NULL/0 = not yet billed and therefore not yet deducted from stock or recognised as revenue.

columns.name: item_id
columns.description: FK to the catalog Item this charge is for — the actual product. Join it for description, category, supplier and cost, none of which are on this row. 0/NULL for a free-text charge with no catalog product behind it.

columns.name: discount_id
columns.description: FK to a Discount applied to this part charge. 0/NULL means none. unit_price is the pre-discount price and no discounted amount is stored, so quoted sums overstate discounted lines.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When this part line was last modified. The only date on the row: there is no added-on or fitted-on date. Time series of parts consumption must use ls_workorders.time_in, or the sale date once billed.

tables.grain: one row per workorder status configured on the account (system-defined and store-created)
tables.description: The lookup for the workshop pipeline: every status a job can be in, system ones plus whatever boards the store invented. Tiny (the reference store has 13 rows) and the single most important table to read BEFORE writing any status filter, because display names are store-configured free text while only system_value is stable across accounts. It defines the pipeline; it holds no jobs, dates or money.
gotchas: Read this table FIRST for any question that names a status. Filtering ls_workorders.status_name on a guessed literal returns an empty result set that looks like a real answer ('no jobs are waiting') rather than an error.
VERIFIED LIVE: system_value is '' (empty string) for custom statuses, not NULL. Use system_value <> '' for 'system-defined' and system_value = '' for 'store invented'.

VERIFIED LIVE: custom boards carry operational meaning invented by the store (TODAY = do it today, TO ORDER = awaiting parts, VAN = mobile/on-site work, Nest, Staff, Non-Bike). Cross-store reporting must map them to system_value semantics manually or exclude them.
Multiple statuses can share the same sort_order, so add workorder_status_id as a tiebreaker for a deterministic listing.
There is no 'is terminal/closed' flag. The closest reliable end-of-pipeline test is system_value IN ('finished','paid'), reinforced by ls_workorders.sale_id IS NOT NULL for genuinely billed work.
This endpoint documents no timeStamp, so statuses cannot be incrementally synced — refetch the whole (tiny) list each run.

columns.name: workorder_status_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the status. Join target for ls_workorders.workorder_status_id. Account-specific — the same id means different things at different stores, so never hardcode one.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Display name shown in the POS. Fully store-configurable free text: VERIFIED LIVE the reference store runs Open, Estimate, Waiting, Finished, 'Done & Paid', Quote, Non-Bike, TODAY, 'TO ORDER', VAN, Staff, 'Finished + Text Sent' and Nest. Matching on a guessed name returns zero rows silently rather than erroring.

columns.name: sort_order
columns.description: Position in POS dropdowns and boards — a display ordering, not a pipeline stage number, and not monotonic with progress. Documented as a string but VERIFIED LIVE numeric; end-of-pipeline system statuses sit at the top of the range (finished = 65000, paid = 65001), so ORDER BY sort_order roughly reproduces the POS board order. Values are not unique.

columns.name: html_color
columns.description: Hex colour the POS paints this status with (e.g. #FF0000). Empty string when unset — cosmetic only, carries no semantics about urgency or completion despite red/green conventions staff may assume.

columns.name: system_value
columns.description: Stable internal identifier for statuses Lightspeed defines and locks (the store cannot rename or delete them). The ONLY status identifier safe to hardcode. VERIFIED LIVE: it is an EMPTY STRING for store-created statuses, never NULL — so 'custom board' is system_value = '' and an IS NOT NULL filter matches every row and does nothing.
columns.enums: open = job open / in progress; estimate = estimate awaiting customer approval; waiting = waiting on parts or customer; finished = work complete, awaiting pickup/payment; paid = checked out and paid; '' (empty) = store-created custom status with no stable meaning

tables.grain: one row per image attached to one workorder
tables.description: Reference photos attached to a job — damage on intake, before/after shots, a picture of the serial plate. Metadata only: the row records the filename, CDN pointers, ordering and size, never the image bytes. Useful for evidencing intake condition and for finding jobs with (or without) photographic documentation; it carries no money, no status and no bearing on charges.
gotchas: Metadata only — no image bytes. Rendering requires composing base_image_url with public_id and fetching over the network; the row alone cannot display anything.
size has no documented unit. Treat it as bytes with a caveat, never state MB as fact.
ordering is a display rank. SUM(ordering) is meaningless; the count of rows per workorder is the image count.
public_id is an unauthenticated pointer to photos of customer property. Treat image URLs as customer data even though the field is named 'public'.
Joining images to a workorder fans out the header row — aggregate to a count per workorder before joining alongside lines or items.
Documented access is per job (GET /Workorder/{workorderID}/WorkorderImage.json), which is N+1 across the account; prefer Workorder.json with load_relations=Images and explode the embedded array.

columns.name: workorder_image_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the image attachment. Identifies the attachment record, not the underlying asset — see public_id for the stored asset.

columns.name: workorder_id
columns.description: FK to the job the image is attached to. The only context this row has; every date, customer and status question requires the join.

columns.name: description
columns.description: Staff-entered caption for the image (e.g. 'scratch on down tube at intake'). Usually blank — absence of a caption says nothing about the photo's importance.

columns.name: filename
columns.description: Stored filename of the image. Often an opaque upload name (IMG_1234.jpg) rather than anything meaningful; do not parse it for dates or content.

columns.name: ordering
columns.description: Display position of this image within the job's image list — a rank, not a count and not a quantity. Never sum it. Ties are possible, so add workorder_image_id for deterministic ordering.

columns.name: public_id
columns.description: Public identifier of the stored asset, combined with base_image_url to build a retrievable URL. Being 'public' it is an unauthenticated pointer to customer-item photography — treat as sensitive and do not republish.

columns.name: base_image_url
columns.description: Base/CDN URL the image is served from. Not a complete link on its own: the usable URL is composed from this plus public_id (and any size transform the client applies).

columns.name: size
columns.description: Documented only as 'the size of the image' with no unit — conventionally bytes for a stored asset, but the docs do not state it and it could be a pixel dimension. Do not present it as MB without verifying against a known file; summing it yields storage volume at best.

columns.name: create_time
columns.description: When the image was uploaded. The genuine event date for the attachment and the right basis for 'were intake photos taken on arrival' — compare it with ls_workorders.time_in. Distinct from updated_at, which moves on any metadata edit.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When the attachment record was last modified (caption edits, reordering). A sync cursor, not the upload date — use create_time for that.

tables.grain: one row per shop (physical store location) on the account, including archived ones
tables.description: The physical store locations on the account. A Shop owns the Registers inside it, the Sales rung through those registers, its own per-shop inventory quantities and Orders, and it carries the location-level defaults: timezone, workshop labour rate, default sales-tax category and default price level. This is NOT a stock bucket in its own right (per-shop quantities live on ItemShop in the inventory domain) and it is NOT a legal entity (that is the Account).
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: the Shop field table publishes NO timeStamp / createTime column, even though most other R-Series objects have one. You cannot ask 'when was this shop last changed' from the documented surface. Do not add a timestamp column by analogy with other endpoints.

VERIFIED LIVE: live Shop payloads return extra keys the V3 field table omits entirely -- companyRegistrationNumber, vatNumber, zebraBrowserPrint, gatewayConfigID (a UUID string, not a number) and networkHealthTool. They are deliberately NOT modelled here because they are not in the published field table; if you need the VAT/ABN number or the modern payments config, read the raw payload and treat it as unversioned.

VERIFIED LIVE: cc_gateway_id is 0 on modern accounts because the real payments configuration moved to the undocumented gatewayConfigID UUID. Never conclude 'this shop cannot take credit cards' from a null cc_gateway_id.

VERIFIED LIVE: every foreign key on this object (contactID, taxCategoryID, receiptSetupID, ccGatewayID, priceLevelID) arrives as integer 0 rather than null when unset. Normalise 0 -> NULL on ingest or LEFT JOINs will silently match nothing while INNER JOINs silently drop rows.

VERIFIED LIVE: single-shop accounts are the common case (the probed store has exactly shop_id 1). shop_id filters and GROUP BYs are then no-ops -- keep them in generated SQL anyway so the same query stays correct when the merchant opens a second store.

time_zone is the single most load-bearing value in the whole org domain. Mixing raw API offsets with SQL date_trunc in server time shifts sales across day boundaries and is the classic source of 'yesterday's total changed'.

Shops are not stock locations in the ShelfLocations sense. ShelfLocations is a separate load_relation (bins/shelves inside a shop); the shop is the inventory OWNER, the shelf location is where it physically sits.
Shop.name is merchant-editable and not unique. Always group and join on shop_id, never on name.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id for the store location. This is the join target for sale.shopID, register.shopID, employee_hours.shop_id, item-shop quantities and orders. Stable forever; archived shops keep their id and keep owning their history.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Store name as it appears on receipts, labels and in the POS shop picker. Free text set by the merchant, not guaranteed unique across shops and not a slug or code.

columns.name: service_rate
columns.description: Default hourly labour/service rate for this location, in the account's base currency (Account.defaultCurrency.code). It is the rate the POS SUGGESTS when a labour line is added at this shop; it is NOT what was actually charged on any given workorder, and it is not a cost rate. Never derive labour revenue from it -- read the actual sale/workorder lines. 0 or null when the shop does no labour.

columns.name: time_zone
columns.description: The store's timezone (IANA-style, e.g. Australia/Sydney). Load-bearing for the entire layer: every datetime the API returns is offset-stamped and every 'today', 'this week' and daily bucket must be computed in THIS zone, not UTC and not the querier's zone. On multi-shop accounts spanning zones, a single account-wide date bucket is arithmetically wrong.

columns.name: tax_labor
columns.description: True when service/labour lines at this shop attract sales tax. Silently changes the tax base: if you assume labour is untaxed on a shop where this is true (typical for AU/GST and most CA provinces), every tax-vs-net reconciliation on service revenue will be off by the labour tax. Applies to the labour line type, not to goods.

columns.name: label_title
columns.description: What heading is printed at the top of product labels for this shop. Pure print configuration -- carries no analytical meaning. Note the enum values are human-readable strings with spaces, not codes, so match them literally.
columns.enums: 'No Title' = labels print with no heading; 'Shop Name' = prints Shop.name; 'Website' = prints the shop's website from the Contact record; 'Phone' = prints the shop's phone from the Contact record; 'Custom' = prints merchant-supplied custom text

columns.name: label_msrp
columns.description: True when a product label should also print the MSRP, but only for items where MSRP is filled in AND MSRP exceeds this shop's own selling price. Conditional on both, so a true value does not mean every label shows an MSRP. Print config only.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True when the location has been archived (closed down / retired). Archived shops STILL own all their historical sales, orders and inventory movements, so filtering archived = false when attributing past revenue silently deletes a whole store's history. Filter it only when listing currently-trading locations.

columns.name: contact_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the Contact record holding the store's street address, phone, email and website. Comes back as 0 (not null) when unset -- normalise 0 to NULL on ingest. The Contact object itself lives in the customers/contacts domain; the payload is duplicated into contact_json here for convenience.

columns.name: tax_category_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the TaxCategory this shop applies to new sales by default (/Account/{accountID}/TaxCategory/{taxCategoryID}). Load-bearing because the category carries the isTaxInclusive flag and the actual rates -- read the wrong one and every tax-exclusive/inclusive split is wrong. This is the DEFAULT only; an individual sale can carry a different tax category.

columns.name: receipt_setup_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the ReceiptSetup record (header/footer text and logo) used by this shop. Joins ls_receipt_setups. Cosmetic print config; returned as 0 when unset.

columns.name: cc_gateway_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the LEGACY credit-card gateway configuration for this shop (ls_cc_gateways). Deprecated in practice: modern Lightspeed Payments accounts leave this at 0 and hold their real payments config in an unpublished gatewayConfigID UUID that the V3 field table does not document. A 0/NULL here does NOT mean the shop takes no cards.

columns.name: price_level_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the default PriceLevel this shop sells at (/Account/{accountID}/PriceLevel/{priceLevelID}). Load-bearing for any 'discount vs list price' analysis: the baseline you compare against is this tier, not necessarily MSRP. A customer or an individual sale can override it.

columns.name: contact_json
columns.description: The shop's full Contact record as returned by load_relations=Contact: Addresses.ContactAddress (address1, address2, city, state, zip, country), Phones.ContactPhone, Emails.ContactEmail, Websites.ContactWebsite. Kept as a blob because Contact is owned by the contacts domain. Beware: R-Series returns a bare object when there is one child and an array when there are several, so guard every path with jsonb_typeof before indexing.

tables.grain: one row per point-of-sale register (till) configured on the account
tables.description: A Register is a single point of sale -- a place where money is received -- and each register keeps a separate cash count per payment type. This table is the lookup behind sale.registerID plus the LIVE open/closed state of each till right now. It is NOT a history of till sessions: past opens and closes live on RegisterCount in the cash-management domain.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: tipEnabled is documented but was ABSENT from the live Register payload on the probed store. Expect NULL on many accounts and never write `WHERE tip_enabled = false` expecting to catch non-tipping tills -- use `IS NOT TRUE`.

VERIFIED LIVE: live Register payloads return two keys the field table omits -- `archived` (boolean) and `ccTerminalID` (UUID of the paired card terminal). They are not modelled here because they are not in the published field table, but it means this table has NO documented way to hide retired tills: a register that shows in ls_registers may be long dead.
VERIFIED LIVE: register foreign keys (openEmployeeID, shopID) arrive as 0 rather than null when unset; normalise on ingest.

is_open and opened_at describe only the CURRENT session. Every question of the form 'when were tills opened/closed', 'how long was the average session', 'who closed the drawer' belongs on RegisterCount, not here.
The Register sortable-field list in the docs is `registerID` only -- there is no timeStamp on this object, so you cannot do incremental sync by modification date. Full re-scan each time.
Each register keeps a SEPARATE cash count per payment type. There is no single 'drawer total' on this object; per-tender expected-vs-counted amounts live on RegisterCountAmount.

columns.name: register_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id for the till. Join target for sale.registerID, RegisterCount.registerID and RegisterWithdraw.registerID. Stable across open/close cycles.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Human label for the till as shown in the POS, e.g. 'Front Register', 'Counter'. Merchant-editable free text, not unique, not a code. Group on register_id, display this.

columns.name: is_open
columns.description: True when the till is open for trading AT THE MOMENT THE ROW WAS FETCHED. This is live mutable state, not a historical fact: a snapshot taken overnight shows every till closed. Never use it to reason about whether a till was open when a past sale was rung -- that requires RegisterCount sessions.

columns.name: opened_at
columns.description: When the CURRENT session was opened, in the shop's timezone. Only meaningful while is_open is true; when the till is closed this retains the stale value from the last open, so 'hours open' arithmetic on a closed till produces a nonsense multi-day number. Not the open time of any past session.

columns.name: tip_enabled
columns.description: True when the Tipping feature is permitted on this register. Documented but frequently absent from live payloads -- treat NULL as 'the account did not report it', which is NOT the same as false. Controls whether tips can be taken, not whether any were.

columns.name: open_employee_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the Employee who opened the current session (/Account/{accountID}/Employee/{openEmployeeID}). Comes back as 0 when unset. This is who UNLOCKED the drawer, not who rang up the sales on it and not who will close it.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the Shop this register physically sits in (/Account/{accountID}/Shop/{shopID}). The only reliable way to attribute a register to a location -- register names are often reused across stores ('Counter' at every branch), so grouping tills by name across a multi-shop account silently merges different physical drawers.

tables.grain: one row per employee login on the account, including archived former staff
tables.description: Biographical and account-login information for staff: names, lock-out and archive state, which role (and therefore which rights) they hold, which shop they are restricted to, and a set of live 'currently attached to' pointers. This is the join target for sale.employeeID, workorder staff, register open/close and time-clock entries. It is NOT a payroll record -- Lightspeed stores no pay rate, salary or employment dates anywhere in the API.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: employee names carry stray trailing whitespace on real accounts (a lastName of 'Leader '). Group and join on employee_id, and TRIM(full_name) before any string comparison or de-duplication.

VERIFIED LIVE: live Employee payloads return an undocumented createTime. It is not modelled here because it is not in the published field table, and even where present it is only a rough proxy for a start date -- it records when the LOGIN was created, which for migrated accounts is the migration date for everyone.

VERIFIED LIVE: all foreign keys on this object (contactID, clockInEmployeeHoursID, employeeRoleID, limitToShopID, lastShopID, lastSaleID, lastRegisterID) arrive as integer 0 when unset, never null. This is especially dangerous on limit_to_shop_id, where 0 means 'no restriction', the exact opposite of a restrictive read.

The three last* columns (last_shop_id, last_sale_id, last_register_id) are live POS cursors, not history. Any report grouped by them is a report about where staff happened to be standing when the sync ran.
Rights resolution has a documented fallback: role rights win, and the employee's own rights apply ONLY when employeeRoleID is unset. Never UNION the two sets unconditionally.

Lightspeed stores no pay rate, wage, salary, hire date or termination date anywhere in the API. Labour-cost questions cannot be answered from this domain at all -- say so rather than deriving a number from service_rate, which is a customer-facing billing rate, not a wage.

Sales credit the employee who RANG UP the sale (sale.employeeID). The mechanic who actually did a workshop job is recorded on the workorder, not the sale, so 'revenue per employee' and 'work done per employee' are different questions with different join paths.
Names are personal data. Do not surface staff names in output unless the question is explicitly about staff.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id for the staff login. Join target for sale.employeeID, EmployeeHours.employeeID, Register.openEmployeeID and RegisterCount open/close employees. Survives archiving, so historical attribution never breaks.

columns.name: first_name
columns.description: Employee's given name. Personal data: do not surface in aggregate reporting unless the question is explicitly about staff. Merchant-typed, so casing and whitespace are inconsistent.

columns.name: last_name
columns.description: Employee's family name. Personal data. Live values commonly carry trailing whitespace ('Leader '), so equality matching on this column silently misses rows -- TRIM before comparing, or better, match on employee_id.

columns.name: full_name
columns.description: Convenience display name built from the two documented name fields; it is not returned by the API as its own key. Use for leaderboards and labels. Because it inherits the whitespace problem from last_name, TRIM it before matching.

columns.name: lock_out
columns.description: True when the employee is locked out of the system and cannot log in to the POS. Distinct from archived: a locked-out employee still counts towards the account's employee limit and is still an active staff record, just suspended. Common for temporary suspension or a forgotten PIN.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: True for former staff. Archived employees do NOT count towards the account's employee limit (that is the documented purpose of the flag). Critically, archived staff still own every sale they ever rang: filtering archived = false when attributing historical revenue silently erases departed staff and makes the remaining team's numbers look larger.

columns.name: contact_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the Contact record with the employee's phone, email and address. Returned as 0 when unset. Often empty for staff even when populated for customers.

columns.name: clock_in_employee_hours_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the EmployeeHours record the employee is CURRENTLY clocked in under (/Account/{accountID}/EmployeeHours/{clockInEmployeeHoursID}). Non-zero means clocked in right this second; 0/NULL means clocked out. This is live state, so it is the only correct source for 'who is on shift now' -- deriving it from EmployeeHours.checkOut IS NULL also catches stale never-closed entries from months ago.

columns.name: employee_role_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the employee's role, which specifies their rights. Load-bearing because of the fallback rule: when this is 0/NULL the employee's OWN rights (ls_employee_rights) apply instead of the role's. Any permissions query that ignores the fallback reports the wrong effective rights for exactly the staff who are configured individually.

columns.name: limit_to_shop_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the single Shop this login is restricted to (/Account/{accountID}/Shop/{limitToShopID}). 0/NULL means the opposite of restricted: the employee may work at ANY shop. Reading 0 as 'shop 0' or as 'no shop access' inverts the meaning.

columns.name: last_shop_id
columns.description: The shop the employee is currently -- or was most recently -- attached to (/API/Account/Shop/{lastShopID}). Transient live POS state that changes every time they log in somewhere. Never use it for historical attribution: 'sales by employee home store' computed from this column reassigns a person's entire history the moment they cover a shift elsewhere.

columns.name: last_sale_id
columns.description: The sale the employee is currently, or was last, working on (/Account/{accountID}/Sale/{lastSaleID}). Transient POS state -- typically an open, incomplete sale on the screen in front of them. It is not 'their most recent completed sale' and must never be used to count sales per employee.

columns.name: last_register_id
columns.description: The register the employee is currently, or was last, attached to (/Account/{accountID}/Register/{lastRegisterID}). Transient POS state, overwritten on every till switch. Not a history of which drawer they worked.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When the employee record was last modified, in the shop's timezone. This is the ONLY sortable/filterable change marker on this object, so it is the incremental-sync key. It ticks on any edit including the transient last* pointers, so it changes constantly during trading and is useless as a proxy for HR events like hire or termination date.

columns.name: contact_json
columns.description: The employee's full Contact record from load_relations=Contact: Phones.ContactPhone, Emails.ContactEmail, Addresses.ContactAddress. Personal data -- staff home addresses and mobile numbers. Frequently empty. Same one-vs-many shape hazard as every R-Series child collection: object when single, array when several.

tables.grain: one row per employee role defined on the account
tables.description: Named permission roles (e.g. Manager, Sales Associate) that bundle a set of rights and are assigned to employees via Employee.employeeRoleID. A role is a REUSABLE RULE, not a grant: the actual right names it confers are rows in ls_employee_role_rights. Roles have no standalone endpoint -- they are only reachable nested inside the Employee resource.

parents.projectFrom: EmployeeRole (single nested object per employee; de-duplicate to get the role catalogue)

gotchas: There is NO GET /EmployeeRole endpoint in the V3 documentation. Roles are only obtainable by scanning Employee.json with load_relations=["EmployeeRole","EmployeeRole.EmployeeRights"] and de-duplicating. A role that no employee currently holds is therefore INVISIBLE to this table -- absence here does not mean the role does not exist.
