Because the source is a per-employee nested object, a naive load produces one row per employee, not one row per role. The grain declared here requires an explicit DISTINCT ON (employeeRoleID).
The role/individual-rights fallback lives on the Employee object, not here: an employee with employeeRoleID unset ignores every role in this table and uses Employee.EmployeeRights instead.
Roles carry no timestamp and no archived flag on the documented surface, so you cannot tell when a role was created, changed or retired.

columns.name: employee_role_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id for the role. Join target for Employee.employeeRoleID. Because roles arrive nested per employee, the same role id appears once for every employee holding it -- de-duplicate on this column when building the catalogue.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Display name of the role as configured by the merchant (e.g. 'Manager', 'Cashier'). Free text, not a fixed enum and not guaranteed unique across ids -- a merchant can create two roles with the same label and different rights.

tables.grain: one row per (role, right) grant -- one right conferred by one role
tables.description: The bridge between a role and the individual rights/privileges it confers, exploded from the EmployeeRights collection nested under EmployeeRole. One row means 'this role grants this right'. This is the effective permission set for any employee whose employeeRoleID is set; employees with no role use ls_employee_rights instead.
gotchas: This is a nested array with the classic R-Series shape hazard: a role with ONE right returns EmployeeRights.EmployeeRight as a bare object, a role with several returns an array. Explode logic that assumes an array silently drops every single-right role.

The documentation publishes no enumeration of right names or ids. Any 'who can do X' query is matching against an undocumented value set -- verify the exact string on the target account before shipping a permission report.
These rights are effective ONLY for employees with employeeRoleID set. Union them with ls_employee_rights unconditionally and you will over-report permissions for individually-configured staff.
A role is exploded once per employee holding it, so the raw explode contains duplicate (role, right) pairs. The declared grain requires DISTINCT.

columns.name: employee_role_id
columns.description: The role conferring this right, carried down from the parent EmployeeRole object during the explode. Not a field on the EmployeeRight element itself -- without it the exploded rows are unattributable.

columns.name: employee_right_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the right/privilege. Stable across roles and accounts, so it is the safe key for 'does this role include right N' checks -- safer than matching the name string.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The right's name as Lightspeed defines it (e.g. discount-application, void, price-override, reporting access). Load-bearing for permission audits because these are the only human-readable handle on what a role can do, yet the docs publish no enumeration of the value set -- do not hard-code an exhaustive list, and use ILIKE matching with care since similarly-named rights differ in scope.

tables.grain: one row per (employee, right) grant made directly to an employee -- effective only when that employee has no role
tables.description: Per-employee rights, exploded from the EmployeeRights collection nested directly under Employee. These are the fallback permission set: the documentation is explicit that an employee's own rights apply ONLY if employeeRoleID is unset. Same EmployeeRight object as ls_employee_role_rights but a different grain (employee-scoped, not role-scoped), so it is deliberately a separate table.
gotchas: These rights are INERT for any employee who has a role. The documented rule is 'if none [no role], then the employee's own rights apply instead of the role's'. Reporting them without checking ls_employees.employee_role_id IS NULL over-states permissions.
Single-vs-array shape hazard again: one right returns a bare object, several return an array. Guard the explode.

There is no standalone EmployeeRight endpoint, so the right CATALOGUE can only be assembled by unioning the distinct (employee_right_id, name) pairs seen across this table and ls_employee_role_rights. Rights nobody has been granted are invisible.
Right names are not an audit trail. Nothing in the API records WHEN a right was granted or by whom.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: The employee the right is attached to directly, carried down from the parent Employee object. Load-bearing because the row is only MEANINGFUL when that same employee's employee_role_id is NULL -- rows for role-holding employees are inert configuration that the POS ignores.

columns.name: employee_right_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the right/privilege, from the same catalogue as ls_employee_role_rights.employee_right_id. The two tables can be compared on this id to diff individual against role permissions.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The right's name as Lightspeed defines it. Same undocumented value set as the role-scoped table; no enumeration is published, so treat any hard-coded list as account-specific.

tables.grain: one row per clock-in/clock-out entry for one employee at one shop
tables.description: Time-clock entries recorded when employees clock in and out of the POS. One row is one shift segment: a check-in, an eventual check-out, the employee and the shop. This is the source for hours-worked and staffing-level questions -- but only for merchants who actually use the Lightspeed time clock. It contains no pay rate, no break tracking, no scheduled/rostered hours and no approval state.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: the probed store returned ZERO rows from this endpoint -- the merchant did not use the Lightspeed time clock (rostering lived in a separate system). An empty result here is NORMAL, not a sync failure. Report 'the store does not use the built-in time clock' rather than reporting zero hours worked.
VERIFIED LIVE: shift length in hours = EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (check_out - check_in)) / 3600.0, and rows with check_out IS NULL must be excluded from every duration sum.

VERIFIED LIVE: Lightspeed stores no pay rate, wage or salary anywhere in the API, so wage cost cannot be computed from this table however you join it. Shop.serviceRate is a customer BILLING rate, not a wage -- multiplying hours by it produces a fabricated number.
Forgotten clock-outs create both NULL check_out rows and absurd multi-day durations once someone belatedly closes them. Sanity-check for shifts over ~14 hours before averaging.
This object has no timeStamp/createTime and its only sortable field is employeeHoursID, so incremental sync must be driven by id watermark or by a checkIn date-range filter, not by modification time.
There is no break, meal-period, overtime or approval concept in this object. 'Hours worked' here is raw clock time, which will not reconcile to a payroll system that deducts unpaid breaks.
Time entries are additive over employees and dates, but only after NULL check_outs are removed; the additivity is on the DERIVED duration, since the object itself publishes no hours measure.

columns.name: employee_hours_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the clock entry (/Account/{accountID}/EmployeeHours/{employeeHoursID}). Employee.clockInEmployeeHoursID points here to mark the one entry that is currently open.

columns.name: check_in
columns.description: Start of the clock-in entry, in the shop's timezone. This is the date to bucket a shift by; a shift that crosses midnight belongs to the check_in day under this convention, so evening-shift hours land on the earlier date. Always present.

columns.name: check_out
columns.description: End of the clock-in entry, in the shop's timezone. NULL while the shift is still open -- and also NULL forever when staff simply forgot to clock out, which is common. Every duration aggregate must exclude NULLs or SUM silently returns NULL/short; every 'still working' query must cross-check ls_employees.clock_in_employee_hours_id to distinguish a live shift from an abandoned one.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the Employee this entry belongs to (/Account/{accountID}/Employee/{employeeID}). Returned as 0 when unset. The person who clocked in -- not necessarily the person who rang up sales during that window, since any logged-in employee can use any till.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the Shop where the clock in/out physically happened (/Account/{accountID}/Shop/{shopID}). Recorded per entry, so a person covering another branch produces entries against that branch -- this is the correct column for labour-hours-by-location, unlike Employee.lastShopID which is transient.

tables.grain: one row -- the identity behind the access token currently in use (singleton)
tables.description: Describes the current API session derived from the access token: which employee granted it, which account and API client it belongs to, and a couple of account-wide facts (shop count, linked eCom URL). It is the authoritative source of the accountID that every other R-Series URL needs. It is NOT a login-history table -- there is exactly one row and it reflects the token you are holding right now.
gotchas: This is a SINGLETON, not a log. There is exactly one row and it describes the token in your hand; it can never answer 'who logged in yesterday' or 'how many sessions were there'.
systemCustomerID is the ACCOUNT id, not a retail customer id. The naming is the single most misleading thing in this domain -- joining it to a Customer table produces confident nonsense.
systemUserID is globally unique across accounts while employeeID is only account-unique. Never use employeeID as a cross-account identity, and never use systemUserID to join inside an account.
The docs list no GET path and no sortable fields for this object; it is a read-only introspection endpoint with no filtering, no pagination and no timestamps.

sessionID and sessionCookie are dead for token-based auth by explicit documentation. If either is populated you are on a legacy cookie session, which behaves differently around rate limits and expiry.

The employee named here is credited with everything the integration writes back. Before attributing sales by employee, check whether ls_session.employee_id appears in the sales data as a synthetic 'API' user.

columns.name: session_id
columns.description: Legacy cookie-session identifier. Explicitly documented as 'Not used for access token sessions', so on any OAuth/access-token integration -- which is every modern one -- this is null or meaningless. Retained only so the documented field is not silently dropped.

columns.name: session_cookie
columns.description: Legacy cookie-session value. Explicitly documented as 'Not used for access token sessions'. Treat as a credential: never log, display or export it, even though it is expected to be empty on token-based integrations.

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Foreign key to the Employee who granted the access token (/Account/{accountID}/Employee/{employeeID}). This is the identity the integration ACTS AS -- every write the integration makes is attributed to this employee, which is why an integration's sales can pollute a staff leaderboard.

columns.name: system_customer_id
columns.description: The account ID (/Account/{accountID}). Despite the 'customer' in the name this has NOTHING to do with retail customers -- it is Lightspeed's internal identifier for the merchant account and it is the {accountID} path segment in every other endpoint URL. Confusing it with a Customer record is the classic misread; confusing it with Account.accountID is safe, they are the same value.

columns.name: system_user_id
columns.description: The employee's identifier at the Lightspeed platform level, unique ACROSS ALL ACCOUNTS -- unlike employeeID, which is only unique within one account. The right key for recognising the same human across multiple merchant accounts; useless as a join key inside a single account.

columns.name: system_api_client_id
columns.description: Unique identifier of the API client (the registered application) associated with the access token. Identifies WHICH integration is calling, not who authorised it. Constant for all tokens issued to the same app.

columns.name: system_api_key_id
columns.description: Unique identifier of the access token itself. Changes when the token is rotated or re-authorised, so it is the natural key for 'which credential is this' and for detecting that a stored token was replaced.

columns.name: ecom_url
columns.description: URL of the associated Lightspeed eCom (C-Series) store, if the account has one linked. Empty/null means no eCom link -- which in turn means online-order questions cannot be answered from this account at all. Its presence is the cheapest test for whether a merchant is omnichannel.

columns.name: shop_count
columns.description: Number of shops on the account, as counted by the platform. Useful as a cheap cross-check that a Shop scan paginated fully, but it does not state whether archived shops are included, so a mismatch against COUNT(*) FROM ls_shops WHERE archived = false is expected and not an error.

tables.grain: one row -- the Lightspeed Retail (R-Series) account associated with the access token (singleton)
tables.description: The merchant account itself: its id, trading name, subscription status, employee licence usage and base currency. This is the legal/billing entity that owns every shop, employee and sale in the layer. WARNING: the V3 documentation publishes NO field table for this object -- every column below is harvested from the documented example payload, so types and null semantics are inferred, not specified.
gotchas: There is NO published field table for the Account object. Every column here is reverse-engineered from the documentation's example payload, so the Postgres types are best guesses and null semantics are unknown. Validate against a live response before building anything load-bearing on account fields.
This is a singleton row. Do not build time series from it: employee_count and status are live values that get overwritten on every sync unless you snapshot them yourself.

default_currency_code is the implicit unit of EVERY money column in the entire semantic layer. No amount field anywhere in R-Series carries its own currency tag. Presenting a total without this code is presenting a number without units.
Account.name is the billing entity, Shop.name is the trading location. On single-shop accounts they usually match, which trains people to conflate them, and then multi-shop accounts break the report.
employee_count excludes archived employees by the documented behaviour of Employee.archived; comparing it against an unfiltered COUNT(*) of ls_employees will always look like a discrepancy.
GET /Account.json (no id) returns the account for your token; GET /Account/{accountID}.json returns a specific one. On a single-tenant token both give the same single row.

columns.name: account_id
columns.description: The account's unique id. This is the {accountID} path segment in every other R-Series URL and is the same value as Session.systemCustomerID. Type inferred from the example payload; the docs publish no field table for this object.

columns.name: name
columns.description: The merchant account name, i.e. the business as Lightspeed bills it. Commonly but not always identical to Shop.name -- on multi-shop accounts the account name is the parent business and each shop has its own trading name. Do not use it as a store label.

columns.name: link
columns.description: Self-referencing API URL for this account resource, as returned in the example payload. Plumbing for HATEOAS-style navigation; carries no analytical meaning and should not be shown to users.

columns.name: system_customer_id
columns.description: Lightspeed's platform-level identifier for the merchant, the same value as Session.systemCustomerID. Again: NOT a retail customer id. Load-bearing because integrations that key their own storage on the wrong one of accountID/systemCustomerID cross-wire tenants.

columns.name: status
columns.description: Subscription/lifecycle state of the account. Load-bearing because a suspended, trial or cancelled account can still serve historical data through the API while no longer reflecting live trading -- a silent source of 'the numbers stopped moving'. The docs publish no enumeration of the possible values, so read the live value rather than assuming 'active'.

columns.name: employee_count
columns.description: Number of employees counted against the account's licence. Per the Employee docs, ARCHIVED employees do not count towards the limit, so this will be lower than COUNT(*) FROM ls_employees and should be compared only against the non-archived count. It is a live counter, not a historical headcount series.

columns.name: employee_limit
columns.description: Maximum employees the account's plan permits. Together with employee_count this is the licence headroom. Hitting the limit blocks creating new logins, which merchants routinely mistake for a bug; it is also why staff records get archived rather than left in place.

columns.name: unique_subscription_identifier
columns.description: Opaque identifier of the billing subscription behind the account, from the example payload. Useful for correlating with Lightspeed billing records; meaningless for retail analytics and not a join key to anything inside the API.

columns.name: default_currency_code
columns.description: ISO code of the account's BASE currency (USD, CAD, AUD...). The single most load-bearing value for money: every amount in every other table in the layer -- sale totals, costs, Shop.serviceRate, register counts -- is denominated in this currency and carries no currency tag of its own. Foreign amounts only ever appear via the purchasing-currency and CurrencyRate mechanisms.

columns.name: default_currency_symbol
columns.description: Display symbol for the base currency ($, £, €). Presentation only -- symbols are ambiguous across currencies ($ is used by USD, CAD, AUD and more), so never infer the currency from the symbol; use default_currency_code.

tables.grain: one row per purchasing currency enabled on the account
tables.description: The non-base currencies the account is configured to PURCHASE in (i.e. buy stock from overseas suppliers), each with the exchange rate recorded against it. Exploded from the purchasingCurrencies collection in the Account example payload. This is a buying-side configuration list, not a selling-side price list and not a live FX feed.
gotchas: Undocumented territory: the Account object has no published field table, so this whole table is harvested from an example payload. Column types, null behaviour and the rate direction are all inferences.

Two independent places record FX in R-Series -- here and the CurrencyRate endpoint -- and nothing guarantees they agree. When they disagree, prefer CurrencyRate, whose direction IS documented (given currency / account currency).

Single-vs-array shape hazard: an account with one purchasing currency very likely returns purchasingCurrency as a bare object rather than a one-element array. Guard the explode or you will drop single-currency accounts entirely.
Purchasing currencies are about BUYING stock. They say nothing about what customers can pay in; selling-side multi-currency is a different mechanism.
Single-currency accounts return an empty collection. Zero rows here is normal, not a sync failure.

columns.name: account_id
columns.description: The account these purchasing currencies belong to, carried down from the parent Account object. Constant on a single-tenant token but required to keep the grain well-defined in a multi-account warehouse.

columns.name: currency_code
columns.description: ISO code of a currency the account may raise purchase orders in (USD, EUR...). Distinct from Account.defaultCurrency.code, which is the currency everything is REPORTED in. A currency listed here does not mean the merchant sells in it.

columns.name: currency_symbol
columns.description: Display symbol for the purchasing currency. Ambiguous across currencies; always label with currency_code, never with the symbol alone.

columns.name: rate
columns.description: Exchange rate recorded for this purchasing currency. The Account object publishes no field table, so the DIRECTION is not documented here -- by analogy with CurrencyRate.rate it should be (given currency / account currency), but that is an inference. Load-bearing: get the direction backwards and every converted cost is out by the square of the rate. Verify against a known PO before using it in arithmetic.

tables.grain: one row per locale Lightspeed publishes globally (a global catalogue, not the account's own setting)
tables.description: The global list of locales available across Lightspeed and their formatting/currency attributes: currency symbol and code, decimal precision, cash-rounding increment, tax naming, date formats and language tag. This is a GLOBAL reference catalogue -- it lists every locale that exists, not the one this account uses. Which locale an account is on is an account Option, not a field here.
gotchas: This is a GLOBAL catalogue of every locale Lightspeed supports, not the account's configuration. Selecting one row from it and calling it 'the store's locale' is wrong -- the account's locale is an account Option value, which is outside this domain.

The endpoint publishes no id field and no timestamps, and the docs state sorting is not available. The name string is the only key, there is no incremental sync, and there is no way to detect that Lightspeed changed a locale's attributes.

cash_rounding_precision is the source of the classic 'cash takings are a few cents off' question. Cash tenders round to this increment, card tenders do not; the difference is expected and should be explained, not reconciled away.

currency_precision and cash_rounding_precision are different things and are easy to swap: the first is storage/display decimals, the second is the physical smallest coin. In AU they are 0.01-precision and 0.05-rounding respectively.

CurrencyDenominations is documented only as 'collection' with no element fields, so it is stored as JSON rather than exploded into a child table -- building one would require inventing column names, which is not permitted.
Locale tax NAMES are cosmetic. Never infer a tax RATE from tax_name1/tax_name2; rates live on TaxCategory in the tax domain and vary per account and per tax class.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Name of the locale. The endpoint publishes no numeric id of any kind, so this string is the only available key -- which makes it fragile: if Lightspeed renames a locale, every reference to it breaks silently.

columns.name: country
columns.description: Country the locale belongs to. The docs do not state whether this is an ISO-3166 code or a display name, so do not join it to country codes from other systems without inspecting a live value first.

columns.name: states
columns.description: States/provinces within the locale, published as a string rather than a structured collection. Expect a delimited list needing parsing; the delimiter is not documented. Relevant because state-level tax setups vary within a country.

columns.name: currency_symbol
columns.description: Currency symbol used for display in this locale. Presentation only; $ is shared by many currencies, so never infer the currency from it.

columns.name: currency_code
columns.description: ISO currency code of the locale. Note this is the locale's currency, NOT the account's -- the account's base currency is Account.defaultCurrency.code and takes precedence for every stored amount.

columns.name: currency_precision
columns.description: Number of decimal places the currency is stored/displayed to. Load-bearing for rounding: rounding to a fixed 2 decimals is wrong for zero-decimal currencies (JPY) and for three-decimal ones (KWD, BHD), producing totals that drift from the POS by a cent per line. Documented as a float even though it is conceptually an integer count.

columns.name: cash_rounding_precision
columns.description: Smallest unit of currency actually used in CASH transactions -- e.g. 0.05 where 1c and 2c coins were withdrawn (AU, CA, NZ). Load-bearing and routinely missed: cash-tendered totals are rounded to this increment while card totals are not, so cash-vs-card reconciliation shows a systematic few-cent gap that is correct behaviour, not an error. Distinct from currency_precision, which governs storage.

columns.name: include_tax_on_labels
columns.description: Whether product labels in this locale print tax-inclusive prices. Load-bearing as a signal of the region's pricing convention: tax-inclusive regions (most of EU/AU/NZ) enter and display prices with tax in them, which changes what a 'price' means before you touch a single sale record. The authoritative per-sale flag is TaxCategory.isTaxInclusive, not this.

columns.name: language_tag
columns.description: Language tag per ISO 639-1 (e.g. 'en', 'fr'). Drives POS and receipt language. Note ISO 639-1 is the two-letter LANGUAGE standard -- it carries no region, so 'en' does not distinguish en-US from en-AU; use country for that.

columns.name: date_format
columns.description: Date format string for the locale, in the API's own format syntax (e.g. 'd/m/Y' style PHP tokens, not strftime and not ISO). Presentation only -- never parse API datetimes with it; API datetimes are returned offset-stamped regardless of locale.

columns.name: datetime_format
columns.description: Date-and-time format string for the locale, same token syntax caveat as date_format. Display formatting only.

columns.name: tax_name1
columns.description: Name of the locale's first tax (GST, VAT, State Tax, TPS...). Explains WHY a TaxCategory is named what it is; the rates themselves live on TaxCategory, never here.

columns.name: tax_name2
columns.description: Name of the locale's second tax, for two-tier regimes such as Canadian GST + PST/QST. Empty in single-tax regions. Its presence is the tell that a region needs two-rate tax handling.

columns.name: currency_denominations_json
columns.description: The locale's note and coin denominations, kept as a JSON blob. Deliberately NOT split into its own table: the V3 documentation publishes the collection but no field table for its elements, so any child columns would have to be invented. Inspect a live response before reading paths out of it.

tables.grain: one row per Lightspeed catalog industry vertical, with its enabled state for this account
tables.description: Lightspeed's built-in retail verticals (Bicycles, Jewelry, Pet, Golf...) and whether each is switched on for this account. Enabling an industry gives the account access to that vertical's shared supplier catalog and its default item templates. Pure configuration reference -- it does not classify products, sales or customers.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: the field-table scrape carried an artifact ('employee:industryID'); the real JSON keys confirmed live are industryID, name and enabled.
VERIFIED LIVE: live responses also return an undocumented catalogIndustryID (the matching id in Lightspeed's shared catalog service). Not modelled here because it is not in the published field table.
The endpoint returns EVERY industry Lightspeed defines, not just the account's. Always filter enabled = true when answering 'what kind of shop is this'.
Industries control catalog access, nothing else. They do not categorise products (that is Category), do not drive tax, and do not appear on sales.
No timestamps and no archived flag on this object; the only sortable field is industryID.

columns.name: industry_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id for the industry vertical. Global to Lightspeed, so the same id means the same vertical on every account -- unlike most ids in this API, which are account-scoped.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Name of the industry vertical (Bicycles, Skateboards, Motorcycles...). Lightspeed-defined, not merchant-editable, so it is safe to match on -- though the docs publish no closed list of values.

columns.name: enabled
columns.description: True when the vertical is switched on for THIS account. Load-bearing because the endpoint returns the full global catalogue regardless: listing rows without filtering on enabled reports every industry Lightspeed offers as though the merchant used them all. Typically exactly one is true.

tables.grain: one row per legacy credit-card gateway configuration referenced by a shop
tables.description: Legacy per-shop credit-card gateway setup: which processor, its credentials, terminal/market identifiers, enabled and test-mode switches, and the mapping from card brands to PaymentType ids. Documented on the Shop endpoint and only reachable via load_relations=CCGateway. This is CONFIGURATION, not transactions -- no charge, settlement or fee ever appears here, and it holds live credentials.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: this whole object is LEGACY. Modern Lightspeed Payments accounts leave Shop.ccGatewayID at 0 and hold their real payments configuration in an undocumented gatewayConfigID UUID on the Shop, so this table is empty on current accounts. Empty is normal and does NOT mean the shop cannot take cards.
There is no standalone GET /CCGateway endpoint. Rows only appear by scanning Shop.json with load_relations=CCGateway, so the grain requires de-duplicating the per-shop nesting.

Six columns are live credentials (login, trans_key, account_num, hash_value, other_credentials1, other_credentials2). They are modelled only because the documentation publishes them; a real ingestion should redact them at the boundary and they must never reach a query result, a log line or an LLM context.

test_mode is the silent revenue-fabricator: charges taken in test mode look like completed payments in the POS but never settle. Always check it before trusting card revenue from a gateway-integrated shop.
The card-brand PaymentType mappings are configuration, not observed volume. A visa_payment_type_id being set says Visa CAN be recorded separately, not that any Visa transaction happened.
Nothing transactional lives here. Charges, declines, voids and settlement are CCCharge; processor fees are ProcessingFee. Both are in the payments domain, not this table.

columns.name: cc_gateway_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the gateway configuration. Shop.ccGatewayID joins here. Because gateways arrive nested per shop, the same id repeats once per shop sharing it -- de-duplicate to reach the declared grain.

columns.name: gateway
columns.description: Name of the payment gateway/processor this shop is wired to. Load-bearing for reconciliation: it tells you WHICH processor's statement the card takings should be matched against. A populated row does not imply the shop actually uses it -- check enabled and test_mode.

columns.name: enabled
columns.description: True when the gateway is switched on. A configured-but-disabled gateway is common after a processor migration, and reading the config as active is how you end up reconciling against the wrong processor.

columns.name: test_mode
columns.description: True when the gateway is in test/sandbox mode. Load-bearing and dangerous: card charges taken while this is true are NOT real money, yet they still appear as completed payments in the POS. A shop left in test mode produces fully plausible revenue that never settles.

columns.name: allow_credits
columns.description: Whether credit-card charges (credits back to a card) are permitted through this gateway. When false, refunds cannot be returned to the original card and staff must use another tender -- which is why refund tender mix sometimes fails to mirror sale tender mix.

columns.name: market_type
columns.description: Market type value sent in the transaction XML (retail, e-commerce, MOTO and similar processor-defined categories). It influences interchange pricing at the processor. Processor-defined value set; the docs publish no enumeration.

columns.name: device_type
columns.description: Numeric code for the type of device used to process card transactions. The code set is processor-specific and undocumented here, so treat the number as an opaque tag rather than decoding it.

columns.name: terminal_num
columns.description: Terminal ID sent in the transaction XML. Identifies the physical/logical terminal to the processor and is usually the key on the processor's own settlement report -- the most useful column here for reconciliation. Not the same as Lightspeed's registerID.

columns.name: login
columns.description: Gateway credential (merchant login). SECRET: never display, log, export or include in any query result shown to a user. Present only so the documented field is not silently dropped; ingestion should ideally store a redaction marker.

columns.name: trans_key
columns.description: Gateway credential (transaction key). SECRET -- treat exactly as a password. Never surface.

columns.name: account_num
columns.description: Gateway credential (merchant account number). SECRET. Despite the name it is a processor account identifier, not a bank account number and not a card number, but it must still never be surfaced.

columns.name: hash_value
columns.description: MD5 hash used to validate the transaction. SECRET (it is effectively a shared signing secret). Also a security smell worth flagging: MD5 is cryptographically broken, which dates this gateway integration.

columns.name: other_credentials1
columns.description: Spare credential slot, used when a processor needs a field beyond login/transKey/accountNum. SECRET; content is processor-specific and undocumented.

columns.name: other_credentials2
columns.description: Second spare credential slot. SECRET; same caveats as otherCredentials1.

columns.name: visa_payment_type_id
columns.description: PaymentType id that Visa transactions on this gateway are recorded against (/Account/{accountID}/PaymentType/{visaPaymentTypeID}). This mapping is the ONLY documented way to split card revenue by brand on gateway-integrated accounts; 0 means unmapped, in which case Visa falls into a generic card tender and brand mix is unanswerable.

columns.name: master_payment_type_id
columns.description: PaymentType id used for MasterCard transactions on this gateway (/Account/{accountID}/PaymentType/{masterPaymentTypeID}). 0 when unmapped.

columns.name: discover_payment_type_id
columns.description: PaymentType id used for Discover Card transactions (/Account/{accountID}/PaymentType/{discoverPaymentTypeID}). 0 when unmapped, which is normal outside North America.

columns.name: american_payment_type_id
columns.description: PaymentType id used for American Express transactions (/Account/{accountID}/PaymentType/{americanPaymentTypeID}). 0 when unmapped. Amex is often deliberately unmapped where the merchant does not accept it.

columns.name: debit_payment_type_id
columns.description: PaymentType id used for debit-card transactions (/Account/{accountID}/PaymentType/{debitPaymentTypeID}). Debit is priced very differently from credit at the processor, so a null mapping here means the cheap and expensive card volume are indistinguishable in the tender mix.

tables.grain: one row per receipt setup configuration referenced by a shop
tables.description: Receipt print configuration: the header block, the general footer message, the workorder and credit-card agreement texts, and the logo image with its pixel dimensions. Documented on the Shop endpoint and only reachable via load_relations=ReceiptSetup. Entirely cosmetic -- useful for reproducing a receipt or auditing legal wording, never for analytics.
gotchas: There is no standalone GET /ReceiptSetup endpoint. Rows exist only by scanning Shop.json with load_relations=ReceiptSetup, then de-duplicating on receiptSetupID.

A blank header does not mean a blank receipt top: the documented behaviour is that the shop's contact information is printed instead. Reporting 'no header configured' as 'receipts have no header' is wrong.

The three text blocks fire under different conditions -- general_msg on every receipt, workorder_agree only on workorder/invoice/quote documents, creditcard_agree only when a card charge is present. Concatenating them reproduces a receipt no customer ever saw.
logo is a RELATIVE URL. Treating it as fetchable as-is fails; resolve it against the account host first.
No timestamps on this object, so you cannot tell when the wording last changed -- which matters if you are trying to establish which terms a customer saw on a given date.
This table has zero analytical value on its own. It exists so receipt reproduction and terms-audit questions have a source, and so the documented fields are not dropped.

columns.name: receipt_setup_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the receipt configuration. Shop.receiptSetupID joins here. Repeats once per shop using it in the nested payload, so de-duplicate to reach the declared grain.

columns.name: header
columns.description: Text printed at the TOP of the receipt. Documented fallback behaviour matters: when left blank, the POS prints the shop's contact information instead, so an empty header does not mean receipts print headerless.

columns.name: general_msg
columns.description: General text printed at the end of ALL receipts (return policy, thanks, opening hours). Applies unconditionally, unlike the workorder and credit-card texts which are conditional.

columns.name: workorder_agree
columns.description: Text printed at the end of workorder receipts, invoices and quotes only. Load-bearing in the legal sense rather than the numeric one: this is the customer agreement wording for service work (liability, storage, abandonment terms), so an audit of what a customer agreed to must read this and not general_msg.

columns.name: creditcard_agree
columns.description: Text printed at the end of a sales receipt that includes credit-card charges -- the cardholder agreement/signature wording. Printed conditionally on the presence of a card charge, so it is absent from cash receipts.

columns.name: logo
columns.description: RELATIVE URL of the logo image file, not an absolute URL and not the image bytes. It must be resolved against the account's asset host before it can be fetched; empty when no logo is configured.

columns.name: logo_height
columns.description: Logo image height in PIXELS as stored, not print millimetres. Used with logo_width to lay the image out on the receipt; 0 when no logo is set.

columns.name: logo_width
columns.description: Logo image width in PIXELS. Paired with logo_height; a width exceeding the printer's dot width is the usual cause of clipped receipt logos.

tables.grain: one row per foreign currency exchange rate the merchant maintains
tables.description: Manually maintained foreign-exchange rates used for multi-currency work. One row per currency code, holding the rate of that currency relative to the account's base currency. The documentation is explicit that these rates are NEVER updated automatically -- they are as fresh as the last time a human typed them, so they are a merchant setting, not a market feed.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: single-currency stores return ZERO rows here. Empty is normal, not a sync failure, and it means multi-currency questions are unanswerable for that account rather than answerable with zero.

VERIFIED LIVE: rates are stale by design -- the documentation states outright that they 'will not be updated automatically'. Never present them as market FX rates; always show updated_at next to any conversion.

The documented direction is (given currency / account currency), so converting INTO the base currency means DIVIDING by rate. This is the opposite of the intuitive reading and produces a plausible-looking wrong number when inverted.
rate is non-additive: summing or averaging rates across currencies is meaningless. The table is a lookup even though it holds a numeric measure.

The account's purchasing currencies carry their own rate values on the Account object. Nothing keeps the two in sync; when they disagree, prefer this endpoint because its direction is the documented one.
This object publishes no sortable-field list in the reference, so filtering and incremental sync options are unknown -- assume a full scan.

columns.name: currency_rate_id
columns.description: Unique numeric id of the rate record (/Account/{accountID}/CurrencyRate/{currencyRateID}). Identifies the ROW, not the currency -- prefer currency_code as the business key since the id can change if a merchant deletes and re-adds a currency.

columns.name: currency_code
columns.description: ISO currency code the rate applies to (USD, CAD...). The account's own base currency is normally absent from this table; if it appears, its rate should be 1 and anything else indicates a misconfiguration.

columns.name: rate
columns.description: Exchange rate of the given currency relative to the account's base currency, documented as (given currency / account currency). Load-bearing because the direction is inverted from what most people assume: to convert an amount FROM this currency INTO the base currency you DIVIDE by rate, you do not multiply. Getting it backwards is out by a factor of rate-squared and still looks plausible. Never SUM or AVG this column across currencies.

columns.name: created_at
columns.description: When the currency-rate record was created, in the shop's timezone. On migrated accounts this is frequently a bulk backfill value identical across every row, so it is not evidence of when the merchant started trading in that currency.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When the rate record was last modified, in the shop's timezone. Effectively the rate's AS-OF date and the only staleness signal available: since Lightspeed never refreshes these automatically, a rate last touched two years ago is being applied to today's transactions. Always surface this alongside any converted figure.

tables.grain: one physical currency denomination available in a locale
tables.description: The note and coin denominations defined for a locale. This is the reference list the POS uses to build its cash-counting screen, so it is what makes a register count reconcile denomination by denomination. Reference data only: it never changes with trading and carries no money of its own.
gotchas: The reference documents this only as an untyped collection on Locale. Column shape is provisional and must be confirmed against a live payload before it is relied on (Tier 0 until probed).

columns.name: locale_id
columns.description: Owning locale. Join to ls_locales to resolve the currency and formatting rules this denomination belongs to.

columns.name: value
columns.description: Face value of the note or coin in the locale currency. Documented only as a collection on Locale, so the per-denomination shape is confirmed at probe time rather than from the reference.

tables.grain: one register close-out — the open-to-close session of a single till, written at the moment the closing count is submitted
tables.description: End-of-day (or end-of-shift) till close-out headers. One row per register session: when the till was opened, when it was closed, and which employee did each. This table is the SPINE for cash reconciliation but holds NO money whatsoever — every counted and expected amount lives in ls_register_count_amounts, joined on register_count_id. It is not a list of trading days and not a list of registers.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: there are NO money columns on this table at all. Any question about cash amounts, floats or over/short must join ls_register_count_amounts on register_count_id.
createTime is the CLOSE time and openTime is the OPEN time. Treating createTime as 'when the record was created' and using it as the session start produces negative or nonsensical durations.

VERIFIED LIVE: sessions can span months. The Ashburton production account contains counts opened 2018-04 and closed 2019-01 because a till was simply never closed. Sanity-filter (closed_at - opened_at) before averaging 'typical session length' or the mean is meaningless.
Session length in hours = EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (closed_at - opened_at)) / 3600.0.
VERIFIED LIVE: page size 100 is the production-safe pageLimit for this endpoint.

There is NO timeStamp field on RegisterCount, unlike most R-Series objects. You cannot ask for 'counts modified since X'. Incremental sync must page by registerCountID ascending and re-poll the tail; edits to old counts will be missed.
The absence of a close-out for a date is NOT evidence that the till did not trade — it means nobody submitted a count. Never infer trading days from this table.
A register can be closed with no corresponding RegisterCountAmount rows if no tenders were configured or counted; use LEFT JOIN when listing sessions.

columns.name: register_count_id
columns.description: Unique id of this close-out. The ONLY documented sortable field on the endpoint, so backfill must page by it ascending. Child tender lines in ls_register_count_amounts join here.

columns.name: closed_at
columns.description: The moment the till was CLOSED and the count submitted. Despite the createTime name this is the END of the session, not a record-creation date — use it, never opened_at, to attribute a close-out to a trading day. Store-local wall time with no timezone offset; do not shift it.

columns.name: opened_at
columns.description: When this till session was opened. Session length = closed_at - opened_at. Store-local wall time, no offset. Misreading this as the count date inverts every duration calculation.

columns.name: notes
columns.description: Free text typed by staff at close. In practice this is where discrepancies and float resets get explained (e.g. 'removed cash to reset the float'). Usually an empty string, not NULL, for routine closes — test with NULLIF(TRIM(notes),'') rather than IS NOT NULL.

columns.name: register_id
columns.description: The till that was counted. Joins ls_registers.register_id (org/location domain). Arrives as 0 when unset; normalise 0 to NULL at ingest so joins do not silently attach to a phantom register.

columns.name: open_employee_id
columns.description: Employee who OPENED the session. The docs give the resolution URL as /Register/{openEmployeeID}, which is a documentation typo — this is an Employee id and resolves against the Employee endpoint. 0 means unset; normalise to NULL.

columns.name: close_employee_id
columns.description: Employee who submitted the count and closed the till. Same documentation typo (/Register/{closeEmployeeID}) — it is an Employee id. This, NOT open_employee_id, is the person accountable for any over/short on this close-out; attributing variance to the opener is the classic mistake. 0 means unset; normalise to NULL.

tables.grain: one payment type's expected-versus-counted pair inside one register close-out
tables.description: The per-tender detail of every till close-out: what the system calculated the drawer should hold for a payment type, against what a human physically counted. This is THE source table for cash over/short and drawer-reconciliation questions. It is not a payments table — it never tells you what was sold, only what was in (or supposed to be in) the drawer at close.
tables.additivityAxis: close-out time within a register + payment_type — calculated and actual are drawer BALANCES at the close instant, not flows. Never sum them across successive register counts (floats carry over from session to session, so the total is fiction). The variance (actual - calculated) IS additive over time and is the only figure safe to total.
gotchas: Over/short = actual - calculated. POSITIVE means the drawer held MORE than expected (overage); NEGATIVE means it was short. Getting the subtraction backwards flips every accusation.

VERIFIED LIVE: staff routinely skip counting non-cash tenders, leaving actual = 0 against a large calculated value. A huge apparent card 'shortage' almost always means 'not counted', not missing money. Filter actual <> 0 before ranking or summing variances, or you will report fiction as theft.
calculated ALREADY includes register adds and payouts. Do not add ls_register_withdraws.amount on top of it to build an expected total — that double-counts the opening float.

VERIFIED LIVE: no live sample was captured for this endpoint on the Ashburton production account; the field list follows the official reference only. Run a small scan and eyeball real values before building anything load-bearing on it.
Summing actual across all rows of ONE close-out gives total drawer contents at that close. Summing across close-outs over time is meaningless because the float carries over — see additivityAxis.
Rows are emitted per CONFIGURED tender, so a store with nine payment types can produce nine rows per close-out, most of them zero on both sides. COUNT(*) here counts tender lines, never close-outs.
The docs type calculated and actual as float. Stage them as numeric(12,2)-style numeric: accumulating binary floats over thousands of lines produces cent-level phantom variances.
There is no timeStamp on this object either. Incremental sync pages by registerCountAmountID ascending; retroactive edits to old counts will not be detected.

columns.name: register_count_amount_id
columns.description: Unique id for this one tender line of one close-out. Sortable, so backfill pages by it ascending.

columns.name: register_count_id
columns.description: The close-out this tender line belongs to. Joins ls_register_counts.register_count_id, which is where the date, register and employee live — this table has no time column of its own. Also documented as sortable, so it doubles as the pushdown key for fetching one count's lines. 0 means unset; normalise to NULL.

columns.name: payment_type_id
columns.description: The tender being counted (Cash, Credit Card, Gift Card, ...). Joins ls_payment_types.payment_type_id. The documented meaning is a truncated sentence ('The this count is for'); it is the payment type foreign key. 0 means unset; normalise to NULL.

columns.name: calculated
columns.description: The 'should have' side: what the system computed the drawer holds for this tender, built from payments taken on it during the session PLUS the signed register adds/payouts (including the opening float, which arrives as a positive RegisterWithdraw). Documented as float; store as numeric so cent-level variance sums do not drift. Never add ls_register_withdraws.amount on top of this — it is already included.

columns.name: actual
columns.description: The physical amount a human counted for this tender at close. Zero is AMBIGUOUS: it means either a genuinely empty drawer or — far more often on card and gift-card tenders — that nobody bothered to count it. There is no documented 'was counted' flag, so 0 must be treated as unknown for non-cash tenders. Documented as float; store as numeric.

tables.grain: one cash add or payout at one register (a single signed drawer movement outside of sales)
tables.description: Cash moving in and out of a till for reasons other than a sale: opening floats, change top-ups, safe drops and petty-cash payouts. The opening count of a register is stored here as a POSITIVE row, not on the register count. These movements feed the calculated side of ls_register_count_amounts. This is emphatically NOT a sales, payments or refunds table — cash revenue questions belong on the sale-payments table.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: the sign convention is confirmed against real production data — +250 recorded as an opening float, -20 recorded as a payout. POSITIVE is cash in, NEGATIVE is cash out.
VERIFIED LIVE: the OPENING COUNT of a register lands here as a positive row, not on RegisterCount. Every 'what float did we start with' question runs on this table, filtered to amount > 0.

Mind the sign in aggregates. 'Cash removed from tills' = SUM(-amount) WHERE amount < 0. 'Cash added to tills' = SUM(amount) WHERE amount > 0. Plain SUM(amount) is the NET and is almost never what was asked.

These are NOT sales or refunds. A payout is not negative revenue and a float is not a sale. Cash takings belong on the sale-payments table; this table only explains why the drawer holds what it holds.
These movements are ALREADY baked into ls_register_count_amounts.calculated. Adding both when building an expected drawer total double-counts the float.
paymentTypeID is virtually always Cash but is not guaranteed to be. Group by payment_type_id rather than assuming a single tender.
No timeStamp field exists on this object. Incremental sync pages by registerWithdrawID ascending and re-polls the tail; edited or deleted movements are not detectable.
VERIFIED LIVE: page size 100 is the production-safe pageLimit for this endpoint.
A payout recorded that did not physically happen manufactures a drawer discrepancy at the next count — treat large uncommented payouts as data-quality suspects, not confirmed cash loss.

columns.name: register_withdraw_id
columns.description: Unique id for this add/payout. The only documented sortable field, so backfill pages by it ascending.

columns.name: amount
columns.description: SIGNED drawer movement. POSITIVE = money INTO the drawer (opening float, change top-up); NEGATIVE = money OUT (payout, safe drop). Documented as float; store as numeric. Because it is signed, a naive SUM(amount) NETS floats against payouts and lands near zero — that number answers no real question.

columns.name: created_at
columns.description: When the add/payout was recorded, store-local wall time with no timezone offset. This is the only time column on the object; there is no separate modification timestamp.

columns.name: notes
columns.description: Reason staff typed for the movement. Documented as 'a note for this payout' but it applies equally to adds. Frequently an empty string for routine floats, so any 'reason for payouts' analysis has poor coverage — test with NULLIF(TRIM(notes),'').

columns.name: employee_id
columns.description: Employee who made the add/payout. Joins ls_employees.employee_id (workforce domain). 0 means unset; normalise to NULL. This is the accountability column for unexplained payouts.

columns.name: payment_type_id
columns.description: Tender that moved. Virtually always Cash in practice, but the field exists because Lightspeed permits adds and payouts of any configured tender — do not hardcode the cash assumption in aggregates. Joins ls_payment_types.payment_type_id. 0 means unset; normalise to NULL.

columns.name: register_id
columns.description: Till the movement happened at. Joins ls_registers.register_id. There is no link to a register count — attributing a movement to a session requires this id plus a created_at BETWEEN opened_at AND closed_at predicate. 0 means unset; normalise to NULL.

tables.grain: one payment type's live running total for one register's CURRENTLY OPEN session, as at the instant the endpoint was called
tables.description: The live 'what should be in this drawer right now' figure, broken down per payment type into the payments taken, the cash added and the cash withdrawn since the register was opened. It answers mid-shift questions (is the drawer right now?) that the close-out tables cannot, because they only exist after a count is submitted. It is NOT history: the numbers reset when the register closes, and successive polls supersede rather than accumulate.
tables.additivityAxis: poll instant per register + payment_type — the endpoint returns the CURRENT running total since the register was opened. Successive reads of the same register replace each other; never union or sum polls across time to build a history.
gotchas: NO published field table exists for this endpoint. Every column here is harvested from the documented example payload and the types are inferred. Probe a live account and confirm shape and signs before making any of it load-bearing.

This is the LIVE running total for the CURRENTLY OPEN session only. Once the register closes the figures reset and nothing is retained — historical 'should have' values live in ls_register_count_amounts.calculated, and that is the table for any question about the past.

The withdraw sign is the single biggest trap. If withdraw arrives as a positive magnitude the expected drawer is payment_total + add_total - withdraw_total; if it arrives signed negative it is payment_total + add_total + withdraw_total. Choosing wrong silently doubles the payout error and the number still looks plausible.
The endpoint is per-register: you must iterate registers yourself. There is no account-wide list form, no pagination, no sortable fields, no filtering and no load_relations.
The response carries NO timestamp. The mirror must stamp its own capture time and treat every refresh as a full replace for that register. Do not build a time series by appending polls.

CalculatedAmount is the array envelope key wrapping the per-payment-type rows (standard R-Series convention), not a value. If a given account instead returns it as a scalar it should equal payment + add + withdraw for the row — verify, never assume.

This table answers 'how much should be in the drawer right now'. That is a different question from 'was the drawer right at close', which is ls_register_count_amounts. Conflating them produces a variance against a moving target.
Because the payload has no register id, a bug that forgets to stamp register_id at ingest silently collapses every register into one set of totals and the result still looks like valid data.

columns.name: register_id
columns.description: The register these running totals belong to. NOT present in the response body — it comes from the request path and must be stamped onto every row at ingest, otherwise a multi-register store's rows are indistinguishable. Joins ls_registers.register_id.

columns.name: payment_type_id
columns.description: The tender this running total is for. Harvested from the documented example payload only — no field table is published for this endpoint — but by R-Series convention it is an integer payment type id and joins ls_payment_types.payment_type_id.

columns.name: payment_total
columns.description: Running total of PAYMENTS taken on this tender since the register was opened — the sales-driven component of the expected drawer. Type is undocumented (example payload only); treat as a money value and stage as numeric. Expected to be positive for takings.

columns.name: add_total
columns.description: Running total of the POSITIVE register-withdraw rows since open: the opening float plus any change top-ups. Corresponds to SUM(amount) WHERE amount > 0 on ls_register_withdraws for the same session. Type undocumented (example payload only); expect a positive number. Named add_total rather than 'add' because ADD is a SQL keyword.

columns.name: withdraw_total
columns.description: Running total of the NEGATIVE register-withdraw rows since open: payouts and safe drops. The SIGN IS UNDOCUMENTED — the example payload publishes no worked figure, so it is unknown whether this arrives already-negative (matching RegisterWithdraw.amount) or as a positive magnitude. Probe a live account before adding or subtracting it. Named withdraw_total to pair with add_total.

tables.grain: one sales-tax configuration (TaxCategory, labelled "Sales Tax" in the Lightspeed UI) on the account
tables.description: The account's sales-tax definitions: up to two named component rates plus the tax-inclusive pricing convention. Sales, shops and the TaxesByDay report all point at a row here, and the defaults here may be overridden per tax class in ls_tax_category_classes. This is RATE CONFIGURATION only - it is not tax collected (that is ls_report_taxes_by_day) and it carries no history, so the current row is the only row that ever existed.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: rates are fractions of 1, not percentages - tax1_rate = 0.1 means 10%. Rendering the raw value as a percent understates by 100x and is the single most common error against this table.

VERIFIED LIVE: an AU store (Ashburton) runs exactly two categories, 'Sales Tax' and 'Labor Tax', both 10% and both tax-inclusive, which makes GST maths uniform there. Do not generalise that to other accounts - is_tax_inclusive may differ per category on the same account.

No rate history exists. timeStamp only says when the row last changed, so historical tax cannot be reconstructed from this table. ls_report_taxes_by_day is the only source for tax actually collected on a past date.

The effective rate for a line is the ls_tax_category_classes override when one exists for that line's tax class, otherwise tax1_rate/tax2_rate here. Reading this table alone overstates tax for zero-rated classes such as gift cards.

At most two component rates are representable (tax1/tax2). Accounts in three-component jurisdictions have their taxes folded by Lightspeed before they reach the API, so component-level reconciliation is impossible.
tax2_name/tax2_rate are empty-string/0 rather than NULL on single-tax accounts; test with `tax2_rate > 0`, not `tax2_rate IS NOT NULL`.

columns.name: tax_category_id
columns.description: Unique id of the sales-tax configuration; the join target for Sale.taxCategoryID, Shop.taxCategoryID and ls_report_taxes_by_day.tax_category_id. Routinely confused with tax_class_id: a CATEGORY is the rate/authority (who you remit to), a CLASS is the item grouping (what is being taxed). The two id spaces overlap numerically, so a mistaken join silently returns plausible rows.

columns.name: is_tax_inclusive
columns.description: true when prices under this category are entered and displayed WITH tax already inside them (AU/NZ/UK convention), false when tax is added on top at the register (US convention). Wrong reading shifts every revenue figure by the whole rate: with true, ex-tax = price / (1 + rate); with false, ex-tax = price. It is a property of the CATEGORY, not of the shop or the item, so one account can legitimately mix both conventions across categories.
columns.enums: true = prices include tax; false = tax calculated and added at the register

columns.name: tax1_name
columns.description: Label of the first component rate as printed on receipts and reports (e.g. 'GST', 'Sales Tax', 'State'). Cosmetic only - the remitting authority is implied by the category, never parsed from this string. Do not key logic on it; stores rename it freely.

columns.name: tax2_name
columns.description: Label of the second component rate (e.g. 'PST', 'County'). Empty string rather than NULL on single-tax accounts. A non-empty tax2_name paired with tax2_rate = 0 means the label was configured and then zeroed, not that a second tax applies.

columns.name: tax1_rate
columns.description: First component rate as a FRACTION OF 1, not a percentage: 0.1 means 10%. Multiply by 100 before displaying. This is the category DEFAULT - it is not necessarily the rate applied to any given sale line, because ls_tax_category_classes may override it for that line's tax class. In most single-tax jurisdictions this is the only rate used.

columns.name: tax2_rate
columns.description: Second component rate, also a fraction of 1; 0 on single-tax accounts. The headline rate equals tax1_rate + tax2_rate only where the jurisdiction stacks the two additively. Jurisdictions that compound tax2 on top of tax1 cannot be expressed by this model, and jurisdictions with three or more components cannot be expressed at all.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When the category record was last modified, in store-local time. A change marker, NOT an effective-from date: there is no rate history table, so a rate edit silently rewrites the apparent past. Never restate historical tax by multiplying old sales by today's tax1_rate - use ls_report_taxes_by_day, which records what was actually collected.

tables.grain: one per-tax-class rate override inside one tax category
tables.description: Rate overrides: the rate a specific tax class attracts under a specific tax category, replacing that category's default tax1_rate/tax2_rate. This is how zero-rated or specially-rated item groups (labour, gift cards, exempt goods) are expressed. A MISSING row means 'use the category default', never 'zero tax' - the distinction is the whole point of the table.
gotchas: DOC GAP: the ground truth documents TaxCategory.TaxCategoryClasses only as an object that 'provides a custom rate for the TaxClass in this TaxCategory' and does NOT enumerate its sub-fields. VERIFIED LIVE: the bike repo, probing a real store, observed rows carrying taxCategoryClassID, taxClassID, tax1Rate and tax2Rate - the four columns modelled here. Confirm the exact keys on the first live call before trusting rate maths.

VERIFIED LIVE: a single override arrives as a bare OBJECT, several arrive as an ARRAY. Normalise to an array before exploding or every one-override category silently yields zero rows and falls back to the wrong default rate.

VERIFIED LIVE: TaxCategoryClass has no standalone account-level GET. Rows exist only inside TaxCategory when load_relations includes TaxCategoryClasses; fetch TaxCategory without that parameter and this table is silently empty, which reads as 'no overrides configured'.
Absence of a row means 'inherit the category default', NOT 'zero tax'. Do not LEFT JOIN and COALESCE the override to 0 - that zero-rates every class that has no override.
Overrides REPLACE the category default rather than adjust it. Adding tax1_rate_override to ls_tax_categories.tax1_rate doubles the rate.
load_relations=TaxCategoryClasses.TaxClass additionally nests the full TaxClass record inside each override, letting you name the class without a second round trip to ls_tax_classes.

columns.name: tax_category_id
columns.description: The owning tax category. The nested payload does not repeat the parent id, so the loader must stamp it onto each exploded child row; without it the override cannot be attributed and every rate lookup collapses to the wrong category.

columns.name: tax_category_class_id
columns.description: Surrogate id of the override row itself. Its only real use is addressing the override for deletion (TaxCategory/{taxCategoryID}/TaxCategoryClass/{taxCategoryClassID}); it has no analytical meaning and should never be grouped on. Nullable if a given account's payload omits it.

columns.name: tax_class_id
columns.description: The tax class this override applies to. Joins ls_tax_classes.tax_class_id. Together with tax_category_id it forms the real grain: one override per (category, class) pair.

columns.name: tax1_rate_override
columns.description: First-component rate for this class under this category, as a FRACTION OF 1 (0.1 = 10%). It REPLACES ls_tax_categories.tax1_rate for lines in this class - it is not an increment and must never be added to the default. 0 here means genuinely zero-rated, which is materially different from the row being absent.

columns.name: tax2_rate_override
columns.description: Second-component override, also a fraction of 1. 0 on single-tax accounts and on classes exempt from the second component. Same replace-not-add semantics as tax1_rate_override.

tables.grain: one tax class label that items and sale lines can carry
tables.description: Labels that group items for tax treatment (Item, Labor, Gift Card, ...). Items and sale lines carry a tax class, and the accounting reports subtotal by it, which makes this the dimension behind service-vs-goods revenue splits. A tax class is NOT a rate: rates live in ls_tax_categories and ls_tax_category_classes.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: expect junk rows. A real store carried a tail of auto-created classes with empty names alongside the three real ones. Filter `name <> ''` before listing classes to a human, but do NOT filter them out of report joins - unnamed classes can still carry money.
VERIFIED LIVE: only 'Item', 'Labor' and 'Gift Card' were named at the probed AU store. 'Labor' is the hook for every service-vs-goods question in this domain.

VERIFIED LIVE: an undocumented `classType` field is returned live with values 'item' and 'service'. It is the cleanest labour/goods discriminator, but it is not in the published field list, so it is not modelled here; falling back to name = 'Labor' is the documented-only route.

TaxClass.SaleLines and TaxClass.Items are documented as type string with URL bodies (/API/V3/Account/{accountID}/SaleLine and .../Item). They are relation pointers, not values - see fieldCoverage.unmapped.
A tax class carries NO rate of its own. Answering 'what rate does Labor attract' requires ls_tax_category_classes joined to ls_tax_categories, and the answer differs per category.

Renaming a class is retroactive across all reports, so tax_class_name in historical report rows reflects today's label, not the label in force at the time. Join on tax_class_id when stability matters.

columns.name: tax_class_id
columns.description: Unique id of the tax class. Joined from Item.taxClassID, SaleLine.taxClassID, ls_report_tax_class_sales_by_day.tax_class_id and ls_report_orders_by_tax_class.tax_class_id. Do not confuse with tax_category_id - the id spaces overlap numerically and a crossed join returns rows rather than an error.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Human label of the class, e.g. 'Item', 'Labor', 'Gift Card'. Frequently EMPTY: Lightspeed auto-creates unnamed classes, so a raw class list shown to a human is full of blanks. 'Labor' (or its local equivalent) is the class that makes service-vs-retail margin analysis possible in ls_report_tax_class_sales_by_day.

columns.name: updated_at
columns.description: When the class record was last modified, in store-local time. A change marker only; renaming a class rewrites its label everywhere retroactively, including in report rows fetched afterwards, so historical reports keyed on tax_class_name can shift meaning.

tables.grain: one tender method configured on the account
tables.description: The tender methods available at the register (Cash, Credit Card, Gift Card, Credit Account, ...), including their refund routing and whether a customer must be attached. This is the lookup behind SalePayment, RegisterWithdraw, RegisterCount and ls_report_payments_by_day. It is configuration only - no money lives here.
gotchas: VERIFIED LIVE: `type` is the tender FAMILY, not the card network - a tender named 'Debit Card' carries type 'credit card'. Card-brand splits need the `name` string or CCCharge data, not this column.
VERIFIED LIVE: live data returns `ecom` and `adjustment` in addition to the five documented type values. Any exhaustive CASE over five values will silently bucket real takings into ELSE.
refund_as_payment_type_id = 0 is a sentinel for 'any payment type may be used', not a foreign key. Wrap it in NULLIF(...,0) before every join or comparison.

VERIFIED LIVE: `archived = true` does not remove history - archived tenders still appear in past payments. Filtering archived rows out of a takings join understates historical revenue with no error raised.

VERIFIED LIVE: two undocumented fields exist on the live resource - a short `code` (SCA = store credit account, SGC = store gift card) and a `channel` tag ('instore' or empty). Neither is in the published field list, so neither is modelled here.

VERIFIED LIVE: one AU store's configured tenders were Cash, Check, Credit Card, Credit Account, Gift Card, Debit Card, eCom, Adjustment and PROMO GIFT CARD - note two distinct gift-card tenders, which a naive name LIKE '%Gift%' would merge.
This table holds no money. Tender-mix questions run against ls_report_payments_by_day or raw SalePayment; this table only names and classifies the ids.
PaymentType has no timeStamp field, unlike TaxCategory and TaxClass, so incremental sync must re-fetch the full (small) list rather than filtering on modification time.

columns.name: payment_type_id
columns.description: Unique id of the tender method; the join target for SalePayment.paymentTypeID, RegisterWithdraw, RegisterCount and ls_report_payments_by_day.payment_type_id. Also the referent of refund_as_payment_type_id on other rows in this same table.

columns.name: name
columns.description: Display name of the tender as staff see it at the register ('Cash', 'Credit Card', 'Debit Card', 'Gift Card', 'Check'). This is the only place a store's own naming survives - `type` collapses several distinct tenders into one family, so card-brand or acquirer splits must be driven from this string.

columns.name: require_customer
columns.description: true when a customer record must be attached to the sale before this tender may be used. Practically this flags account-bearing tenders (store credit, on-account, loyalty), so it is a decent proxy for 'this payment creates or settles a customer balance' when no ledger data is available.

columns.name: archived
columns.description: true when the tender has been retired from the register. Archiving does NOT remove history: past payments keep referencing the archived id. Filtering `archived = false` inside a join to payments therefore silently deletes historical takings and makes old months look smaller. Filter it only when listing tenders currently available for use.

columns.name: internal_reserved
columns.description: true for predefined system tenders that a store cannot edit or delete (the set published in the API's Defined Values section). Useful for separating Lightspeed-managed plumbing - gift card, credit account, eCom, adjustment - from tenders the store created itself. Not a proxy for 'real money': system tenders carry genuine takings.

columns.name: type
columns.description: The tender FAMILY, used for grouping takings into cash/card/gift/account buckets. It is NOT the card network and NOT the acquirer: a row named 'Debit Card' carries type 'credit card'. Grouping tender mix by this column merges debit with credit and hides the store's own tender naming, which produces a plausible but wrong tender-mix chart.
columns.enums: Documented five: cash, gift card, credit account, credit card, user defined. VERIFIED LIVE: 'ecom' (online payments pushed into the POS) and 'adjustment' (system balancing entries) also occur, beyond the documented five.

columns.name: refund_as_payment_type_id
columns.description: The tender that refunds of this tender must be issued as (e.g. Gift Card refunds as Gift Card, Credit Account as Credit Account). ZERO IS A SENTINEL meaning 'any tender may be used for the refund' - it is NOT a foreign key to payment type 0. Joining it raw drops or mis-attributes every unrestricted tender; convert with NULLIF(refund_as_payment_type_id, 0) before joining.

tables.grain: one payment type per shop per day, split by the layaway flag
tables.description: Lightspeed-computed daily takings totals by payment type, shop and layaway flag, built for accounting-package export. The canonical source for tender mix over long ranges: one request replaces thousands of raw sale records. It measures MONEY RECEIVED, not revenue recognised, so it will not tie to sale totals.
gotchas: startDate and endDate are REQUIRED query parameters (ISO dates) on this endpoint. They must be injected from the question's date range at request time, not hard-coded as base params, and a request without them does not return the full history.

VERIFIED LIVE: this is TAKINGS (money received), not revenue. Deposits, layaway payments, gift-card loads and on-account settlements appear here on the day cash moved, which will not reconcile to a sum of sale totals for the same period. Reconciling the two is a category error, not a data bug.
is_layaway splits the grain, so a single tender can produce two rows for the same day and shop. `WHERE payment_type_id = X` returns up to two rows per day; aggregate or filter the flag explicitly.
VERIFIED LIVE: the response envelope key is taken from the doc's field-section name (PaymentsByDay) because the docs publish no sample body. Verify the real key on the first live call.
No register, employee, customer or sale dimension exists here. Per-register cash-up, per-staff takings and per-customer payment questions all require raw SalePayment/RegisterCount instead.
The docs do not state whether refunds appear as negative amounts or as separate rows. Check one known refund day against raw SalePayment before assuming amount is a gross positive.

columns.name: day
columns.description: The aggregation day these payments were taken on. The docs type it datetime, but the value is a day bucket, not an instant - there is no time-of-day detail here at all, so intraday or shift-level takings questions cannot be answered from this table.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: The shop where the money was taken. Joins ls_shops.shop_id (location). Multi-shop accounts get one row per shop per tender per day, so omitting shop_id from a GROUP BY silently blends stores.

columns.name: is_layaway
columns.description: true when the row totals payments taken against a LAYAWAY (a deposit toward goods not yet handed over), false for ordinary sale payments. It splits the grain: the same tender on the same day at the same shop can appear twice. Treating layaway deposits as revenue overstates the period, and filtering them out understates cash banked - decide which question is being asked.
columns.enums: true = layaway/deposit payments; false = ordinary sale payments

columns.name: amount
columns.description: Total money taken under this payment type on this day at this shop (the docs call it the subtotal for the payment type). This is takings, not revenue: gift-card loads, layaway deposits and on-account settlements all land here on the day cash moved. The docs do not state the sign convention for refunded tenders, so do not assume every value is positive.

columns.name: payment_type_name
columns.description: Denormalised tender name as of report generation. Convenient for grouping without a join, but it reflects the CURRENT name - a renamed tender changes historical labels. Group on payment_type_id when the series must stay stable.

columns.name: payment_type_id
columns.description: The tender this total is for. Joins ls_payment_types.payment_type_id to reach the family (`type`), archived flag and refund routing.

tables.grain: one tax category per shop per day
tables.description: Lightspeed-computed daily tax totals by tax category and shop, built for accounting-package export and marked read-only in the docs. The canonical source for GST/sales-tax remittance figures over long ranges, and the ONLY source for tax actually collected on a past date - tax rates carry no history, so it cannot be recomputed.
gotchas: startDate and endDate are REQUIRED query parameters (ISO dates), injected per question from the asked date range. Not base params - the values are dynamic.
Read-only report: no write operations exist against this endpoint.

The grain is tax CATEGORY, not tax class. This answers 'how much tax do I remit', never 'which products were taxed'. Class-level splits come from ls_report_tax_class_sales_by_day, which has no tax figure at all - the two axes never meet in one table.
tax_amount is a combined figure across the category's tax1 and tax2 components. Two-tax jurisdictions (GST + PST) cannot decompose remittance from this endpoint.
