Tax collected here will NOT equal ls_report_tax_class_sales_by_day.subtotal multiplied by ls_tax_categories.tax1_rate: per-class overrides, exempt classes and line-level rounding all differ. Recomputing and reporting a discrepancy is a false positive.
VERIFIED LIVE: the response envelope key is taken from the doc's field-section name (TaxesByDay); the docs publish no sample body. Verify on the first live call.
Because tax rates hold no history, this table is the only correct answer to 'how much tax did we collect in <past period>'. Never back-compute historical tax from current rates.

columns.name: day
columns.description: The aggregation day the taxes were collected on. Typed datetime in the docs but the value is a day bucket. Collection day, not liability date: a sale on the last day of a period lands in that period regardless of when the goods ship.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: The shop where the tax was collected. Joins ls_shops.shop_id (location). On multi-shop accounts that remit separately, this is the column that splits the liability.

columns.name: tax_category_id
columns.description: The tax category (rate/authority) the total belongs to. Joins ls_tax_categories.tax_category_id. This is the CATEGORY axis, not the class axis - it answers 'who do I remit to', not 'what got taxed'.

columns.name: tax_category_name
columns.description: Denormalised category name as of report generation. Reflects the current label, so renaming a category retroactively relabels history; group on tax_category_id for stable series.

columns.name: tax_amount
columns.description: Total tax collected for this category on this day at this shop. It is a COMBINED figure: even though a category can define two component rates (tax1/tax2), this report does not split them, so GST-plus-PST jurisdictions cannot separate the components here. This figure will not equal subtotal x tax1_rate because per-class overrides, exempt lines and per-line rounding all intervene - trust this number over any recomputation.

tables.grain: one shop per day
tables.description: Lightspeed-computed daily discount totals by shop, built for accounting-package export. The cheap way to answer 'how much did we give away' over long ranges without scanning raw sales. Deliberately coarse: there is NO per-discount, per-item or per-staff breakdown here.
gotchas: startDate and endDate are REQUIRED query parameters; the docs specify ISO 8601 values. Injected per question, not base params.

VERIFIED LIVE: there is NO discount-name breakdown here, only shop and day. 'Which discount cost us the most' and 'who authorises the most discounting' cannot be answered from this table - they need Sale/SaleLine discount fields plus the Discount lookup.
The sign convention is undocumented. Do not assume discount_amount is a positive give-away; verify against one raw sale before adding or subtracting it.

Whether a manual line-price override counts as a discount is unstated. If register staff type a lower price rather than applying a named discount, the give-away may never appear here, making discounting look smaller than it is.
This is the ONLY table in the domain with no tax dimension at all, so discounts cannot be attributed to a tax class or category. Discount-adjusted margin by class is not derivable.
VERIFIED LIVE: the response envelope key is taken from the doc's field-section name (DiscountsByDay); no sample body is published. Verify on the first live call.
Zero-discount days may be omitted from the response rather than returned as 0. Averages computed over returned rows will overstate the daily mean.

columns.name: day
columns.description: The aggregation day the discounts were given on. Typed datetime in the docs but the value is a day bucket. Days with no discounts may be absent rather than zero, so a time series must be joined against a generated calendar to avoid gaps reading as continuity.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: The shop where the discounts were given. Joins ls_shops.shop_id (location). This is the only dimension besides day, so it is the finest cut available.

columns.name: discount_amount
columns.description: Total value of sale discounts given on this day at this shop (the docs call it the subtotal of sale discounts). The docs do not state the SIGN convention, so whether it must be added to or subtracted from a subtotal is unverified - check one known day against a raw sale before wiring it into a net-revenue formula. Also unstated: whether manual price overrides at the register count as discounts here, or only named discount rules.

tables.grain: one tax class per shop per day
tables.description: Lightspeed-computed daily sales subtotals broken down by tax class and shop, carrying BOTH a FIFO and an average cost basis for the same goods. Built for accounting-package export. The cheapest route to margin by tax class (service versus retail) over long ranges, and the only place two alternative COGS bases sit side by side.
gotchas: startDate and endDate are REQUIRED query parameters (ISO dates), injected per question rather than fixed as base params.

VERIFIED LIVE: the envelope is AMBIGUOUS in the docs - the endpoint resource is TaxClassSalesByDay but the docs title its field section 'SalesByTaxClassAndDay'. The bike repo shipped the resource name and flagged it for verification on the first live call.

subtotal is EX TAX. On tax-inclusive accounts (is_tax_inclusive = true) it will sit below the sale totals users recognise from the POS by exactly the tax rate. That gap is correct, not missing revenue.

fifo_cost and avg_cost are two ALTERNATIVE cost bases for the SAME goods. Sum either, never both, and never switch basis between periods being compared - margin will move for reasons that have nothing to do with trading.
VERIFIED LIVE: subtotal - fifo_cost matches Lightspeed's own profit reporting. Use FIFO as the default basis when a question just says 'margin'.

Service classes ('Labor') show near-zero fifo_cost because labour carries no stock cost, so margin by tax class reads close to 100% for services. That is real, not a data error, and it means blended margin is dominated by the service/goods mix rather than by pricing.

This report carries NO tax amount despite the name. Tax collected is in ls_report_taxes_by_day, which is keyed by category rather than class - the class and category axes never appear in the same table.
No item, category, customer or employee dimension. This is the cheapest margin-by-class source but it cannot go finer; product-level margin needs raw SaleLine data.

columns.name: day
columns.description: The aggregation day of these sale totals. Typed datetime in the docs but the value is a day bucket - no time-of-day, so no trading-hour or shift analysis is possible from this table.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: The shop these sales were rung at. Joins ls_shops.shop_id (location). Omitting it from a GROUP BY blends stores with different pricing and cost bases.

columns.name: tax_class_id
columns.description: The tax class the totals belong to. Joins ls_tax_classes.tax_class_id. This is the CLASS axis (what was sold), not the category axis (who is remitted) - this report carries no tax figure at all, so it cannot answer remittance questions.

columns.name: tax_class_name
columns.description: Denormalised class name as of report generation ('Item', 'Labor', 'Gift Card'). Reflects the current label, so a renamed class retroactively relabels history; group on tax_class_id for stable series. May be empty for the auto-created unnamed classes that still carry money.

columns.name: subtotal
columns.description: Sales subtotal for this class on this day at this shop, EX TAX. Comparing it directly to tax-inclusive sale totals from a tax-inclusive category understates by the whole rate, which reads as a plausible shortfall rather than an error. This is the revenue side of every margin calculation in this table.

columns.name: fifo_cost
columns.description: Cost of goods sold in this group valued First In First Out - an EXTENDED total for the group, not a unit cost. subtotal - fifo_cost is what Lightspeed's own profit reporting shows. It is one of TWO alternative bases in this row; adding it to avg_cost double-counts COGS and halves reported margin.

columns.name: avg_cost
columns.description: Cost of the same goods valued at weighted-average cost - the ALTERNATIVE basis to fifo_cost for the identical sales, not an additional cost. Its name reads like a per-unit average, which is the trap: treating it as a unit figure and multiplying by quantity, or summing it alongside fifo_cost, both produce plausible wrong margins. Pick one basis and hold it across every period being compared.

tables.grain: one tax-class cost subtotal within one received purchase order
tables.description: Lightspeed-computed accounting report of purchase orders RECEIVED from vendors, broken down per order and subtotaled by tax class, with vendor identification. The cheap way to summarise restocking spend by day, vendor and class over long ranges. Its two shipping/other cost columns are whole-order values repeated on every row, which is what makes the table non-additive as a whole.
gotchas: startDate and endDate are REQUIRED query parameters; the docs specify ISO 8601 values. Injected per question, not base params.

VERIFIED LIVE: total_ship_cost and total_other_cost are WHOLE-ORDER values repeated on every tax-class row of the order. Summing them across a multi-class order double- or triple-counts freight. Use MAX() per order_id or aggregate to order level in a subquery first - this is the single most expensive mistake against this table and the docs call it out explicitly.

VERIFIED LIVE: the envelope is AMBIGUOUS in the docs - the endpoint resource is OrdersByTaxClass but the docs title its field section just 'Orders'. The bike repo shipped the resource name and flagged it for verification on the first live call.
VERIFIED LIVE: rows exist per RECEIVED order day. Orders placed but not yet arrived never appear, so this table cannot answer 'what is on order' or 'what have we committed to spend'.
order_id repeats across tax-class rows. COUNT(*) counts subtotals, not orders; use COUNT(DISTINCT order_id).

cost is supplier cost, not retail. Comparing it to ls_report_tax_class_sales_by_day.subtotal as if it were revenue for the same goods is doubly wrong: different valuation AND different timing (received versus sold).

The report does not apportion freight or other charges across tax classes, so true landed cost per class is not provided. If you need it, allocate total_ship_cost + total_other_cost pro rata on cost yourself - and be explicit that the allocation is yours, not Lightspeed's.
The report gives no quantity, item or unit-cost detail, so unit-cost inflation cannot be measured here; that needs OrderLine data from the purchasing domain.

columns.name: received_date
columns.description: The day the order was RECEIVED, not the day it was placed. Typed datetime in the docs but the value is a day bucket. Because the report is keyed on receipt, orders that are open, in transit or cancelled never appear at all - this table cannot measure purchase commitments, only arrivals.

columns.name: shop_id
columns.description: The shop the order belongs to. Joins ls_shops.shop_id (location). On multi-shop accounts this is how restocking spend is attributed to a store.

columns.name: vendor_id
columns.description: The vendor (supplier) this line is for. Joins ls_vendors.vendor_id. Note the docs phrase it per LINE, but the grain is order x tax class, so every row of one order carries the same vendor.

columns.name: vendor_name
columns.description: Denormalised vendor name as of report generation. Convenient for grouping without a join, but it reflects the current name - a renamed or merged vendor retroactively relabels history. Group on vendor_id when the series must stay stable.

columns.name: tax_class_id
columns.description: The tax class the cost subtotal belongs to. Joins ls_tax_classes.tax_class_id. This is the axis that repeats within an order and therefore the axis that makes order-level columns dangerous to sum.

columns.name: tax_class_name
columns.description: Denormalised tax class name for this subtotal. Same retroactive-rename caveat as elsewhere; may be empty for auto-created unnamed classes that still carry cost.

columns.name: cost
columns.description: Subtotal COST (what you paid the vendor) for items of this tax class on this order - not retail value, not landed cost. This is the one genuinely additive measure on the table: it may be summed across rows, orders, vendors and days. It excludes freight and other charges, which live in the two order-level columns.

columns.name: order_id
columns.description: The purchase order this row is part of. Joins ls_orders.order_id. It REPEATS across the order's tax-class rows, so COUNT(*) counts subtotals rather than orders - use COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) for an order count.

columns.name: total_ship_cost
columns.description: The ENTIRE order's shipping cost, repeated verbatim on every tax-class row of that order - the docs say explicitly not to sum it. SUM(total_ship_cost) over a multi-class order multiplies freight by the number of classes, producing an inflated but entirely plausible spend figure. Take MAX() per order_id, or aggregate to order level first.

columns.name: total_other_cost
columns.description: The ENTIRE order's other/ancillary charges, repeated on every tax-class row exactly like total_ship_cost, with the same explicit do-not-sum warning in the docs. Same mitigation: MAX() per order_id or a per-order subquery before rolling up.
